Phenomenological Grounding: distinct things occur in awareness.
nodes.soWhat: Without this, there is no grounded starting point — no phenomena, no distinctions, no qualities, no connections, and no awareness. Nothing to reason about, nothing to reason with.
nodes.search: phenomenological grounding primitives phenomenon distinct quality association awareness experience starting point vocabulary

sections.title: Observations
items: Something is happening.
What occurs is not all the same — there are differences within it.
Each difference is something specific: red, hot, hungry, loud.
Some of these specific things feel connected — red is like blue, sweet goes with strawberry.
All of this occurs — and that occurring is itself something, not nothing.

items.text: Distinct things occur in awareness.
items: Things happen (1.1.1), they are not all the same (1.1.2), each one is something specific — a quality (1.1.3), they occur with felt connections to each other — associations (1.1.4), and their occurring IS awareness (1.1.5).

This is the foundation — the most basic description of experience, from which everything that follows is built. Every observation, identification, and conclusion later in the tree traces back to these starting points.

items.title: No grounded starting point exists
items.detail: Every concept in the tree — information, identity, truth, reality, reasoning — is built from the observations established here: that phenomena occur, that they are distinct, that they have specific character (qualities), that they connect (associations), and that their occurring IS awareness. Without these, there is nothing to point at when grounding a claim and nothing to build later observations from.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The primitive vocabulary from which all later terms are built.
items: "Phenomenon" — anything that occurs (1.1.1).
"Distinct" — not the same as something else (1.1.2).
"Quality" — a singular distinct phenomenon (1.1.3).
"Association" — a quality that occurs with multiple phenomena (1.1.4).
"Awareness" — the quality of occurrence (1.1.5).
Plus the connector vocabulary grounded along the way: what, one, a, the, that, each, from, than, which, of, have, as, like, with, together, and, or, similar, any, group, given, presence, absence.
The next step: identifying what these phenomena carry — information — and the structures it forms (1.2 — Epistemological Grounding).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Nothing whatsoever is happening — since holding that position is itself something happening.
Experience is a single undifferentiated occurrence with no internal distinctions.
Distinct phenomena have no specific character — distinctions exist but carry no content.
Qualities occur in total isolation with no felt connections between them.
Awareness is a separate entity behind experience — a "watcher" that observes from the outside.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: What structures or patterns qualities form — requires the epistemological vocabulary (1.2).
Who or what is aware — the question of a self or subject is addressed later (1.3.7).
Whether or not the qualities experienced correspond to anything beyond experience — requires ontological vocabulary (1.3).
Why anything occurs at all — mechanism questions are deferred to Node 2.

items.title: This is so basic it says nothing — everyone already knows things happen in their experience.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The entire section is a laborious way of saying 'I experience stuff.'
Every conscious person already knows this. Building five nodes to arrive at something this obvious seems like wasted effort.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: A section that tells you what you already know does not do useful work.
Grounding or foundations are only valuable if they provide new information or insight.
If a claim is obvious to everyone, spelling it out is redundant rather than methodologically important.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: The section's purpose is not to inform — it is to ground. Every technical term used later (information, identity, truth, reality, reasoning) needs to trace back to something undeniable.

The progression is also not as trivial as it looks: it separates occurrence from distinction from specificity from connection from presence — five observations that are often conflated but are genuinely different.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The section is basic by design — it establishes the floor.

Its value is not in surprising you but in giving every downstream claim an explicit, unchallengeable starting point. The alternative is starting from undefined terms and hoping no one asks what they mean.

items.title: All of this could be an illusion — how do you know any of it is real?

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: How do you know any of this is real? You could be a brain in a vat, dreaming, or running in a simulation.
If you can't rule that out, then 'phenomena occur' is just what the illusion looks like from the inside — and that is not a foundation.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: If experience could be fabricated (dreamed, simulated), then claims grounded in experience inherit that unreliability.
"Grounded in experience" means "claiming experience is veridical" — that what occurs accurately represents what exists.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: This section does not claim that what occurs is real, accurate, or external. It claims only that occurrence is happening, that it contains distinctions, and that those distinctions have specific character. A dream contains all of these. A hallucination contains all of these. A simulation contains all of these.
The second commitment above is where the objection breaks — this never claims experience is veridical. It claims only that it occurs.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Either the illusion itself occurs — in which case occurrence, distinction, and quality are all present and this holds — or nothing occurs at all, not even the appearance of experience. To reject this, the objector must commit not to the claim that experience is misleading, but to the claim that there is no experience whatsoever.
The question "is it real?" requires these primitives to even be asked.

items.title: These five steps could be collapsed into fewer — the distinctions between them are artificial.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Why separate "phenomena occur" from "distinct phenomena occur" from "qualities occur"? These seem like slightly different ways of saying the same thing. The granularity seems forced rather than natural.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Conceptual distinctions that aren't experientially separable (you don't experience them as separate moments) are artificial rather than genuine.
Parsimony of vocabulary is preferable to explicitness — fewer terms is better unless each one captures a genuinely different experience.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Try collapsing any two of the five. Can you eliminate distinction without losing specificity? Can you eliminate connection without losing presence?
Each step depends on the one before it — occurrence must precede distinction, which must precede specificity. The ordering is not arbitrary.
The concern should be tested: if two steps are truly identical, show the collapse. The tree's structure will reveal whether or not anything was lost.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The five steps are the order in which each aspect is *identified and named*, not the order in which they are *experienced*. The cost of collapsing is hidden dependencies; the cost of separating is mild redundancy. The tree chooses explicitness over brevity.

nodes.claim: Epistemological Grounding: information can be identified, compared, and defined.
nodes.soWhat: Establishes that phenomena carry information, that this information forms recognizable structures that can be identified, compared, and defined — grounding the capacity for inquiry that the rest of the sieve depends on.
nodes.search: epistemology information identification comparison knowledge features patterns classes types questions ignorance learning

sections.title: Observations
items: Phenomena carry specific, distinguishable content — the redness of one thing, the sweetness of another, the similarity between them.
This content forms structures: features belong to phenomena, patterns repeat across features, classes group patterns together.
Structures can be compared — sameness and variation between information are noticed, not inferred.
Phenomena fall into distinct types: wanting, sensation, temporal experience, physical occurrence, emotion, thought, and relation — each sharing a fundamental feature.
Information can be sought and found: a pull toward what something is, and then the identification arrives — or it does not.
Information has context — where the same information has different significance in different contexts.

items.text: Information can be identified, compared, and defined.
items: "Identified": phenomena carry information (1.2.1.1) — qualities and associations — that forms features (1.2.1.3), patterns (1.2.1.6), and classes (1.2.1.9). A phenomenon's identity (1.2.1.4) is its distinct set of features. Identification (1.2.1.5) is the awareness of that identity. Phenomena fall into distinct types based on fundamental features (1.2.5). A question (1.2.6.1) directs wanting at specific information; when the information occurs, that is an answer (1.2.6.2), and the result is knowledge (1.2.6.3). When it does not, the result is ignorance (1.2.6.4). Learning (1.2.6.5) and forgetting (1.2.6.6) are the transitions between them.
"Compared": information can be observed for sameness (1.2.3) or variation (1.2.4) — the basis of matching and mismatching. Comparison (1.2.2) is the act of observing these relationships.

"Defined": classes have scope (1.2.7.1) and boundaries (1.2.7.2), information has meaning within a scope (1.2.7.3), a definition is the identifiable features of a scope's boundary (1.2.7.7), and "all" of a scope includes both known and unknown instances (1.2.7.4–6) — general claims extend beyond what has been encountered.

items.title: No capacity for inquiry — and no path from experience to definition
items.detail: Without epistemological grounding, phenomena occur (1.1) but carry no identifiable information, form no recognizable structures, and support no comparison or definition. Experience becomes an undifferentiated flow with nothing to single out, match, distinguish, seek, or define.

children.title: No identification
children.detail: Without information, features, patterns, and classes, no phenomenon can be singled out or recognized. Information that occurs cannot be sought, found, held, or lost — there is no structure for inquiry and no path to knowledge.

children.title: No comparison
children.detail: Without sameness and variation, nothing can be matched or mismatched. There is no basis for saying two things are alike or different — and therefore no basis for testing, evaluating, or distinguishing claims.

children.title: No definition
children.detail: Without scope, boundary, meaning, and definition, classes cannot be delimited and general claims cannot extend beyond what has been encountered. "All" collapses to "all I've seen" — and the sieve's goal of distinguishing what is true from what is false has no foundation.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The complete epistemological vocabulary — everything needed to describe how information is structured, compared, and known.
items: Information and structure: "information," "feature," "identity," "identification," "pattern," "sameness," "variation," "class" (1.2.1).
Comparison: "comparison," "match," "mismatch" (1.2.2–1.2.4).

Types of phenomena: "type," "willful," "intensional," "temporal," "physical," "emotional," "mental," "relational" — and the full vocabulary within each type, including wanting, direction, success, failure, sensation, perception, memory, change, event, imagination, thought, possibility, correlation, expectation, consistency, cause, effect, and more (1.2.5).
Inquiry: "question," "answer," "knowledge," "ignorance," "learning," "forgetting" (1.2.6).
Scope and definition: "scope," "boundary," "meaning," "context," "definition," "all," "every," "some," "none," "rest," "complete," "open," "closed" (1.2.7).
The next step: grounding what "reality" is — what exists independently of want — so that knowledge can be evaluated against something beyond experience itself (1.3 — Ontological Grounding).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Phenomena occur but carry no distinguishable information — experience is an undifferentiated mass with nothing to single out.
Information exists but cannot be compared — there is no basis for sameness, variation, or matching.
Information can be encountered but never known — inquiry has no structure and no possible outcome.
General claims cannot extend beyond what has been encountered — "all" collapses to "all I've seen."

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not knowledge corresponds to what actually exists — the distinction between knowledge and truth requires the ontological grounding (1.3).
Whether or not the patterns and classes identified here reflect mind-independent structures — requires the ontological vocabulary of independence and reality (1.3).
What methods reliably distinguish knowledge from error — requires the vocabulary of logic (1.4) and reasoning (1.5).
Whether or not a method that justifies falsehood can be trusted — addressed at (1.6).

items.title: This is just categorizing experience — real epistemology needs justification, truth conditions, and logic.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Epistemology since Plato has centered on justified true belief — not just having information, but having information that is true and well-supported. This branch defines identification, comparison, and definition without ever addressing truth, justification, or logical validity.
An epistemological grounding that ignores these is not epistemology at all — it is taxonomy of experience dressed up as knowledge theory.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Genuine epistemology requires truth conditions, justification, and logical structure at the foundational level.
Without these, the framework cannot distinguish knowledge from organized delusion — systematic categorization of experience that happens to be wrong.
Deferring truth and justification to later nodes means this branch is incomplete and cannot legitimately claim to ground knowledge.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 demands the full apparatus of epistemology at the foundation. But truth (correspondence with reality), justification (reasons for belief), and logic (valid inference) each require their own vocabulary — vocabulary that depends on what this branch establishes. You cannot assess whether or not knowledge "corresponds to reality" without first grounding what knowledge is. You cannot reason about justification without first grounding what information, comparison, and patterns are.

Commitment #2 raises the real concern: can this framework distinguish knowledge from systematic error? At this level, no — and it explicitly acknowledges this in Unknowns. The distinction between knowledge and correct knowledge requires ontological vocabulary (1.3). But the concern does not show that the foundation is wrong — only that it is incomplete. An incomplete foundation that is correct is better than a complete framework built on ungrounded assumptions.

Commitment #3 confuses "incomplete" with "illegitimate." The branch grounds the experiential structures that truth, justification, and logic will later operate on. Calling it illegitimate because it doesn't yet include those layers is like calling a foundation illegitimate because the building isn't finished.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This branch grounds the experiential structures — information, comparison, knowledge, and definition — that truth conditions, justification, and logic operate on. These later layers require this foundation; they do not replace it. The branch is incomplete by design: it establishes the base that the ontological (1.3), logical (1.4), and reasoning (1.5) layers build upon.

items.title: The framework is circular — it uses identification, comparison, and knowledge to establish identification, comparison, and knowledge.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: To identify a "feature," you must already be able to single out information. To compare, you must already recognize sameness. To know, you must already distinguish having information from lacking it. To define, you must already recognize boundaries and scope. The framework presupposes the very capacities it claims to ground.
Any attempt to ground epistemology from within experience faces this problem: the tools of investigation are the tools being investigated.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Grounding a capacity requires using something other than that capacity — otherwise the grounding is circular.
The framework uses identification to ground identification, comparison to ground comparison, knowledge to ground knowledge, and definition to ground definition.
Circularity at the foundation undermines everything built on it.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 sets a standard that no foundational investigation can meet — including the objector's own. Any critique of the framework uses identification (singling out the problem), comparison (noting the difference between circular and non-circular reasoning), and knowledge (claiming to know that circularity is a flaw). If the standard is applied consistently, it defeats itself.

Commitment #2 misdescribes what the framework does. It does not use identification to *prove* identification. It *points at* the experience of singling out information and gives it a label. The observations — red distinguished from blue, a pattern recognized across features, a question asked and answered — are experiential data, not conclusions derived from prior epistemological theory. The framework is ostensive (pointing at experience), not inferential (deriving from premises).

The circularity objection arises whenever foundations are being laid. The response is the same at every level: awareness of a capacity is not the same as a theory of that capacity. Recognizing that identification occurs does not require a prior theory of identification — it requires the experience itself, which is the starting point (1.1.1).

subSections.label: Correction
items: The framework does not derive identification from identification. It points at experiential data — the occurrence of features, patterns, comparisons, knowledge, and definitions — and labels what is observed. The method is ostensive, not inferential. Awareness of a capacity is what the framework describes; a theory of that capacity is what it produces. These are not the same, and the first does not depend on the second.

items.title: Phenomenological categories are subjective — different people carve up experience differently, so this isn't a universal grounding.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Different cultures, languages, and individuals categorize experience differently. Some languages have dozens of words for snow; others have one. Some traditions treat emotion and sensation as the same type; others separate them sharply.
If the epistemological categories (features, patterns, types, classes) depend on who is doing the categorizing, they aren't a universal grounding — they're one perspective among many.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Phenomenological categories are culturally or individually determined, not universal.
A grounding that varies from person to person cannot serve as a foundation for claims about truth and knowledge.
The specific types and structures identified in this branch reflect one way of carving up experience, not the only way.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 conflates the *labels* for experiential structures with the *structures themselves*. Different languages may have different words for the experience of recognizing sameness — but the experience of recognizing sameness occurs regardless of the word used. The framework identifies the experiential structures, not the linguistic labels.

Commitment #3 is partly right: the specific type-boundaries (willful vs. intensional, emotional vs. physical) could be drawn differently. But the observation that phenomena fall into *some* types based on fundamental features is not culturally dependent — it is an observation about the structure of experience. whether or not the boundary between emotion and sensation falls exactly here or slightly there does not undermine the observation that different types of phenomena occur.

The relevant test is not "does every culture draw the same boundaries?" but "does every experiencing being encounter distinct information, recognize patterns, compare, and come to know?" These structural features are what the branch grounds. The specific categories are ways of organizing the structures — they are revisable without undermining the foundation.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The branch grounds experiential structures — information, patterns, comparison, knowledge, and definition — not culturally specific labels. Different traditions may organize the structures differently, but the structures themselves (that phenomena carry distinguishable information, that patterns repeat, that knowledge and ignorance are distinct states, that classes can be bounded and defined) are what the grounding identifies. The specific type-boundaries are revisable; the structural observations are not.

nodes.claim: Ontological Bridge: reality is what exists independently of want — including myself.
nodes.soWhat: The bridge from experience to reality. Within experience, certain phenomena are independent of willing — and this is what 'real' means here. Without this bridge, nothing in experience is more than experience itself; with it, the whole vocabulary of knowledge, error, and discovery becomes available.
nodes.search: ontological bridge, reality, independent, want, will, object, limit, nature, structure, existence, mind-independent, phenomenology, ontology

sections.title: Observations
items: Pushing against a wall that does not give way.
Returning to a notebook hours later and the words still there, saying what they said.
Willing pain to stop and the pain continuing.
A calculation working out to a result that cannot be forced to be otherwise.

items.text: Ontological Bridge: reality is what exists independently of want — including myself.
items: Phenomena that do not correlate with want are limits (1.3.1). Limits have consistent features — their nature (1.3.2) — and form structures (1.3.3). A structure with a nature is an object (1.3.4.1), existing independently of observation (1.3.4). Reality (1.3.5) is all such objects, connected by relationships (1.3.6). "I" am one of them (1.3.7) — the object that will is, which exhibits features independent of any want's direction.

What is bridged, and what is not required: the bridge is not an inference from experience to something behind experience. It is the recognition within experience that certain phenomena do not correlate with willing. "Independent of willing" IS what "real" means at this level — not something beyond the experience of it. The bridge is crossed by noticing, not by theorizing.

items.title: Experience never reaches anything beyond itself
items.detail: Without the bridge, experience is a closed stream — what occurs has no feature that distinguishes it from what would occur if willing ran the show.

children.title: Knowledge loses its target
children.detail: If nothing is independent of wanting, there is nothing for a claim to match or miss. Asking "is this true?" has no standing outside "is this what I want to be true?" — and the distinction between true and false collapses into preference.

children.title: Error becomes impossible
children.detail: Being wrong requires something to be wrong about. Without a reality independent of will, "mistaken" has no meaning — whatever one wants to be the case simply is.

children.title: Discovery collapses into imagination
children.detail: Finding out what is the case requires a difference between what is and what is imagined. Without that difference, there is no distinction between noticing and inventing, between learning and deciding.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The complete ontological vocabulary built across this branch.
items: Core terms: "limit" (1.3.1.4), "nature" (1.3.2), "structure" (1.3.3), "object" (1.3.4.1), "existence" (1.3.4.2), "observation" (1.3.4.3), "reality" (1.3.5), "relationship" (1.3.6).
Self-reference terms: "I," "me," "myself," "my," "mine," "self," "my body," "voluntary," "involuntary" (the whole 1.3.7 branch).

Plus connector vocabulary grounded along the way: constraint, boundary, against, system, composition, network, exist, perceive, appear, real, unreal, connection, link, between, embodied, inhabit, fatigue, pain, reflex, autonomic.
The next step: logical structures (1.4) — how reality, once established, supports reasoning about what is and what is not the case.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Reality is nothing beyond willing — wanting something to be the case makes it so.
Reality is entirely beyond experience — no phenomenon within experience can reveal it, so reality is inaccessible.
The self is outside reality — reality is external, and "I" stand apart from it.
Experience is all there is — there is no distinction between what is felt and what is the case.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: The full contents of reality — what objects there are in total. Only encountered objects are established here.
Whether or not reality is finite or open-ended — whether there is a complete catalog.
What, if anything, accounts for reality having the specific features it does. The question of a source for reality is not addressed here.
Whether other "I"s exist — whether what is named in 1.3.7 is unique or one of many such objects.
The full structure of relationships among objects — specific laws, regularities, and connections are not enumerated.

items.title: Everything described is still inside experience — no actual bridge to anything mind-independent has been crossed.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The wall that does not give way is an experienced wall. The notebook returned to is an experienced notebook. Calling parts of experience "mind-independent" just renames them. Berkeley's challenge stands: to conceive of something unconceived is already to conceive it. Nothing genuinely outside the mental stream has been established.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Genuine mind-independence requires something outside any possible experience.
2. Everything this framework points to is inside experience.
3. Therefore, no actual bridge has been built — only a rearrangement of experience.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 is the load-bearing assumption and defines "mind-independent" in a way that requires what cannot be given — something outside any possible experience. But this is not what the framework means by "independent of want." The criterion (1.2.5.7.4) is operational: variations in a feature do not correlate with variations in a specific want's direction. That relation is directly accessible within experience.

Commitment #2 describes the framework correctly but draws the wrong conclusion. The wall's resistance does not correlate with the want to push through; the pain does not correlate with the want for it to stop. These are phenomena in experience that are independent of wanting. The objection demands independence-from-experience; the framework claims and establishes independence-from-want. Those are different relations.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The bridge is not to something outside experience. It is to something within experience that does not correlate with wanting. Whether what is independent of want also corresponds to something entirely outside experience is a further question — one the framework neither settles nor requires. The distinction between what is willed and what is not is directly accessible and is what the bridge delivers.

items.title: Your criterion is too weak — a convincing simulation or deceiving demon would satisfy it, but would not be genuine reality.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: If I am in a simulation, the walls still resist me, the notebook still waits where I left it, pain still does not yield to willing — yet nothing is real in the way the word is supposed to mean. Reality should be what exists independently of any mind at all, not just independently of my particular willing. The framework's criterion cannot distinguish genuine reality from a sufficiently thorough illusion.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. The concept of reality requires independence from all minds, not just from my will.
2. A convincing simulation satisfies the framework's criterion without being real.
3. Therefore, the framework does not establish genuine reality.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 imports a standard the framework neither uses nor needs to meet at this level. What is established here is what reality means when first approached — the operational concept of what does not correlate with my will. Whether or not phenomena that meet this criterion are also independent of every possible mind is a further, downstream question.

Commitment #2 points to something correct but mistakes the consequence. At this level, a sufficiently thorough simulation would indeed be practically indistinguishable from unsimulated reality. That is not a defect of the framework; it is an accurate description of epistemic position. Asking whether what one encounters is simulated requires the concept of reality to already be in hand. The framework grounds that concept; it does not purport to settle every question askable with it.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This grounds reality in what is experientially available — what does not correlate with my will. Whether some of what meets this criterion is also independent of all possible minds is a separate question requiring further distinctions. The framework does not foreclose that inquiry; it provides the operational concept of reality that makes it possible.

items.title: You haven't actually reached objects — only patterns. Calling a pattern an "object" imports a theoretical posit that experience does not deliver.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Direct experience gives correlations: this sensation follows that action, this feature appears with that feature. An "object" is something beyond the correlation — a thing the pattern is of. Russell, Mach, and the sense-data tradition showed that moving from patterns to objects requires an inference that experience does not support. The framework has reached patterns and called them objects.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Direct experience delivers only patterns, not objects.
2. "Object" must be a theoretical posit beyond the pattern.
3. Therefore, no genuine bridge to objects exists — the framework smuggles in what it cannot deliver.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 imports a specific theory of what "object" must mean. The framework's definition (1.3.4.1) is different: an object is a structure with nature — a set of limits (1.3.3) with consistent features (1.3.2). Every element is something present in experience. Limits are phenomena that do not correlate with will; consistent features are those that hold across encounters. Nothing is posited beyond what the observations deliver.

Commitment #1 conflates pattern with posit. A pattern with consistent independent features just is what the framework calls an object. Naming the pattern as a structure, its independent features as its nature, and the structure-with-nature as an object, is not adding a hidden entity behind the pattern. It is noticing that the pattern has the specific form the word "object" is defined to name here.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Object is defined within the framework as structure with nature — every element directly available in experience. No hidden entity is posited behind patterns; the patterns themselves, having independent features, meet the definition. A different concept of "object" that requires something beyond patterns would belong to a different framework with different grounding; the one used here is built entirely from what the observations deliver.

nodes.claim: Logical Grounding: statements can be true or false, and new statements can be derived from existing ones.
Reasoning verifies whether or not a statement is true or not.
A method of reasoning that justifies falsehood can't distinguish it from truth.
"I want to know what is actually true — not what I want to be true."
Phenomena occur.
nodes.soWhat: Without this, there is nothing to reason about, nothing to observe, and no starting point for any inquiry.

items.text: Something is happening.
items: A "phenomenon" is anything that occurs. "Thing" means the same at this level.
This is the starting point — nothing more basic is available to point at. Any pointing is itself an occurrence.

items.title: Without phenomena, there is nothing — not even the rejection
items.detail: If nothing occurs, there is no distinction to be noticed, no quality to be pointed at, no association to be felt, no awareness to register anything. There are no observations, no statements, no thoughts — not even the thought that nothing is happening.

children.title: The rejection consumes itself
children.detail: The rejection is itself an occurrence — a thought, a doubt, a denial. There is no standpoint from which the claim is rejected without that standpoint also being something occurring. The denial does not produce an alternative — it collapses into an instance of what it denies.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The vocabulary of "phenomenon" and "occur" — the most primitive terms in the tree, from which all later terms are built.
items: "Phenomenon" — anything that occurs. Synonyms: thing, happening, occurrence.
"Occur" — to happen, to be present. Synonyms: happen, appear, is.
The next observation: whether or not what occurs is uniform or varied — whether or not there are distinctions within it (1.1.2).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: "Nothing whatsoever is happening" — since holding that position is itself *something* happening.
A more basic starting point — occurrence is the floor. There is nothing beneath it to appeal to.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: What is occurring — no specific content has been identified yet.
Whether or not what occurs is uniform or varied — this is addressed in the next node (1.1.2).
Who or what is experiencing the occurrence — the question of a self or subject is addressed later (1.3.7).
Why anything occurs at all — mechanism questions are deferred to Node 2.

items.title: This is trivially true — analytically true statements can't serve as foundations.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: 'Phenomena occur' is true by definition — a phenomenon is something that occurs. This isn't a discovery; it's a tautology. Tautologies carry no information: 'triangles have three sides' tells you nothing about any actual triangle.
If your foundation is analytically true, it is unfalsifiable and therefore empirically empty — it cannot do the work of grounding anything because it excludes no possibilities.
Coherentists (BonJour) and pragmatists (Rorty) would add: foundations aren't needed at all; beliefs are justified by their relationships to other beliefs, not by resting on self-evident truths.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Analytically true statements are informationally empty — they tell you nothing about the world because they exclude no possibilities.
A foundation must be substantive (could be false) to carry weight — unfalsifiable claims are load-free.
Foundationalism itself is optional — coherentism or pragmatism can do the same work without requiring self-evident starting points.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 is plausible for scientific claims, where informationally empty statements do no work. But foundations aren't scientific claims — they play a different role. Ask: what would it look like if 'phenomena occur' were *false*? Not false in a hypothetical way, but actually false — nothing occurring at all. In that case, there are no beliefs, no coherence relations, no justificatory chains, no objections. The coherentist framework the objector prefers (commitment #3) cannot even *begin* without something to cohere about.

This is not the kind of triviality that 'triangles have three sides' has. That statement is derivable from definitions and excludes nothing. 'Phenomena occur' is not derivable — it reports the presence of the raw material that all claims, definitions, and derivations operate on.

Commitment #2 asks that the foundation could be false to carry weight. But a foundation for geometry that 'could be false' — say, 'parallel lines might or might not meet' — is weaker than one that holds necessarily. The objector is asking for vulnerability where the role requires stability.

The real concern behind the objection is that a claim this basic might not *do enough work* — that it's too thin to support anything. But the test of a foundation is not whether it asserts much. It is whether anything can be said at all without it. 'Phenomena occur' passes that test: its negation removes the possibility of any assertion, including the objector's own.

subSections.label: Correction
items: 'Phenomena occur' is not informationally empty in the way 'triangles have three sides' is. It reports the presence of the material that all further claims operate on — and its negation eliminates the possibility of any claim at all, including the objector's.

The coherentist alternative (beliefs justifying beliefs) requires content for beliefs to be about, and that content is phenomena occurring. The foundation's triviality is its strength: it cannot be denied without undermining the denier's own activity.

items.title: 'Phenomena occur' has the form of a claim but no determinate content — what does it actually rule out?

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: 'Phenomena occur' appears to say something — but what state of affairs would make it false?
If nothing could make it false, it has no empirical content. It has the grammatical form of a claim but may be what Carnap called a pseudo-statement — grammatically correct but meaningless.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: A genuine claim must have a determinate negation — it must rule out some possible state of affairs.
"Phenomena occur" has no determinate negation — "phenomena do not occur" is not a coherent state of affairs anyone could inhabit or describe.
A claim that cannot be meaningfully denied cannot do foundational work — it is indistinguishable from saying nothing.

subSections.label: What's Missing

items.text: Commitment #3 mistakes what foundational work requires. A foundation does not need to rule things out — it needs to provide the vocabulary that later claims use.
items: 'Phenomena occur' gives downstream nodes their raw material: features, identity, patterns, comparison, and knowledge all build on it.

items.text: Commitment #2 is actually evidence *for* this, not against it.
items: The negation is incoherent because occurrence is the condition for all coherence.
The objector cannot describe 'no phenomena occurring' without using phenomena (their own thinking, their words) to do so.
The objector's demand — 'give me something falsifiable' — applies to empirical claims within a framework. This establishes the framework itself.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The claim's undeniability is not a defect — it is what makes it foundational.
The negation of 'phenomena occur' requires phenomena (your own thinking and speaking) to be stated. The objector's tools are made of the material they are trying to reject.

items.title: This assumes an observer — something can only 'occur' if it occurs *to* something.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Every example of occurrence you can point to is one you witnessed. The concept of 'something happening' seems to require 'something it happens to.' This isn't just an empirical observation — it may be a conceptual truth.

Strawson's argument that experience requires a subject, the Buddhist concept of *vijñāna* (consciousness as always consciousness-of), and ordinary grammar ('it rains' — but what is 'it'?) all suggest that occurrence without a subject is not a coherent concept.
The node asserts subjectless occurrence without establishing that the concept is even intelligible.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 'Occurrence' is conceptually parasitic on 'subject' — the concept of something happening requires the concept of something it happens to.
Every introspective access to occurrence goes through a subject — you can't observe occurrence independently of being the one observing.
Subjectless occurrence is not parsimonious; it is incoherent — it strips away a necessary condition and presents the remainder as self-sufficient.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 is true but proves the opposite of what the objector intends. Yes, every occurrence you access is one you are experiencing. But that doesn't show that occurrence *requires* a subject — it shows that your *access to* occurrence goes through experience. The question is whether or not the subject is part of *what occurrence is* or part of *how you encounter it*.

Commitment #1 derives its plausibility from commitment #2: because you always encounter occurrence as a subject, you assume subjecthood is part of occurrence itself. But this is like concluding that because you always see objects from a perspective, objects inherently possess a perspective. The perspective is in the seeing, not in the object. The subject may be in the encountering, not in the occurring.

Commitment #3 claims subjectless occurrence strips a necessary condition. But what the node actually describes is occurrence as it is given — before the vocabulary for 'subject' or 'observer' has been built. At this level, the observation is: *this is happening*. The 'to whom?' question is real and important, but it uses vocabulary ('to,' 'whom') that requires concepts (directedness, agency) not yet available.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The node does not assert that occurrence is subjectless — it observes occurrence before the vocabulary for subjects exists. 'Phenomena occur' is the observation. 'To whom?' is a real question — and it requires the concepts of awareness (1.1.5), identity (1.2.1.4), and eventually selfhood (later branches) to answer.
The node's silence about subjects is not a denial of subjects; it is the order of construction.

items.title: Consciousness is an illusion — nothing is actually happening. (Eliminativism)

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Some philosophers and neuroscientists argue that consciousness does not exist — that there is no 'what it is like' to experience anything.
On this view, what you call 'experience' is a construction of the brain, and the brain is wrong about its own inner states.
If this is right, nothing is genuinely 'happening' in the way this claims.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: What you call experience is a theoretical posit — part of a theory about what the brain does, not raw data.
If the theory is wrong, the 'data' it posits (qualia, phenomenal consciousness) may not exist either.
The correct description of what the brain does may not include experience at all.

subSections.label: What's Missing

items.text: Try this: hold the position that 'nothing is happening' while reading this sentence. Red, hot, pressure, hungry — none of these have ever occurred to you, including the reading of this very sentence.
items: You are reading. That reading is something happening.
If you hold that the reading is an illusion — that illusion is also something happening.
The position consumes itself: denying occurrence requires occurrence.

The commitments above target a richer notion of consciousness — qualia with metaphysical status, unified subjects, irreducible phenomenal properties. This claims none of that. It claims only: *something is happening*. The bar is as low as it can possibly be.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Eliminativism operates above this claim's level. It denies that folk-psychological concepts (beliefs, qualia, consciousness-as-a-thing) accurately describe what exists.
It does not — and cannot — deny that *something* is happening. The theorizing that denies occurrence is itself something occurring.

nodes.claim: Distinct phenomena occur.
nodes.soWhat: Without this, everything would be a single undifferentiated occurrence — no features, no comparisons, no identifications, and nothing to reason about.
nodes.search: distinct different separate plural multiple not same variety differentiation multiplicity phenomenon

sections.title: Observations
items: Red is not hot.
Pressure is different than hunger.
Ouch is not strawberry.
2 is not an arm.
"2 + 2 = 4" is not a flying pig.
"The earth is flat" is not "The earth is round".

items.text: Distinct phenomena occur.
items: Phenomena are "distinct" when one is not like the another.

items.title: Phenomena collapse into a single undifferentiated occurrence
items.detail: If phenomena are not distinct, then red would be indistinguishable from hungry — which would be the same as ouch — which would also be the same as a flying pig. There is no "this" versus "that" — only a single, featureless happening. Without distinctions, there is nothing to identify, nothing to compare, and nothing to reason about.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The vocabulary of "distinct" — not the same as each other.
items: "Distinct" — not the same as something else. Synonyms: different, separate, other.
"Multiplicity" — the occurrence of more than one distinct phenomenon.
Also grounded: "what" (pointing at a specific phenomenon), "one" / "a" / "the" / "that" / "each" (singling out), "from" / "than" / "which" (comparing), "uniform" (what distinctness rules out).
The next observation: what specifically makes phenomena distinct from each other (1.1.3 — qualities).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: What occurs is a single undifferentiated phenomenon with no internal distinctions.
Differences between phenomena are imposed or constructed rather than observed — at this level, the distinction is directly given, not inferred.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: What makes phenomena distinct from each other — the specific *character* of their differences is not yet identified (addressed in 1.1.3).
How many distinct phenomena there are — no count or enumeration is established.
Whether or not the distinctions are fundamental or superficial — that question requires vocabulary not yet built (1.2.5.7).

items.title: Distinction requires a criterion — you haven't said what makes them different.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: You say phenomena are distinct — but you haven't said *what* makes them different.
Claiming a difference without identifying the property that differs leaves the claim empty.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Noticing a difference and knowing *what* differs are the same act — you can't have one without the other.
An observation without an explanation of what was observed is incomplete.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: You notice that red is not the same as hungry before you can say why. The observation is immediate — it does not wait for an explanation.
Commitment #1 inverts the actual order: you observe first, then explain. The specific character of what differs (qualities) is the next node (1.1.3).

subSections.label: Correction
items: This registers the observation of difference, not its explanation.
Requiring the explanation before the observation reverses the order of how you actually encounter things.

items.title: Distinction is an artifact of attention, not a feature of experience.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: William James described infant experience as a 'blooming, buzzing confusion.'
Before attention carves experience into separate items, there may be no genuine boundaries — only a continuous field.
If so, what this calls 'distinct phenomena' only become distinct when you attend to them.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Pre-attentive experience is continuous — boundaries between phenomena are imposed by attention, not found.
Attention is prior to distinction: things become distinct because you attend to them, not the other way around.
If distinction depends on attention, it is something you generate rather than something that occurs.

items.text: Commitment #2 inverts the observable order. You attend to red because it is already not-hot, not-hungry, not-pressure — the difference is what draws your attention.
items: James's 'buzzing confusion' describes being *overwhelmed by too many distinctions*, not the absence of distinction.
If experience were genuinely undifferentiated before attention, attention would have nothing to select from — no edge, no gradient, no salience.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Attention selects *among* distinctions already present — it does not create them.
Red being not-hungry does not require focusing on one and ignoring the other. That difference is what makes focusing possible.

items.title: All distinctions are ultimately unreal — reality is one undifferentiated whole. (Monism)

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Major philosophical and religious traditions — Advaita Vedanta, Parmenides, some Buddhist schools — hold that multiplicity is illusory.
What appears as distinct phenomena is ultimately one undivided reality.
On this view, the observation of distinctness is a product of ignorance, not a feature of what exists.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Experiential distinctions derive their legitimacy from ultimate reality — if reality is one, experienced distinctions are errors.
Observing a difference commits you to the *reality* of that difference, not just the *experience* of it.
Illusion (*maya*) is not just 'experienced as real' but 'falsely experienced as real' — and 'falsely' disqualifies the observation.

subSections.label: What's Missing

items.text: Commitment #1 carries the objection's force — and it is a large assumption. Why should an observation about experience require ultimate-reality backing to count?
items: The Advaita tradition itself acknowledges that *maya* is experienced as real, even within its own framework.
Red is not hungry *within experience*, regardless of whether or not that distinction is ultimately real.
The monist can consistently hold both: distinctions are not ultimately real AND experiential distinctions occur.

Commitment #1 also faces a structural problem the monist rarely examines: the claim 'reality is one' is itself a distinction — it distinguishes the one from the many, the real from the illusory, the correct view from the incorrect. The monist must draw experiential distinctions (between their position and competing positions, between maya and Brahman, between ultimate and conventional truth) in order to articulate the claim that distinctions are unreal. If the principle 'all distinctions are unreal' is applied consistently, it dissolves itself — including the distinction between the monist's view and any other view.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not distinctions are ultimately real is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied.
Within experience, red is not hungry. The monist does not need to deny experienced distinction to hold that ultimate reality is one — and the major monist traditions don't.

nodes.claim: Qualities occur.
nodes.soWhat: Without this, distinct phenomena would have no specific character — nothing to single out, identify, or refer to.
nodes.search: quality qualia character content specific label name red hot hungry sweet distinct phenomenon

sections.title: Observations
items: Red.
Blue.
Hot.
Cold.
Sweet.
Hungry.
Ouch.
Loud.

items.text: Qualities occur.
items: A "quality" is a singular distinct phenomenon (1.1.2). Red is a quality. Hot is a quality. Hungry is a quality.

items.title: Nothing specific to identify or refer to
items.detail: Without qualities, there is nothing specific to single out, compare, or refer to. Features, patterns, and classes all depend on having specific qualities to work with. The entire epistemological grounding (1.2) has no raw material.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The vocabulary of "quality" — a singular distinct phenomenon.
items: "Quality" — a singular distinct phenomenon. Synonyms: character, content.
Also grounded: "of" (the quality OF a phenomenon), "have" (a phenomenon HAS a quality), "as" (occurring AS a quality), "seem" (how something SEEMS — its quality as presented).
The next observation: whether or not there are felt connections between qualities (1.1.4 — associations).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Distinct phenomena are nameless and interchangeable — with nothing specific about any of them.
Distinction is purely negative — just "not-X" — with no positive content.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not qualities occur in isolation or in connection with each other — addressed in the next node (1.1.4 — associations).
What structures or patterns qualities form — requires vocabulary not yet built (1.2.1).
Whether or not qualities are fundamental or superficial — addressed later (1.2.5.7).

items.title: Qualities are theoretical posits, not observational data.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Sellars argued that there is no uninterpreted 'given' in experience. What you call a 'quality' is already shaped by concepts, language, and prior learning.
Redness is not raw data — it is a product of your visual system, your culture, your language. Without these, there is no 'red' to observe.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: There is no layer of experience that is genuinely pre-conceptual — all awareness is already structured by learned or innate frameworks.
Calling something a "quality" assumes it is a natural unit of experience, but the boundaries of qualities are imposed by the perceptual system.
If qualities are framework-dependent, they cannot serve as neutral starting points.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 assumes that framework-dependence disqualifies something as observational. But even in Sellars' own account, the framework must have *something to organize*. If all qualities were entirely imposed, any framework would produce any output from any input — there would be no constraint on what the system could classify.
The fact that your perceptual system consistently classifies certain inputs as red and never as bitter means the qualitative character constrains the framework, not only the reverse.

Commitment #1 is the strong form, and it proves too much: if no experience is pre-conceptual, then the concepts themselves have no experiential ground, and the account of conceptual imposition has nothing to be imposed *upon*.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This does not claim qualities are pre-conceptual in Sellars' sense — it does not take a position on what produces them. It observes that whatever shows up in awareness has specific character: this, not that. whether or not that specificity is "given" or "constructed" is a question about the source of qualities, not about whether or not qualities occur.
The Sellarsian can consistently hold that all quality-experience is framework-shaped and still acknowledge that the shaped result has specific character — which is all this registers.

items.title: Qualities are subjective — they depend on the observer, not on reality.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The same physical stimulus can produce different experiences in different observers. What you see as red may not be what someone else sees as red.
If qualities depend on you, they cannot ground objective claims about experience.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: If a quality depends on the observer's perceptual apparatus, it is "merely subjective" and cannot ground anything beyond that observer's experience.
The subjective/objective distinction is prior to and more fundamental than any claim about qualities.
"Subjective" means unreliable or not foundationally useful.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 is doing all the work and is never stated. The objection assumes that "subjective" means "unreal" or "unreliable." But this is not claiming qualities are objective features of a world existing independently of experience. It is noting that qualities occur.
The subjective/objective axis — which requires vocabulary for objects, observers, and independence not yet built — is orthogonal to occurrence.

There is a further problem with commitment #1 that the objector should notice. The distinction between subjective and objective is itself identified through subjective experience — you observe that different people see colors differently, which is an observation made through your own perceptual apparatus. If observer-dependence disqualifies a quality from grounding anything, then the subjective/objective distinction is itself disqualified, since it is grounded in observation. The objector needs subjective experience to be reliable enough to identify the subjective/objective distinction. Once they concede that, the node's claim (qualities occur in experience) uses the same reliability they've already accepted.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The question of whether or not qualities are observer-dependent or world-dependent requires concepts from later nodes. This registers only that qualities occur. Their source and status are deferred, not denied.

items.title: Qualities are secondary — what really exists are structures, relations, or dispositions.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Structural realists argue that what really exists are relations and dispositions, not qualities.
'Red' is just a label for a particular frequency of light hitting your retina in a particular way. The real story is the structure, not the feel.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: The ultimate constituents of reality are structures, relations, or dispositions — not qualitative properties.
Qualities as experienced are products of a causal chain, and the chain's real elements are non-qualitative (wavelengths, neural patterns).
Derivatives cannot serve as primitives — if qualities are produced by something else, that something else is more fundamental.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 conflates causal priority with observational priority. The causal story of how redness is produced (wavelengths → retina → cortex → experience) may be correct, but the thing at the *end* of that chain — the experienced quality — is where observation starts.

You cannot observe a wavelength without experiencing a quality (the reading on a meter, the color of a spectral line). The structural realist's own account of structures and relations is itself given through qualities — the quality of seeing a diagram, reading an equation, noting a pattern.
Commitment #2 assumes that the causal explanation replaces the datum it explains, but the explanation itself relies on qualitative experience at every step.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Qualities may be causally downstream of structures, wavelengths, and neural patterns. But they are observationally upstream of all of these — every account of structure, disposition, or relation is given through experienced qualities. This starts where observation starts, not where causation starts.

nodes.claim: Associations occur.
nodes.soWhat: Without associations, qualities would occur in isolation — no felt connections, no groupings, no basis for identifying patterns or comparing anything.
nodes.search: association connection link relation together like similar grouping belonging synthesis and or with

sections.title: Observations
items: Red is like blue.
Hungry is like thirsty.
Pleasure is like pain.
Two is like three.
Redness and sweetness — together in a strawberry.
Hotness and the ache of a burn — together.

items.text: Associations occur.
items: An "association" is a quality that occurs with multiple phenomena — the felt sense that they are alike, belong together, or go with each other. The likeness between red and blue is an association.

items.title: Qualities occur in total isolation
items.detail: If there are no associations, then red has no connection to blue, hunger has no connection to thirst, and hot has no connection to ouch. Each quality occurs as a standalone, disconnected occurrence with no felt links to anything else. Without connections, there is nothing to group, nothing to compare, and no way to recognize what belongs with what.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The vocabulary of "association" — a quality that occurs with multiple phenomena.
items: "Association" — a quality that occurs with multiple phenomena. Synonyms: connection, link, relation.

Also grounded: "like" (one phenomenon IS LIKE another), "with" (a quality occurs WITH another), "together" (phenomena go TOGETHER), "and" (this AND that — connecting), "or" (this OR that — alternatives within a group), "similar" (alike), "any" (any one of a group), "group" (phenomena connected by association).
The next step: identifying awareness as the quality of occurrence (1.1.5) — completing the phenomenological grounding.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Qualities occur in total isolation with no felt connections between them.
Felt connections between phenomena do not occur — every quality occurs in isolation with no "likeness" or "togetherness."

sections.title: Unknowns
items: What specific structures associations form — requires vocabulary built later (1.2.1 — features and patterns).
Whether or not associations reflect real connections or are merely felt — requires the ontological vocabulary (1.3).
The formal types of associations (similarity, belonging, sequence, etc.) — identified in the types of phenomena (1.2.5).

items.title: Connections between experiences are constructed by inference, not given in experience.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Hume argued that what you call a 'connection' between two things is really just one thing following another. You see lightning, then hear thunder — but the connection is something your mind adds.
If connections are inferences rather than observations, this is describing something the mind does, not something that occurs.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: The felt quality of "these go together" is a product of repeated co-occurrence, not a distinct observation.
Habit and inference are the source of experienced connections; the connections themselves are not in the experience.
Only individual qualities are genuinely given; their relationships are always added by the mind.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 creates a problem Hume himself recognized. If individual qualities (1.1.3) are the only genuine data, and their connection is added by habit, then habit itself has no data to work from — because noticing that A and B *co-occurred* already requires registering a connection between them.

The very concept of "constant conjunction" presupposes that you observe A-and-B rather than just A, then just B, with no link. For repeated co-occurrence to generate a habit, the co-occurrence itself must be noticed each time — which is an association.
Commitment #3 tries to eliminate associations from the data layer, but the mechanism it offers to replace them (repeated conjunction) depends on associations being in the data layer.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The experience of connection — red *with* this shape, warmth *with* this surface — is what makes conjunction observable in the first place. Hume's "constant conjunction" requires that the co-occurrence be noticed, and that noticing is itself an association. You cannot get from isolated qualities to habitual connection without already having experienced togetherness.

items.title: These "connections" are learned, not given — you learn to associate red with strawberry through experience.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The association between red and strawberry comes from seeing strawberries that are red — repeatedly, over time.
Associations are products of learning and memory, not primitive occurrences.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Associations between specific phenomena (e.g., red and strawberry) are products of repeated experience, not primitive occurrences.
If specific associations are learned, the general phenomenon of 'association' is also learned — there is no primitive associative quality.
A foundational claim about association must distinguish innate connections from acquired ones to be meaningful.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: The objection conflates specific associations (red-strawberry) with the occurrence of association as such. This is not claiming that any particular association is innate or unlearned. It is noting that felt connections between phenomena occur — as established at (1.1.1).
Whether or not specific associations are learned or given is a separate question that requires temporal vocabulary (memory, learning) not yet built (1.2.5.3, 1.2.6.5).

subSections.label: Correction
items: This observes that associations occur — not that specific associations are innate. The mechanism by which particular associations form (learning, memory, pattern recognition) is a later question. The observation that felt connections between phenomena occur (1.1.1) at all stands regardless of how any specific connection came about.

items.title: 'Like' already requires comparing, which hasn't been defined — this node smuggles in comparison.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: 'Like' already requires comparing two things. But comparison hasn't been defined yet — that is node (1.2.2).
If connection uses comparison, and comparison hasn't been established, this is borrowing vocabulary it hasn't built.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Noticing similarity IS comparing — there is no pre-comparative similarity.
The felt quality of "these go together" is the *result* of comparing, not raw material for it.
Dependency order requires that no node use a concept defined later.

subSections.label: What's Missing

items.text: The objection assumes that comparison produces similarity.
items: But the observation is the reverse: similarity is what makes comparison possible. You compare *because* you already notice likenesses and differences — the felt connection is prior to any formal act of comparing.

The second commitment is where the objection breaks: it gets the dependency backwards. The association ("these go together") is the raw material; comparison (1.2.2) is the later identification of what that connection involves.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The association is not the result of comparing — it is what makes comparing possible. Convention 4 (observation before abstraction) applies: the specific observation (felt likeness) comes before the general identification (comparison).

nodes.claim: Awareness is the occurrence of a quality or association.
nodes.soWhat: Without this, occurrence would add nothing to a quality — there would be no difference between a quality occurring and not occurring, and no ground for presence or absence.
nodes.search: awareness experience consciousness given presence absence there-ness occurring phenomenal

sections.title: Observations
items: Red occurring.
Hot occurring.
Hungry occurring.
Ouch occurring.
The likeness between red and blue occurring.
The togetherness of sweet and strawberry occurring.

items.text: Awareness is the occurrence of a quality or association.
items: "Awareness" is the quality of occurrence — the "there-ness" of a quality or association. "Red occurs" and "awareness of red" say the same thing.

items.title: Occurrence adds nothing
items.detail: If awareness is not the quality of occurrence, then occurrence has no character of its own. "Red occurring" and "red not occurring" would have no felt difference — the "there-ness" that distinguishes presence from absence would vanish.

children.title: Presence and absence become indistinguishable
children.detail: Everything that follows depends on the difference between a quality being present and being absent. If occurrence has no quality, this difference has no ground — and the observation that things happen (1.1.1) loses its content.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The vocabulary of "awareness" — the quality of occurrence.
items: "Awareness" — the quality of occurrence of a quality or association. Synonyms: experience, consciousness (at this level).
Also grounded: "given" (what is present in awareness), "presence" (the occurring of a quality or association), "absence" (the non-occurring of a quality or association).

Completes the phenomenological grounding (1.1). The parent claim — "distinct things occur in my awareness" — is now fully built: phenomena (1.1.1) are distinct (1.1.2), are qualities (1.1.3) with associations (1.1.4), and their occurrence IS awareness.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Occurrence has no quality of its own — there is no "there-ness" to distinguish presence from absence.
Awareness is a separate entity behind occurrence — a "watcher" that observes qualities from the outside.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Who or what is aware — the question of a self or subject is addressed later (1.3.7).
Whether or not awareness is continuous or intermittent — requires temporal vocabulary (1.2.5.3).
What awareness is "made of" or how it arises — mechanism questions are deferred (Node 2).

items.title: There's something it's 'like' to experience redness, beyond it just happening.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Nagel's 'what it is like' and Chalmers's 'hard problem' suggest that awareness is more than just occurrence — there is a felt quality, a subjective character, to being aware.
Defining awareness as just 'the occurrence of a quality' leaves out this subjective dimension entirely.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: There is a gap between "occurrence" and "experienced occurrence" — something can happen without there being anything it's like for it to happen.
The hard problem reveals a genuine gap in what exists between physical processes and experience.
"Mere occurrence" is a coherent category — things can occur without any phenomenal character.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: At this level, "mere occurrence" is not a coherent category. Every occurrence that has been described since (1.1.1) — redness, hotness, the likeness between phenomena — already IS experiential. Redness doesn't "merely happen" like a thermostat reading; it occurs with its full phenomenal character.

Commitment #3 collapses here: at the experiential level, there is no such thing as characterless occurrence. The hard problem arises only when trying to explain awareness from the outside (from physics or neuroscience). From the inside — which is where this starts — there is no gap to bridge.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This is not claiming that awareness is "nothing special." It is claiming that awareness is not a separate entity added to occurrence. The "what it's like" IS the quality of occurrence. The hard problem is about explaining awareness from a third-person perspective. This describes it from the first-person perspective, where no explanation is needed — only recognition.

items.title: This conflates passive awareness with active attention — they're different in kind.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Background awareness (the hum of traffic you're not attending to) and focused attention (the word you're reading right now) are qualitatively different. Cognitive science treats them as distinct systems (dorsal/ventral attention networks, global workspace vs. peripheral processing).

Defining awareness as 'the occurrence of a quality' covers both without distinguishing them. If the definition can't capture this difference, it's too coarse to be useful — like defining 'weather' as 'atmospheric conditions' without distinguishing hurricanes from sunshine.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: The difference between background awareness and focused attention is a difference of *kind*, not degree — they involve different cognitive systems and produce qualitatively different experiences.
A definition that subsumes both without distinction fails to capture something important about the structure of experience.
The relevant difference (kind, not degree) must be captured at the *definitional* level, not deferred to later nodes.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 makes the specific claim that background awareness and focused attention differ in *kind*, not degree. This deserves direct engagement. The cognitive science is real: different neural systems underlie each. But the question is whether or not different underlying systems produce different *kinds* of experience or different *degrees* of the same experience.

The objector needs to provide a case where the transition from background to foreground awareness involves a qualitative *break* — a point where the experience stops being one thing and starts being another. Consider: the background hum of traffic gradually becomes loud enough to bother you. At what point did it change *kind*? The hum gains detail, salience, and centrality continuously. There is no break point.

Commitment #3 asks the definition to capture this difference *here*, at the definitional level. But the definition of 'color' need not distinguish red from blue to be correct. Red and blue are different — importantly different — but they are both colors. The difference between them is a difference *within* the category, not evidence that the category is too coarse.

The objector's real concern is that the definition papers over something important. It doesn't — it identifies the genus. The species (background vs. focused) differ in qualities that the tree already has vocabulary for: intensity (1.2.5.2.1) and direction (1.2.5.1.2, where attention is wanting directed at a specific quality).

subSections.label: Correction
items: Background awareness and focused attention are both occurrences of qualities — the definition is correct about the genus. They differ in intensity and direction, which are already available as vocabulary.
The difference is real and captured by the tree — but it is a difference between *types* of awareness, not evidence that the definition of awareness is wrong.

items.title: If awareness = occurrence of a quality, then rocks are aware — this entails panpsychism.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: A rock heats up — a quality (temperature) occurs. By this definition, the rock is aware. If the definition entails panpsychism, then either panpsychism is true (which most people find absurd) or the definition is wrong.

You can't define awareness so broadly that heating rocks qualify and then act surprised when panpsychism follows. Constitutive panpsychists (Chalmers, Strawson, Goff) take this seriously, but most philosophers and scientists consider it a *reductio* of any definition that generates it.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Physical processes (rock heating) and phenomenological occurrences (experiencing warmth) are the same kind of event — both are 'occurrences of qualities.'
If the definition covers both, it entails panpsychism.
Panpsychism is absurd or at minimum an unacceptable cost, so the definition must be wrong.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 is where the objection breaks. The objector treats 'the rock heats up' and 'warmth occurs' as the same event described differently. But are they? 'The rock heats up' describes a physical process with a temperature change measurable by thermometer. 'Warmth occurs' (in the sense the tree has been using since 1.1.1) describes an experiential quality — the felt character of warmth as it shows up in awareness.

The entire tree has been built within the experiential domain: 'phenomena occur' (1.1.1) meant phenomena as experienced, 'qualities occur' (1.1.3) meant qualities as experienced, and 'awareness is the occurrence of a quality' (this node) means awareness as it shows up experientially. The rock's temperature change is not in this domain unless you already assume it is — which is exactly what the panpsychist does.

The objector's argument has the structure: 'If X applies to everything, it entails panpsychism.' But X (the definition) applies only to *phenomenological* qualities, and whether or not rocks have phenomenological qualities is the contested premise, not a consequence. Commitment #2 works only if commitment #1 holds — only if physical processes and phenomenological occurrences are already established as the same kind of event. They aren't; that's the debate.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The definition operates within the domain of phenomenological qualities — the domain the entire tree has been building in since 1.1.1. Physical processes enter this domain only if they involve phenomenological qualities, which is precisely what panpsychism asserts and its critics deny.
The definition doesn't settle this — it tells you what awareness is, not what has it. The panpsychism debate is about the scope of the phenomenological domain, not about the definition of awareness.

items.title: Awareness could be a separate entity and presence would still be distinguishable from absence.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Maybe awareness is a *separate thing* — an entity, a 'witness' — that observes occurrence from the outside.
If so, distinguishing presence from absence does not require awareness to *be* occurrence. A separate observer could do the same job.
This would mean this conflates what is observed (occurrence) with you (awareness).

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Awareness is a substance or entity that encounters qualities from outside, rather than being identical with their occurrence.
This separate entity can distinguish presence from absence using something other than occurrence itself having intrinsic character.
The "watcher" model is at least as parsimonious as the "occurrence IS awareness" model.

subSections.label: What's Missing

items.text: If awareness is separate from occurrence, then occurrence itself contributes nothing — it has no character of its own. The separate entity must do all the work: it must distinguish "red present" from "red absent" using something other than occurrence.
items: But what does it encounter? If occurrence has no character, there is nothing *there* for the separate entity to engage with — no difference between a quality (1.1.3) occurring and not occurring until the entity acts. This doesn't solve the problem — it relocates it.
