Now the separate entity needs its own account of how it detects presence versus absence, and that account will either reintroduce occurrence-as-a-quality (arriving back at this claim's definition) or leave the mechanism unexplained.
Commitment #3 fails: the watcher model adds an assumption (a separate entity) without resolving what it was supposed to resolve.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The separate-entity model assumes that "occurring" is an empty placeholder that needs an external witness to gain content. But the observation is the opposite: occurring already HAS content — the "there-ness" of red is not added by a watcher, it is what red's occurring consists in.
Positing a separate entity to do what occurrence already does is an extra assumption with no observational ground at this level.

nodes.claim: Phenomena are identified by features and patterns.
nodes.soWhat: Establishes how we identify phenomena (by their features) and recognize what they have in common (by their patterns). Comparison and knowledge depend on this vocabulary.
nodes.search: features patterns information identity identification sameness variation class epistemological vocabulary

sections.title: Observations
items: Redness, sweetness, shape — each a distinct feature that, together, identifies a strawberry.
Redness belongs to the strawberry, not to the thunder. Heat belongs to the flame, not to the song.
Red, blue, green — they share something in common, a color. So do hot, warm, cold — temperature. So do sweet, sour, bitter — taste.
A red apple and a red strawberry — same in one way (color, fruit), different in others (taste, shape, texture).
Color and brightness are both visual. Taste and smell are both chemical. Sight and smell are both senses. Patterns themselves have patterns.

items.text: Phenomena are identified by features and patterns.
items: What awareness contains — qualities and associations — is "information." Information belongs with phenomena as distinct "features." A phenomenon's unique set of features is its "identity," and being aware of that identity is "identification."
Features share qualities — "patterns." Features are the same or vary within a pattern. Patterns themselves share qualities — "classes."
Together: features tell you what THIS thing is, and patterns tell you what KIND of thing it is.

items.title: Phenomena carry no identifiable information
items.detail: Without features and patterns, phenomena occur but carry nothing recognizable. There is nothing to say about what a phenomenon IS (no identity), nothing to notice it shares with other phenomena (no patterns), and nothing to compare or know. Comparison, matching, mismatching, and knowledge all require phenomena to have identifiable features and recognizable patterns.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The epistemological vocabulary built across this section's nine nodes.
items: "Information" — a quality or association (1.2.1.1). "Belongs with" / "of" / "has" — information is of a phenomenon (1.2.1.2).
"Feature" — a distinct piece of information (1.2.1.3). "Identity" — a unique set of features (1.2.1.4). "Identification" — awareness of identity (1.2.1.5).

"Pattern" — a shared quality across features (1.2.1.6). "Sameness" — alike in a pattern (1.2.1.7). "Variation" — different in a pattern (1.2.1.8). "Class" — a shared quality across patterns (1.2.1.9).
Plus connector vocabulary grounded along the way: about, same, identical, type, category, attribute, property, characteristic, vary, differ.
The next step: comparing information across phenomena — comparison (1.2.2), matching (1.2.3), and mismatching (1.2.4).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Phenomena have no identifiable information — nothing to single out or refer to about them.
Information floats free without belonging to any phenomenon.
Phenomena have no unique identity — no distinguishing feature-set.
Features have nothing in common — no shared qualities, no patterns.
Classification requires something beyond shared qualities — an external authority or convention.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: How to compare information across phenomena — addressed by comparison (1.2.2).
Whether or not features and patterns correspond to anything beyond experience — ontological questions deferred to (1.3).
How identification relates to language, memory, or learning — deferred to later nodes.
How many levels of classification exist — the recursive structure allows indefinite nesting but no enumeration is possible.

items.title: Imposing categories like 'feature,' 'pattern,' and 'class' onto experience reifies what is fluid.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Experience is fluid and continuous. Imposing rigid categories like 'feature,' 'pattern,' and 'class' onto it carves up what is actually a flowing stream.
These categories may distort what they claim to describe.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Genuine experience is continuous flow, not a collection of discrete identifiable items.
The act of identifying features and patterns is an intellectual operation that transforms what it describes — the description is not faithful to the original.
Any vocabulary that carves experience into units has already departed from experience as it actually occurs.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 applies to itself. Bergson's own description of "continuous flow" uses identifiable terms: "flow," "duration," "continuity." These are themselves features of experience that have been identified and named. The claim that experience is "undivided" is itself a division — between divided and undivided experience.
If the act of identifying always distorts, then the identification of experience as "flowing" is equally distorted, and Bergson's own account cannot get off the ground.
Commitment #1 states that experience is continuous, but this observation is made *using* the very capacity for distinction and identification that the objection claims is distortive.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The vocabulary here does not claim experience occurs as a list of separate items lined up for inspection. It identifies aspects of experience that are distinguishable within whatever form experience takes — including continuous flow. A flowing river has distinguishable features (speed, temperature, direction) without ceasing to flow. Identification is not dissection.

items.title: Features, patterns, and classes are cognitive constructs imposed by the mind, not found in experience.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Constructivism (Goodman, late Wittgenstein) holds that the mind doesn't discover features and patterns — it imposes them. Which features you notice depends on your perceptual training, language, culture, and expectations.
There is no 'neutral' experience that comes pre-carved into features. The appearance of structure in experience is the result of cognitive work, not a passive reception of what's there.
If the mind constructs the features, then 'phenomena are identified by features' describes a cognitive act, not an observation.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: The features and patterns available in experience are products of cognitive processing — imposed, not found.
If the mind constructs the features, then calling those features 'observations' is begging the question against constructivism.
There is no middle ground between 'mind-independent features' and 'arbitrary cognitive impositions' — features are either found or made.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 is the false binary that gives the objection its force. The constructivist presents two options: features are mind-independent (realism) or mind-imposed (constructivism). But notice what both options share: features are present in experience. The realist says they're present because reality put them there. The constructivist says they're present because the mind put them there. Both agree on the *presence*; they disagree on the *source*. The node claims only the presence.

The constructivist might push back: 'But calling features *observations* already sides with realism — it implies they were found, not made.' This is commitment #2, and it depends on commitment #3 (the false binary). If 'observation' necessarily means 'passive reception of mind-independent facts,' then yes, the node smuggles in realism. But the node defines observation more minimally: the awareness of what is present in experience. The constructivist's own position requires this — when Goodman says the mind constructs features, he must be aware of the features the mind constructs. That awareness is what the node calls observation.

There is also a self-referential consequence the constructivist should confront: to say 'the mind imposes features,' the constructivist has identified a specific feature of experience (the mind-imposing quality) — which, on their own account, is also a cognitive construction. This doesn't refute constructivism. But it clarifies something important: the constructivist trusts their own constructed identification of construction. 'Constructed' cannot mean 'therefore untrustworthy,' or the constructivist's own analysis is untrustworthy. If 'constructed' means 'mind-dependent but still informative' — which it must, for the constructivist to do their own work — then the node's features are also mind-dependent but still informative, and constructivism is compatible with the node rather than opposed to it.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Realism and constructivism disagree about whether or not features are found or made. Both presuppose that features end up present in experience. The node names that shared presupposition.

Calling this an 'observation' doesn't side for or against realism — it means awareness of what is present, which the constructivist's own account requires in order to say 'the mind imposes *these* features rather than *those*.'

items.title: These definitions carry ontological commitments — 'identity,' 'information,' and 'class' imply metaphysical positions.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: "Identity" implies essences or substances. "Information" implies processing or encoding. "Class" implies real, built-in categories in nature (natural kinds). The definitions appear neutral but smuggle in philosophical positions about what exists.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Terms like "identity," "information," and "class" unavoidably import their richer philosophical meanings even when defined minimally.
You cannot use a philosophically loaded term in a philosophically "innocent" way — the baggage always comes along.
Minimal definitions are covert smuggling because readers will hear the richer meaning.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 is genuinely worth considering — and the response should not dismiss it. There is a real question about whether or not stipulative narrowing of a term fully brackets its connotations.

But the alternative is inventing new terms for every concept (abandoning ordinary language entirely) or avoiding terms that have richer senses (leaving the reader with no recognizable vocabulary). The pragmatic resolution: each term is defined at the experiential level only, and the richer senses are explicitly deferred to later nodes with more vocabulary.

The objection also undermines itself on its own terms. If a philosophically loaded term cannot be used innocently (commitment #2), then the objector's own vocabulary fails the same test. 'Ontological commitment' presupposes a specific framework for relating language to existence (Quine's). 'Smuggling' presupposes a theory of hidden content. 'Neutral starting point' presupposes a theory of epistemic innocence. The objector uses loaded terms to identify other terms as loaded. If the principle 'loaded terms always import their richer meanings' is applied consistently, the objector cannot state their objection without importing the very kind of baggage they're criticizing. The principle, taken seriously, makes all philosophical conversation impossible — not because of these specific definitions, but because of how language works.

subSections.label: Correction
items: You don't need a theory of essences to identify a strawberry, a theory of processing to have information, or a theory of natural kinds to notice that color and brightness are both visual. These nodes capture the experiential sense of each term. The question about what exists are real, important, and deferred — not denied.

nodes.claim: A comparison is observing sameness or variation between information.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the everyday act of noticing how information is alike or different. Matching and mismatching both build on this.
nodes.search: comparison compare contrast between alike unlike similar different relate

sections.title: Observations
items: A strawberry and an apple, both red.
A strawberry and a lemon, one red, one yellow.
Two notes played back to back, same or different pitch.

items.text: A comparison is observing sameness or variation between information.
items: "Observing" here is awareness (1.1.5) — a comparison is the awareness of sameness or variation between information.
Every observation above is a comparison: two reds alike, red and yellow different, two pitches the same or not.

items.title: No two pieces of information are ever observed as alike or different
items.detail: Without comparison, a strawberry and an apple are never 'both red.' A repeated sound is never 'the same note again.' Sameness and variation exist within patterns (1.2.1), but never between them. Pattern (1.2.3), identity (1.2.4), and every subsequent node that depends on relating one thing to another loses its ground.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Comparison" — the awareness of sameness or variation between information.
Also grounded: "compare," "contrast," "between" (in the relational sense), "alike," "unlike."
The next step: comparison has two possible outcomes — sameness (match, 1.2.3) and variation (mismatch, 1.2.4).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Information exists in isolated pieces with no way to relate them.
Sameness and variation are properties within patterns but never observed across pieces of information.
Relating information requires something beyond observing sameness or variation — an external rule or authority.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: What it means when compared information is the same — addressed by match (1.2.3).
What it means when compared information varies — addressed by mismatch (1.2.4).
How comparison relates to reasoning, inference, or abstract thought — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Comparison requires a subject — who is doing the comparing?

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Comparison seems to be an act performed by someone. Without a subject, there is no one to look at two pieces of information and notice sameness or variation.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Comparison is an act performed by a subject — it requires someone to hold two items side by side.
Without a subject, there is no agent to notice sameness or variation between two pieces of information.
Any account of comparison that omits the comparer is incomplete — the subject is a necessary condition, not an optional addition.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: This defines comparison as it shows up in experience — not as an act that requires a subject. The strawberry and the apple are both red — that sameness is present in awareness without a theory of who notices it. "Subject" is a later concept (1.3.7).

Commitment #2 (without a subject, there is no one to perform the comparison) applies equally to the objector's own activity. Raising an objection IS an act: the objector is comparing this node's claim to their own view and judging it deficient. If acts require actors, the objector needs an actor to perform this very comparison. But at this level, 'subject' hasn't been built yet — the objector is performing comparison without a subject, right now, in exactly the way they claim is impossible. The objection demonstrates what it denies.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Comparison is the occurrence of sameness or variation between information.
whether or not this requires a subject who compares is a legitimate question — but the vocabulary for 'subject' has not been built at this level (see 1.3.7). The question is deferred, not dismissed.

items.title: Comparison is a judgment, not an observation." (Empiricism)

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Noticing that two things are the same or different looks like something the mind *does* — a judgment, an inference — not something that passively occurs.
You compare the apple and the strawberry, conclude they share redness, and call that a match. The comparison is an act of judgment, not an observation.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: There is a layer of raw experience that contains no judgments — and comparison is a judgment applied to that raw layer, not part of it.
The sense-datum / raw-experience distinction is real and prior to comparison.
Noticing sameness requires cognitive effort beyond mere exposure.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 assumes a judgment-free layer of experience that comparison is applied *to*.

But if even the most basic experience already contains comparative structure — if you can't experience red and blue without some sense of their likeness — then there is no such layer. Two reds being alike is as immediately present as redness itself.
The distinction between comparison and inference is scope: comparison names what is present in awareness; inference (1.5.1) arrives at a new statement from existing ones.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Comparison is at the observation level, not the reasoning level. The cognitive processes that may underlie comparison are downstream questions about mechanism. Here, comparison names what shows up — not how it shows up.

nodes.claim: A match is sameness between compared information.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the outcome of comparison when sameness is found. Types and knowledge both depend on recognizing matches.
nodes.search: match fit agree correspond same common shared

sections.title: Observations
items: A strawberry's red and an apple's red — the same color.
A C note on a piano and a C note on a guitar — the same pitch.
The warmth of a fire and the warmth of sunlight — the same quality.

items.text: A match is sameness between compared information.
items: A "match" is when comparison finds sameness — the compared information shares a quality.
Every observation above is a match: the same color, the same pitch, the same warmth.

items.title: Sameness is observed but never constitutes a relationship between information
items.detail: Comparison finds sameness or variation, but without match there is no name for the sameness outcome. Sameness occurs within patterns, but nothing connects it across compared pieces of information.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Match" — sameness between compared information.
Also grounded: "fit," "agree," "correspond," "in common."
The next steps: types (1.2.5) group phenomena by matching features, and knowledge (1.2.6) compares answers against observations.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Sameness is observed but never constitutes a relationship between compared information.
Agreement or correspondence requires something beyond observed sameness — an external criterion or rule.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: What happens when matched information groups phenomena — addressed by types (1.2.5).
How matching relates to truth or verification — deferred to later nodes.
Where the boundary of sameness falls in ambiguous cases — a question of where to draw the line, not of whether or not matching occurs.

items.title: Perfect sameness never occurs — no two things are exactly the same.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: No two experiences are identical in every respect. A strawberry's red and an apple's red are never precisely the same shade. Strict sameness is an idealization that never actually obtains.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: True sameness requires identity in every respect — two things match only if they are identical.
If no two things are ever perfectly identical, then 'match' names an idealization, not an observation.
A definition of match that allows partial or approximate sameness is too loose to do real work.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Match does not require total identity between phenomena — it requires sameness in the compared respect. Two reds match in color even if the apple and strawberry differ in shape, taste, and size. Match is sameness between compared information, not sameness in every possible way.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Match is always relative to what is being compared. The concern about perfect sameness targets a claim this does not make. Two reds are a match in color; the same two things may mismatch (1.2.4) in other respects.

items.title: What counts as 'the same' is subjective — matching depends on the observer.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Cultural and individual differences in categorization mean that what one person calls "the same red," another might distinguish as different shades. If matching is observer-dependent, it has no objective basis.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: If observers disagree about where the boundary of sameness falls, sameness has no objective basis.
Observer-dependence in boundary placement means there is no fact of the matter.
Any observer-dependent element contaminates the entire concept.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 is the key assumption: the objector treats any observer-dependent aspect as disqualifying the whole concept.

But the disagreement is about *where the line falls*, not about *whether or not sameness exists*. Both positions agree that sameness, when observed, constitutes a match. This defines the relationship; it does not prescribe where the line falls.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Disagreements about specific matches are about where to draw the line — not about whether or not matching happens. This defines comparison as it shows up in experience, not as a claim about where all observers must agree.

nodes.claim: A mismatch is variation between compared information.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the outcome of comparison when variation is found. Distinction, conflict, contradiction, and error all build on this.
nodes.search: mismatch disagree conflict differ difference distinction unlike

sections.title: Observations
items: A strawberry's red and a lemon's yellow — different colors.
The sound of a drum and the sound of a flute — different timbres.
The taste of sugar and the taste of salt — different qualities.

items.text: A mismatch is variation between compared information.
items: A "mismatch" is when comparison finds variation — the compared information differs.
Every observation above is a mismatch: different colors, different timbres, different qualities.

items.title: Variation is observed but never constitutes a relationship between information
items.detail: Comparison finds variation, but without mismatch there is no name for the variation outcome. Variation occurs within patterns, but nothing connects it across compared pieces of information.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Mismatch" — variation between compared information.
Also grounded: "disagree," "conflict" (in the informational sense), "differ" (between compared pieces).
Together with match (1.2.3), comparison now has both possible outcomes named. The next steps — types (1.2.5) and knowledge (1.2.6) — build on both.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Variation is observed but never constitutes a relationship between compared information.
Disagreement or conflict requires something beyond observed variation — an external rule or judgment.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: How mismatch relates to contradiction — deferred to (1.4.3).
How mismatch relates to error or falsity — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Everything always varies — mismatch is trivially universal and match is the real problem.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Nothing is ever truly the same — everything is in flux.
If all things always differ, mismatch is trivially universal. Match, not mismatch, is the phenomenon that needs explaining.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: If variation is universal — everything always differs from everything else — then mismatch is trivially true and carries no information.
Match, not mismatch, is the phenomenon that requires explanation, since it is the exception rather than the rule.
A concept that applies to everything equally cannot serve as a meaningful distinction.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 confuses the *default status* of a phenomenon with its *triviality*. The Heraclitean's own worldview depends on variation being real, important, and worth naming: 'everything is in flux' is precisely a name for universal variation. If naming a universal phenomenon is trivial, the Heraclitean's own doctrine is trivially named. But the Heraclitean clearly thinks their naming adds something — it identifies what they see as the fundamental character of reality. This node does the same: it identifies mismatch as always available in experience. The Heraclitean and the node agree on the phenomenon; they disagree only about whether or not naming it at this granularity is worthwhile — and the Heraclitean has already conceded that naming universal phenomena IS worthwhile by naming one themselves.

Commitment #3 (universal applicability = vacuity) also proves too much. Breathing is always happening; that doesn't make it trivial to biology. Gravity is always operative; that doesn't make it trivial to physics. The question is not whether or not mismatch is universal, but whether or not the node accurately describes what it is. Universality doesn't answer that question.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Mismatch being universally available is a feature, not a defect — and the Heraclitean's own worldview depends on it being so. The node names what the Heraclitean also names: universal variation.
The disagreement is about granularity, not about whether or not the phenomenon is real.

nodes.claim: Phenomena are associated in distinct "types".
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the experience that phenomena don't just occur — they occur in recognizably different ways. Wanting, sensing, remembering, imagining, and relating are not just different contents but different kinds of occurrence. Without types, all phenomena are the same kind of thing.
nodes.search: types kinds categories phenomenological willful temporal physical emotional mental relational intensity classification associated distinct

sections.title: Observations
items: Wanting something and seeing something feel different — not just in content but in kind. The wanting has directedness; the seeing does not.
Remembering a taste and imagining a taste are recognizably different — even when the content is the same.
A sensation and an emotion about that sensation are distinguishable — the pain is one thing, the frustration about it another.
Noticing that clouds tend to bring rain feels different from noticing the color of the clouds — one is about a relationship between phenomena, the other about a quality within one.

items.text: Phenomena are associated in distinct "types".
items: A "type" (1.2.5.8) is a recognized grouping of phenomena that share a fundamental feature — a way of occurring that distinguishes them from other phenomena. Wanting, sensing, remembering, imagining, and relating are not just different contents but different types of occurrence.

The types grounded across this section's seven branches: willful phenomena (1.2.5.1) — wanting, direction, success, failure, endorsement, resistance, desire, will. Intensities (1.2.5.2) — degree, sensation, perception, satisfaction, frustration. Temporal phenomena (1.2.5.3) — present, sequence, past, memory, recognition, novelty, step, change, event. Physical phenomena (1.2.5.4) — location, extension, arrangement. Emotional phenomena (1.2.5.5) — unified wanting-sensation experiences. Mental phenomena (1.2.5.6) — imagination, visualization, thought, possibility, future. Relational phenomena (1.2.5.7) — correlation, expectation, hope, independence, consistency, fundamental, superficial, cause, effect.

items.title: All phenomena are the same kind of thing
items.detail: Without types, phenomena are a flat, undifferentiated stream. Wanting and sensing, remembering and imagining, relating and occurring — all have the same standing. The entire structure of experience collapses into a single category with no internal distinctions.

children.title: No distinction between wanting and sensing
children.detail: Without willful and intensity types, the directedness of a want and the intensity of a sensation are indistinguishable. Hunger-as-desire and hunger-as-stomach-sensation are the same thing. Agency, satisfaction, and frustration all lose their basis.

children.title: No distinction between experiencing and constructing
children.detail: Without temporal and mental types, perceiving something present and imagining something absent are the same kind of occurrence. Memory, thought, possibility, and the future all collapse into undifferentiated occurrence.

children.title: No distinction between content and connection
children.detail: Without relational types, the qualities of phenomena and the structures between them have the same standing. That honey is sweet and that clouds tend to bring rain are the same kind of observation. Correlation, independence, cause, and effect cannot be recognized as distinct from the phenomena they relate.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The full phenomenological type vocabulary built across this section's eight children.
items: Willful (1.2.5.1): wanting, direction, success, failure, outcome, endorse, resist, desire, will.
Intensity (1.2.5.2): intensity, sensation, perception, satisfaction, frustration.
Temporal (1.2.5.3): present, sequence, past, memory, recognition, new, step, change, event.
Physical (1.2.5.4): physical, location, extension, arrangement.
Emotional (1.2.5.5): emotion, angry, joyful, afraid, sad, excited.
Mental (1.2.5.6): imagination, visualization, thought, possibility, future.
Relational (1.2.5.7): correlation, expectation, hope, independence, consistency, fundamental, superficial, cause, effect.
Type (1.2.5.8): type, kind, category, class, sort.
With phenomenological types established, the epistemological grounding (1.2) can build on the full vocabulary of how phenomena occur.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: All phenomena are the same kind of thing — there is no recognizable difference in how wanting, sensing, remembering, imagining, and relating occur.
Types are imposed by theory, not recognized in experience — grouping phenomena into kinds requires a framework external to experience itself.
Types are arbitrary — any grouping is equally valid, and the divisions drawn here have no experiential basis.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not these seven types exhaust all phenomenological types — other types may exist beyond those grounded here.
Whether or not types have sharp boundaries or overlap — a phenomenon might belong to more than one type. The boundary between types is not fully addressed.
Whether or not phenomenological types correspond to real divisions in what exists — the ontological status of types is deferred to later analysis (1.3).

items.title: These types are culturally learned categories, not features of experience itself.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Different cultures carve up experience differently. Some languages have no word for "emotion" as distinct from "sensation." Some philosophical traditions deny the wanting-sensing distinction entirely. If the types were genuinely in experience, everyone would recognize them. The fact that they vary by culture suggests they are learned categories imposed on a more basic, undifferentiated flow.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Cultural variation in how experience is categorized shows that types are learned, not experienced.
2. If types were features of experience itself, they would be universally recognized in the same way.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 confuses labeling with recognizing. Different cultures may label the types differently or draw the boundaries in different places — but the observations do not depend on labels. Wanting something and seeing something feel different in kind. Remembering a taste and imagining a taste are recognizably different. These distinctions are available before any cultural framework names them.

Cultural variation in *labeling* types is consistent with the types being experientially present. The same variation exists for color — different languages carve up the color spectrum differently, but this does not show that colors are culturally constructed rather than experienced.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Cultural variation in labeling does not show that types are absent from experience. The experiential distinctions — wanting versus sensing, remembering versus imagining — are available before any framework names them. Different cultures may label them differently, just as different languages divide the color spectrum differently without color being culturally constructed.

items.title: Experience is a unified stream — dividing it into types is artificial.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Experience does not arrive pre-sorted. Eating a meal involves sensation, wanting, emotion, memory, anticipation, and spatial awareness all at once — a single unified experience. Dividing this into seven types is an analytical exercise that fragments what is actually whole. The stream-of-consciousness tradition and phenomenologists like James emphasize that experience is continuous, not categorized.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Experience is fundamentally unified and continuous, not divided into types.
2. Dividing experience into types fragments something that is whole and distorts its character.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 confuses co-occurrence with indistinguishability. Eating a meal involves wanting, sensing, remembering, and anticipating all at once — but each is recognizably different from the others within that unified experience. The wanting is not the sensing. The memory is not the anticipation. They co-occur without being the same.

Types do not require experience to arrive pre-sorted. They name distinctions within the stream — distinctions the observations make concrete. A unified experience can have recognizably different aspects without those aspects being artificially imposed.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Types name recognizable distinctions within a unified experience, not fragments imposed on it. Wanting and sensing co-occur during a meal — but the wanting is recognizably different from the sensing. Co-occurrence does not mean indistinguishability.

nodes.claim: Questions result in knowledge or ignorance.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the entire structure of inquiry — from the initial want for information through to the states that result and the transitions between them.
nodes.search: questions knowledge ignorance inquiry answers learning forgetting epistemology knowing

sections.title: Observations
items: Seeking and finding — a pull toward information, then the information arrives, and the pull subsides.
Seeking and not finding — the same pull, but no information arrives, and the pull persists.
What was once unknown becomes known — the shift is felt, not merely logical.
What was once known becomes unavailable — the shift back is equally felt.
Every case of seeking information ends in one of two states: the information occurs, or it does not.

items.text: Questions result in knowledge or ignorance.
items: A "question" is a want for specific information (1.2.6.1). An "answer" is the occurrence of that information (1.2.6.2). When an answer occurs, the result is "knowledge" (1.2.6.3). When it does not, the result is "ignorance" (1.2.6.4).
These states are not permanent. "Learning" is the change from ignorance to knowledge (1.2.6.5). "Forgetting" is the change from knowledge to ignorance (1.2.6.6).
Together, these ground the complete structure of inquiry: a want directed at information, its possible outcomes, and the transitions between them.

items.title: No structure of inquiry — and no basis for distinguishing what is known from what is not
items.detail: Without recognizing that questions result in knowledge or ignorance, the entire experience of seeking information collapses into undifferentiated wanting. There is no distinction between having an answer and still looking for one, no difference between knowing and not knowing, and no basis for describing how knowledge is gained or lost. The epistemological grounding — that information can be "known" — has no foundation.

children.title: Reasoning has no starting point
children.detail: Reasoning (1.5) evaluates whether or not statements are true. But evaluating a statement requires recognizing what is known and what is not — which requires the question-knowledge-ignorance structure. Without it, reasoning has nothing to work with.

children.title: Truth and falsehood cannot be distinguished
children.detail: The sieve's governing claim — that some things are true and some are false — requires the capacity to know which is which. Without knowledge and ignorance as grounded states, "knowing which is which" has no experiential meaning.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The complete vocabulary of inquiry.
items: "Question" — a want for specific information (1.2.6.1). Synonyms: inquiry, wondering.
"Answer" — the occurrence of a question's wanted information (1.2.6.2). Synonyms: response, finding.
"Knowledge" — when an answer occurs (1.2.6.3). Synonyms: knowing.
"Ignorance" — when an answer does not occur (1.2.6.4). Synonyms: not knowing, unknowing.
"Learning" — the change from ignorance to knowledge (1.2.6.5). Synonyms: discovering, finding out.
"Forgetting" — the change from knowledge to ignorance (1.2.6.6). Synonyms: losing knowledge.
Also grounded: "ask," "seek," "found," "known," "unknown," "understand," "discover," "realize," "forgotten."
The next step: recognizing that a class extends beyond what has been asked about — that "all" includes instances in both knowledge and ignorance (1.2.7).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Wanting information and wanting anything else are structurally identical — there is no distinct kind of want that targets information.
Questions can never be met — the concept of an answer has no experiential ground.
Having an answer and not having one are the same state — knowing and not knowing are indistinguishable.
Knowledge, once acquired, cannot be lost — or, conversely, knowledge that was never held cannot be gained.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not answers correspond to what is actually the case — the distinction between correct and incorrect knowledge requires ontological vocabulary not yet built (1.3).
What methods reliably produce learning — requires the vocabulary of reasoning (1.5).
Whether or not ignorance extends beyond questions actually asked — the scope of "all" within a class is addressed next (1.2.7).
Whether or not knowledge requires justification in addition to having an answer — requires later vocabulary (1.5).

items.title: Knowledge and ignorance aren't binary — real epistemic states include degrees of confidence, partial understanding, and uncertainty.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Real knowing is rarely all-or-nothing. A name half-remembered, a route partially known, a concept grasped in outline but not in detail — these are neither full knowledge nor full ignorance.
A binary framework that admits only "answer occurred" or "answer did not occur" cannot capture the epistemic states people actually experience.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Epistemic states are continuous, not binary — they range from complete ignorance through degrees of confidence to full knowledge.
The binary framework forces partial states into one category or the other, losing information about the real state.
Any adequate epistemology must represent degrees of knowledge at the foundational level.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 describes something real: partial knowledge exists. But consider what "partially knowing a route" involves. Some questions about the route have been answered (the first three turns), and others have not (what comes after the bridge). The partial state is not a third category between knowledge and ignorance — it is knowledge about some questions and ignorance about others.

The apparent continuity arises because complex situations involve many questions, each of which is individually in one state or the other. A name "on the tip of the tongue" is a case where some features of the answer have occurred (its length, its first sound) while others have not (the full name). Each sub-question is individually resolved or not.

Commitment #3 asks the framework to represent degrees at the foundational level. But degrees of confidence require additional vocabulary — comparison between how well an answer matches what is wanted — that builds on this foundation rather than replacing it.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Partial knowledge is real, but it is not a third state between knowledge and ignorance. It is the coexistence of knowledge about some questions and ignorance about others within the same topic. The binary applies to each question individually; apparent gradation arises from the multiplicity of questions involved.

items.title: This makes knowledge entirely dependent on wanting — but facts are facts whether or not anyone asks about them.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The structure ties knowledge to questions, and questions to wanting. But the boiling point of water is 100°C whether or not anyone wants to know. Knowledge should describe a relationship between a person and a fact, not between a person and their wants.
Making knowledge want-dependent turns epistemology into psychology — it's about what people happen to seek, not about what is true.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Facts exist independently of anyone wanting to know them — their status as knowledge does not depend on a question being asked.
The framework confuses the *process* of coming to know (which involves wanting) with the *state* of knowledge (which does not).
An adequate definition of knowledge must be independent of wanting.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 raises a real distinction — between what is the case and what is known. But this distinction belongs to the ontological grounding (1.3), which separates what occurs from what exists independently. At this level, the question is experiential: what does it mean to *have* knowledge, not what makes something *true*.

Commitment #2 claims the state of knowledge is independent of wanting. But consider: in what sense does someone "know" something they have never encountered, never asked about, and have no awareness of? The boiling point of water is what it is regardless of wanting — but *knowing* the boiling point requires that the information be present. The information's presence is the answer; the wanting was the question that made its arrival recognizable as knowledge rather than mere occurrence.

Commitment #3 wants knowledge detached from wanting entirely. But even the objector's preferred framework (facts independent of wanting) requires that a person *have* the fact — which is what this definition identifies. The independence of facts from wanting is about truth, not about knowledge. Truth is addressed later (1.3).

subSections.label: Correction
items: This defines knowledge as the experiential state of having an answer — which requires a question. Whether or not the information that constitutes the answer is true independently of wanting is a question about truth and reality, not about knowledge. The distinction between what is known and what is true requires ontological vocabulary addressed at (1.3).

nodes.claim: Definitions have context and meaning.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds what a definition is, what context and meaning are, and how general claims extend beyond what is known.
nodes.search: all every universal scope boundary meaning meaningful class instances known unknown generalization totality open closed possible

sections.title: Observations
items: "All colors of the rainbow" — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. A scope where additional members are not possible.
"All colors" — a scope where additional unknown members are possible, since a never-seen color is imaginable.
A blade cutting flesh — different meaning in a surgery, different meaning in an assault. The scope determines the significance.
"All past events" — a scope where most members are unknown, with each accounted for including those with no memory of them.

items.text: Definitions have context and meaning.
items: A "scope" is the membership of a class (1.2.7.1). A "boundary" is the difference between what is in a scope and what is not (1.2.7.2). Information is "meaningful" when it belongs to a scope (1.2.7.3). A "definition" is the identifiable features of a boundary (1.2.7.7).
"All" is each member of a scope (1.2.7.4). A scope is "open" when additional unknown members are possible (1.2.7.5). A scope is "closed" when additional members are not possible (1.2.7.6).
"All" applies to both open and closed scopes. For a closed scope, "all" is the known membership. For an open scope, "all" includes members in ignorance.

items.title: General claims collapse to reports about what has been encountered
items.detail: Without scope, boundary, and completeness, "all birds have feathers" becomes "every bird encountered so far has feathers" — with no extension beyond current knowledge. Every generalization is a summary of past experience. And without meaning, the same phenomenon in different contexts has no recognized difference in significance.

children.title: Patterns become unreliable beyond the observed
children.detail: A pattern (1.2.1.6) identified across known instances has no bearing on unknown instances. The sameness observed so far says nothing about what has not yet been observed — making every pattern provisional in a way that prevents it from grounding further reasoning.

children.title: Knowledge has no structure for what remains to be learned
children.detail: Learning (1.2.6.5) fills in specific answers, but without a scope that includes what is unknown, there is no framework for recognizing what remains to be learned.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The complete scope and quantifier vocabulary built across this section's six children.
items: "Scope" / "domain" / "range" (1.2.7.1). "Boundary" / "border" / "criterion" (1.2.7.2). "Meaning" / "meaningful" / "significance" / "context" (1.2.7.3). "Definition" / "define" / "defined as" (1.2.7.7).
"All" / "every" / "each" / "none" / "some" / "rest" / "complete" (1.2.7.4). "Open" (1.2.7.5). "Closed" (1.2.7.6).
General claims — "all birds," "every color" — now have grounded scope, including what has not been encountered.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: "All" means only "all that have been encountered" — general claims have no scope beyond past experience.
A class has no instances beyond those already known — the class is identical to its known members.
Phenomena have fixed significance regardless of context — meaning does not change with scope.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not claims about "all" are justified — the reliability of generalizations requires reasoning vocabulary (1.5).
Whether or not an open scope's unknown members share the same patterns as its known members — the problem of induction, deferred.
How the relevant scope is selected when a phenomenon belongs to multiple scopes — deferred.

items.title: Scope and boundary are redundant with class — adding new terms does no additional work.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: A class (1.2.1.9) already identifies a shared quality among patterns. "Scope" and "boundary" are just different angles on the same concept. The additional labels do no new work.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: A class already refers to everything that has the shared quality.
"Scope" and "boundary" add no information beyond what "class" already provides.
The additional labels are unnecessary.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 conflates three distinct recognitions. A class identifies that patterns share a quality — "redness, blueness, greenness are alike." A scope identifies what has that shared quality — "what belongs to 'color.'" A boundary identifies what distinguishes members from non-members — "what makes redness a color and loudness not." These are similarity, membership, and criterion — each independently observable.

subSections.label: Correction
items: A class identifies a shared quality among patterns. A scope identifies what has that shared quality — the membership. A boundary identifies what distinguishes members from non-members — the criterion. The three concepts are related but distinct: grouping, membership, and criterion.

items.title: Including unknown instances in "all" smuggles in a metaphysical claim about unobserved entities.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Saying "all birds includes birds never seen" presupposes that unseen birds exist. But existence claims about unobserved entities go beyond phenomenological description — they require ontological commitments not yet established (1.3).

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Referring to unknown members requires the ontological claim that they exist.
Ontological claims about what exists independently of experience belong to (1.3).
Without the ontological claim, "all" means only "all experienced instances."

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 reads the node as claiming that unknown members *exist independently*. But an open scope (1.2.7.5) is one where additional unknown members are possible — the thought of an unseen bird matches recognized patterns. This is epistemological: the scope has room for members not yet encountered. Whether or not those members exist independently is ontological (1.3) — not addressed here, neither endorsed nor denied.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This is an epistemological claim, not an ontological one. "All" of an open scope includes members not yet encountered because additional unknown members are possible — the boundary does not rule them out. Whether or not unknown members exist independently of experience is an ontological question (1.3) — not addressed here, neither endorsed nor denied.

nodes.claim: Phenomena occur independently from want — a limit.
nodes.soWhat: Names the general phenomenon and its category: across outcomes, sensations, and thought, what occurs is not given by wanting. This is what a "limit" names — the foundation for reality as something other than want, and for the concepts (nature, structure) that build on it.
nodes.search: limit independent want phenomena correlate reality encounter

sections.title: Observations
items: A weight in the hand, unchanged by wanting it lighter.
Rain continuing outside, regardless of wanting it to stop.
A memory surfacing unbidden, without having been wanted.
A standing tree, unchanged by wanting it fallen.

items.text: Phenomena occur independently from want — a limit.
items: Outcomes (1.3.1.1), sensations (1.3.1.2), and what is thought about or imagined (1.3.1.3) all fail to correlate (1.2.5.7.1) with want (1.2.5.1.1). Across domains, what occurs does not track what is wanted.

A "limit" (1.3.1.4) is the label for what is independent from want — any phenomenon, or any feature of a phenomenon, whose occurrence is not given by wanting. The weight of what is held, the continuing rain, the unbidden memory, the standing tree — all limits.

Limit is not a property located in things. It names a relationship between two observed occurrences — the want, and the phenomenon — that do not correlate. Resistance is one shape this takes; independence is the more general phenomenon.

items.title: There is no category of what is not given by wanting — everything encountered is an extension of will.
items.detail: Without recognizing that phenomena occur independently from want, outcomes, sensations, and what is thought about all collapse into wanting itself. Every failure becomes a failure of wanting; every sensation becomes something wanted; every occurrence becomes something thought into being. Reality as something other than preference — as what is encountered rather than willed — has no foothold, and the concepts that depend on a limit (nature, structure, what is real as distinct from what is wanted) lose their unit.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this branch.
items: "Limit" (1.3.1.4) — what is independent from want.
Also grounded: "constraint," "boundary" (in the sense of what does not yield to want), "against" (in the sense of independence from want, not active opposition).
The next steps: the features that make up a limit (nature, 1.3.2), and how limits group together into wholes (structure, 1.3.3).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Phenomena correlate with want — that wanting is what brings outcomes, sensations, and occurrences into being.
What is encountered is an extension of wanting — that there is no category of what is independent of want.
Limit is a property located in objects rather than a relationship between want and phenomenon.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not limits have an underlying source — external substance, law, brute fact — is not addressed here. This names the phenomenon of independence from want, not its metaphysical ground.
Whether or not a want can itself be a limit to another want is not addressed here — the claim names the relationship between want and phenomenon at this level; the reflexive case awaits later nodes.

Whether or not what is currently encountered as a limit can shift through practice, technique, or knowledge is not addressed — the claim names the structure of encounter, not a prediction about any specific limit's permanence.

items.title: Volition shows that phenomena DO correlate with want — willed movements, willed speech, willed attention all track wanting closely.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Ordinary action refutes the claim. Wanting to raise an arm, speak a word, walk across a room — all regularly succeed. Wanting to attend to the feet brings those sensations forward. Wanting to think about a topic brings thoughts about that topic. Volition is the clear case of want tracking what occurs, and it is pervasive in daily experience.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Volitional cases show wants whose outcomes, sensations, or thoughts regularly coincide with the wanting.
2. If any broad class of phenomena coincides with want, phenomena do not occur independently from want.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 conflates two patterns. Cause (1.2.5.7.8) was already grounded earlier as a want whose direction correlates with an event — a specific recognized sub-pattern. The general claim here is broader: across all domains, wanting on its own does not bring about what is wanted.

Even in volitional cases, what occurs proceeds by way of limits not given by wanting. The arm moves only as the arm can move — according to its weight, its joints, its attachment. Attention shifts only among sensations already present. Thought-content that tracks willing does so because willing adds to bare thought the cause-pattern from (1.2.5.7.8). The observations show the broader field: a held weight is not lightened by wanting, rain is not stopped by wanting, memories surface without being wanted, trees stand unchanged.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the broader pattern — phenomena in general occur independently from want. Whether or not specific narrower sub-patterns (cause at 1.2.5.7.8, volition at 1.2.5.1.8) show recognized correlations is a separate phenomenon established elsewhere. Those cases hold only where what is independent of want already permits, and their scope is a small band within the wider field.

items.title: Calling this "independence from want" smuggles mentality into inanimate phenomena — walls and trees have no relationship to wanting at all.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Walls, weights, trees, and rain have no mental states. Saying they are "independent from want" makes them sound as though they stand in some relation to wanting — registering it, resisting it, or indifferent to it. Independence is a relational term, and relations require both sides to be the kind of thing that can relate. Applying it to objects imports mentality into them.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Inanimate phenomena (walls, weights, rain, trees) have no mental states.
2. Saying a phenomenon is "independent from want" attributes a relation-to-want to the phenomenon itself.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 misreads where the independence sits. The claim does not place wanting into the wall or the tree. It names two observed occurrences — a want (wanting the tree to fall) and a phenomenon (the tree standing) — and says they do not correlate (1.2.5.7.1).

The independence is a feature of the encounter between two observed occurrences, not a property inside either one. The observations make this visible: wanting a held weight lighter and the weight being what it is are two separate occurrences. Nothing is being attributed to the weight itself.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names a relationship between observed occurrences, not a property of things. Whether or not any phenomenon has intrinsic mental qualities is not addressed here — the claim only tracks the non-correlation between want and what occurs. The label "limit" belongs to the phenomenon as encountered, not to any attributed inner state.

items.title: Reality does conform to want — manifestation, placebo, strong belief, and self-fulfilling expectation all show want shaping what occurs.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Long traditions and well-studied effects claim that want, belief, or intention shape what occurs. Placebo reduces felt pain. Expectation shapes perception. Manifestation practices report tangible shifts. Across many accounts, reality does track wanting. The claim that phenomena occur independently from want denies this body of evidence.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. There are documented cases where wanting, believing, or expecting produces shifts in what occurs (placebo, psychosomatic effects, expectation-shaped perception).
2. If wanting ever shifts what occurs, phenomena do not in general occur independently of want.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 uses "correlate" too broadly. Correlation (1.2.5.7.1) names a recognized, recurring pattern — one event often following another. Scattered, context-bound, frequently-failing effects are not the recognizable pattern the broad claim addresses.

Placebo and similar effects are narrow, scaffolded, and fragile. Across the full field — held weights, rain, unbidden memories, standing trees — wanting is not what reliably brings phenomena about. Even where specific shifts occur, they proceed within much larger webs of what is not given by want (bodily chemistry, environment, prior states). Those webs themselves are limits.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the broad pattern. Whether or not narrower sub-patterns (placebo, expectation effects, specific practices) show local correlations in constrained domains is a separate question, already left open in the child nodes. Those effects occur within a wider field of independence, not outside it. The broader pattern — phenomena occur independently from want — holds across the full range of what is encountered.

nodes.claim: Nature is the set of features for a limit.
nodes.soWhat: Names the feature-set that makes a limit the limit it is. Lets any limit be referred to by its collected features — "the nature of water," "the nature of an arm's movement" — without listing them one by one.
nodes.search: nature features limit set properties characteristics

sections.title: Observations
items: A held stone: heavy, cold, rough, dense.
A heard bell: ringing, sustained, pitched, decaying.
A lifted arm: weighted, jointed, reaching, muscular.
A standing tree: rooted, branching, swaying, rough-barked.

items.text: Nature is the set of features for a limit.
items: A "nature" is the collected features (1.2.5.3.1) of a limit (1.3.1.4). The stone's nature is the set {heavy, cold, rough, dense}; the bell's nature is {ringing, sustained, pitched, decaying}. The features that belong together as the limit's own make up its nature.

"The nature of X" refers to X's feature-set as a single thing — useful when all the features are operating together and pulling them apart misses the point. A stone's weight, its coldness, and its roughness are not separately what makes encountering the stone what it is; the bundle is.

items.title: Limits have no collected identity — each feature stands alone.
items.detail: Without recognizing nature, a limit's features can only be listed one by one, with no way to refer to them as belonging together. The stone is heavy, the stone is cold, the stone is rough — but there is no phrase for the stone's feature-set as a single thing. Limits lose the coherence of being recognizable wholes, and the concept of a structure built from limits (1.3.3), or of the way limits pattern themselves, has no unit to work with.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Nature" — the set of features for a limit. The stone's nature is {heavy, cold, rough, dense}; the arm's nature is {weighted, jointed, reaching, muscular}.
Also grounded: "character," "makeup," "what it is like" (in the sense of a limit's collected features).
The next step: how limits group together into larger wholes (structure, 1.3.3).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: A limit is nothing more than any single feature — that each feature stands for the whole.
Features belong to no particular limit — that any feature can be reassigned to any limit without remainder.
Nature is something hidden behind features rather than the features themselves collected.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not a limit's nature is fixed or can change over time is not addressed here — the claim names the feature-set at the level of encounter, not its permanence.
Whether or not two limits can share the same nature is not addressed here — the claim names what a nature is, not how natures compare across limits.

Whether or not there is an essence behind or beneath a limit's features is not addressed here — the claim identifies nature with the feature-set as encountered, and does not speak to deeper metaphysical structure.

items.title: A limit must have some essence beyond its features — otherwise a stone losing one feature would become a different limit entirely.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: A stone that warms up is still the stone. A bell that stops ringing is still the bell. If nature were identical to the feature-set, changing any feature would change the limit — which contradicts how limits are ordinarily encountered. There must be something that makes the stone the stone apart from its current features.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. A limit can undergo feature-change while remaining the same limit (warmed stone, silenced bell).
2. If a limit persists through feature-change, nature cannot be identical to the current feature-set — some underlying essence must ground the identity.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 introduces a question about persistence through change that this claim does not try to answer. Nature here names the set of features for a limit as encountered — what makes the stone presently encounterable as the stone it is.

Whether or not there is continuity across changes, or what grounds such continuity, is a further question — it depends on concepts (identity, persistence, essence) that are not yet grounded. The observations show what is available now: a held stone presents as heavy, cold, rough, dense; that set is its nature as encountered.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the collected features of a limit as encountered. Whether or not an essence stands behind those features, or what preserves identity across feature-change, is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. The observations show the feature-sets that are recognizable now; the metaphysics of persistence awaits vocabulary not yet built.

items.title: Calling this a "set of features" treats distinct feelings as though they were list items — reducing lived limits to arithmetic.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: A held stone is not experienced as a list. Its heaviness, coldness, and roughness blend into a single encountered thing. Saying nature is a "set" imposes a discrete, list-like structure on what is lived as unified and continuous. The label falsifies the phenomenon by formalizing it.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. A limit is encountered as a unified whole, not as a list of items.
2. A "set of features" imposes list-structure where none is actually encountered.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 conflates how something is encountered with how it can be referred to. A held stone does present as a unified encounter — that is exactly the point of having a label for the whole feature-set as one thing.

The features are already grounded (1.2.5.3.1) as distinct pieces of information. Recognizing them as belonging together — as the stone's nature — does not pull them apart; it gives the unified encounter a name. The observations make this visible: {heavy, cold, rough, dense} is how the held stone is describable when features are named; the nature is that bundle held together.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names a feature-bundle as a single referable thing. Whether or not the features are experienced as discrete or continuous is a separate question about how features are encountered — already addressed where features themselves were grounded. The label operates at the level of the bundle, not the granularity of the experience.

items.title: Different observers notice different features, so a limit has no single nature — nature is just the observer's description.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: A geologist and a child hold the same stone and note different features. A musician and a passerby hear different features in the same bell. If the feature-set varies with who is encountering the limit, then nature is not a property of the limit — it is a description the observer makes. The label treats description as though it were structure.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Different observers notice different features of the same limit.
2. If the feature-set varies with the observer, the feature-set is observer-dependent rather than a feature of the limit itself.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 extrapolates from variation in what is noticed to variation in what is there. Noticing is a narrower phenomenon than encountering. Two observers notice different features of the same held stone, but neither finds features they wanted to find and that were not there — the stone's heaviness is encountered whether or not it is noted, its coldness whether or not it is commented on.

Because each limit is independent of want (1.3.1), the features encountered are not given by who is looking. Which features get picked out in a given description may vary; the feature-set that is there to be picked out does not vary with the wanting.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the feature-set of a limit as what is encountered, independent of want. Whether or not different observers' descriptions pick out overlapping or disjoint subsets of features is a separate question about noticing and attention. The nature is what is there to be encountered, not what any particular description captures.

nodes.claim: A structure is a set of limits.
nodes.soWhat: Names what is encountered when multiple limits belong together as one thing — a maze, a body, a room. Lets any such whole be referred to as a collected set of limits without enumerating them, and opens the way to talking about how reality is built from more than single limits.
nodes.search: structure set limits composition whole arrangement system

sections.title: Observations
items: A room: walls, floor, ceiling, door, window.
A tree: trunk, branches, leaves, roots, bark.
A hand: palm, fingers, knuckles, nails, skin.
A maze: walls, passages, corners, dead ends.

items.text: A structure is a set of limits.
items: A "structure" is the collected limits (1.3.1.4) that belong together as one encountered thing. The room is the set {walls, floor, ceiling, door, window}; the hand is the set {palm, fingers, knuckles, nails, skin}. Each item in the set is itself a limit; the structure is their belonging-together as a referable whole.

"The structure of X" refers to the limit-set that makes up X — useful when the whole is what is being encountered, not any single limit on its own. A hand is not a finger, or a palm, or a knuckle; it is all of those as one thing.

items.title: Nothing can be encountered beyond single limits.
items.detail: Without recognizing structure, there is no category for the room as a room, the tree as a tree, the hand as a hand. Each limit stands alone — the wall, the floor, the ceiling — with no phrase for their belonging-together. Every encounter with a world made of multiple limits at once loses its name, and the concepts that depend on collected limits (bodies, environments, the ordered wholes that make up reality) have no unit to work with.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Structure" — a set of limits. The room, the tree, the hand, the maze — each a structure made from its limits.
Also grounded: "composition," "system," "network," "build," "whole" (in the sense of a set of limits encountered together).
The next step: how natures and structures combine — a structure with nature becomes an object, and the concepts that follow from reality's being built from ordered sets of limits.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Only single limits exist — that nothing is ever encountered as more than one limit at a time.
Structures are only words — that collected limits have no encountered unity beyond being named together.
A structure is something other than its limits — a further entity added alongside them.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not a structure's limits are arranged in any specific way — spatial, causal, hierarchical — is not addressed here. The claim names the collected set; arrangement and internal relations await vocabulary not yet built.
Whether or not a structure can lose or gain limits and remain the same structure is not addressed here — the claim names the set at the level of encounter, not its persistence.

Whether or not there is a principled boundary between a structure and its surroundings — what counts as belonging to the set — is not addressed here. The claim points at encountered wholes; the criterion for membership is a further question.

items.title: A pile of bricks is a set of limits too, but it is not a structure — this definition collapses heaps into structures.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: A heap of sand, a scatter of loose stones, a random assortment of objects on a table — each is a set of limits, yet none is what is ordinarily called a structure. A structure has arrangement, connection, organization. Defining structure as any set of limits loses the distinction between a house and the pile of bricks it could be made from.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Everyday usage reserves "structure" for arrangements, not heaps.
2. A definition that counts unorganized limit-sets as structures is too broad — it misses what distinguishes structure from mere collection.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 asks for arrangement-level distinctions that require vocabulary not yet built. Arrangement, organization, and connection between limits are further concepts — they depend on how limits relate inside a set, which is a later question.

What is available at this level is the bare phenomenon: multiple limits encountered as belonging together. The observations show clear cases — room, tree, hand, maze — where this belonging is immediate. Whether the set is a pile of bricks or a wall built from them, both count as sets of limits. The finer distinction between arranged and unarranged sets awaits concepts that come after.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the bare phenomenon of limits-belonging-together as a set. Whether or not further distinctions (arranged vs. heaped, organized vs. loose) carve structures into sub-kinds is a separate question that depends on vocabulary not yet available. The broad label stands as the foundation that those later distinctions will build on.

items.title: There are no structures — only limits. Saying a set of limits is itself a thing adds a fictional entity alongside the real ones.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The hand is real. The palm, fingers, knuckles are real. But "the hand" as something beyond those limits is a name for a collection, not a further entity. Claiming the set exists in addition to its members double-counts. What is encountered is the limits; "structure" adds nothing real.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. The limits that make up a purported structure are what is genuinely encountered.
2. Treating the set of those limits as itself a thing posits an entity beyond what is encountered.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 misreads what the label adds. The claim does not posit a structure as an additional limit alongside the ones in the set. It names the belonging-together of the limits as a referable thing — the same limits, grouped, with a name.

The observations make this visible: a hand is encountered as one thing, not as five separate encounters of fingers and a palm. A room is entered, not assembled from the walls one at a time. The unity is in the encounter, not a new entity added beside the limits. The label names that unity so it can be referred to.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the belonging-together of limits, not a further entity. Whether or not any metaphysical weight attaches to the set beyond its members is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. The label tracks what is already present in encountering limits as groups.

items.title: What counts as belonging to a structure is arbitrary — observers choose which limits to group, so structure is just a way of talking, not a feature of reality.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Where does a tree end — at its outermost leaves, at its dripline, at its root-tips? Is the door part of the room or part of the hallway? Every purported structure has fuzzy edges, and where the set cuts off depends on the observer. If membership in the set is not given by the limits themselves, structure is imposed, not encountered.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. The boundary of any purported structure admits observer-dependent variation.
2. If what belongs to the set is observer-dependent, the set itself is not a feature of what is encountered — only a way of talking about it.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 extrapolates from unclear cases at the edges to the entire claim. Many encounters present no such fuzziness: a hand is encountered as a hand, a room as a room, without the boundary being chosen. The observations show immediate cases where the belonging-together is given, not imposed.

Because each limit is independent of want (1.3.1), so is the collection of limits that is encountered as belonging together. Where precisely the boundary sits may be a further question in some cases, but the encounter of limits-as-one-thing is not produced by wanting. A tree is encountered as a tree whether or not its exact edge is at issue.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the encounter of limits-as-a-set. Whether or not every case of such an encounter has a sharp, non-negotiable boundary is a separate question. The claim points at what is present in encounters like the room, the tree, the hand, the maze — multiple limits belonging together as one encountered thing — whether or not the boundary in any case is precisely drawn.

nodes.claim: Ontological Bridge: objects exist independently of observation and want.
nodes.soWhat: Completes the move from phenomenology to ontology. With object, existence, and observation in place, and the independence of an object's nature from both observation and want established, experience contains a population of objects encountered as not-made-by-the-observer. Reality as what is met rather than willed or produced has its ground — and the concepts that follow (reality as the full population, relationships between objects) can stand on it.

sections.title: Observations
items: A room left and returned to, its cup, chair, and table where they were.
A stone on the path, its weight what it is regardless of what is wanted of it.
Turning a corner to find a building that was there all along.
A world extending beyond the current scene — rooms behind doors, paths not walked, objects out of sight.

items.text: Ontological Bridge: objects exist independently of observation and want.
items: An object (1.3.4.1) is a structure (1.3.3) with nature (1.3.2) — a set of limits cohering into a unit with features of its own. Existence (1.3.4.2) is the occurrence of an object. Observation (1.3.4.3) is the perception of an object.

Objects do not depend on observation. Their nature holds across observations (1.3.4.5) and does not co-vary with observation at all (1.3.4.6). The set of possible objects exceeds what is currently observed (1.3.4.7); observation itself brings new objects into view (1.3.4.4).

Objects do not depend on want. A limit (1.3.1.4) is what is independent of wanting, and an object is built from limits — its features are limits, its structure is a set of limits. What is wanted of the stone, the room, the tree does not produce or alter their features.

This is the bridge from phenomenology to ontology. Experience arrives with a vocabulary for what is encountered rather than made: objects that are met, whose features hold regardless of what is wanted and whether they are observed. Reality as a population of such objects comes into view.
