Nothing is ever wanted, so nothing succeeds or fails. There is no difference between a craving that just showed up and a commitment that is actively maintained. The entire domain of motivation — wanting, pursuing, endorsing, resisting — has no experiential basis, and everything that depends on it has nothing to build on.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The willful vocabulary built across this section's eight nodes.
items: "Wanting" / "want" — a phenomenon with felt directedness (1.2.5.1.1). "Direction" — the wanted information (1.2.5.1.2). "Success" — the occurrence of what is wanted (1.2.5.1.3). "Failure" — the non-occurrence of what is wanted (1.2.5.1.4). "Outcome" — a success or failure (1.2.5.1.5).

"Endorse" — a want directed toward the occurrence of another want. "Resist" — a want directed against another want (1.2.5.1.6). "Desire" — an unwanted want (1.2.5.1.7). "Will" — a wanted want (1.2.5.1.8).
Plus connector vocabulary grounded along the way: urge, pull, target, aim, purpose, goal, achieve, satisfy, fail, miss, craving, temptation, willing, deliberate.
The next steps: phenomena that depend on wanting — intensity (1.2.5.2), and eventually striving, volition, and compulsion.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: No phenomenon is ever directed toward anything — wanting is indistinguishable from sensation.
Wanting exists but has no identifiable target — direction is a quality with no object.
No wanting is ever satisfied — success and failure have no experiential basis.
All wants are on equal footing — no want is ever endorsed, resisted, or evaluated by another want.
The difference between a craving that arrived unbidden and a deliberate commitment is illusory — there is no basis for distinguishing desire from will.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: What causes desires to occur or wills to form — mechanism is deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not wanting is reducible to physical processes — deferred to later nodes.
Who or what wills — deferred to the self (1.3.7).
Whether or not wants outside awareness exist — deferred to later nodes.
What patterns emerge across outcomes — deferred to relational phenomena (1.2.5.7).

items.title: Willful phenomena are not a separate domain — wanting is just a complex arrangement of sensations.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Maybe wanting, direction, success, failure, desire, and will are just labels for complex physical states.
Hunger is stomach contractions plus low blood sugar. Success is just an occurrence that happens to follow a neural state.
If everything 'willful' can be fully described in physical terms, no separate willful domain exists.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Wanting is a label for a complex arrangement of physical sensations — no separate 'willful' quality exists.
Any phenomenon labeled 'willful' can be fully described in terms of non-willful components (sensations, neural states).
If reduction to non-willful components is possible, a separate willful domain is an unnecessary posit.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Wanting has a quality that sensations lack: directedness. Hunger is not just stomach contractions — it includes a pull toward food that the sensation alone does not have. Success is not just an occurrence — it is the occurrence of what was wanted. Each node identifies a structure within experience that non-willful phenomena do not exhibit.

Two phenomena can share a mechanism and still be observably distinct. Redness and loudness may both reduce to neural firing, yet they are different qualities. The same applies to wanting: it may reduce to physical processes and still be an observable quality in its own right.

Apply the reductionist's own principle consistently: if sharing a substrate (neural firing) means wanting and sensing are 'really the same,' then redness and loudness are also 'really the same' (both reduce to neural activity), warmth and pressure are 'really the same' (both reduce to receptor activation), and every qualitative distinction in experience collapses into 'neural events.'

The reductionist does not accept this for perception — they maintain that seeing and hearing are genuinely different experiences despite reducing to the same physical substrate. They cannot then deny the same status to sensing and wanting. Commitment #1, consistently applied, doesn't just eliminate the wanting/sensing distinction — it eliminates every experiential distinction, including the ones the reductionist needs to describe their own experimental observations.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not willful phenomena are reducible to non-willful components is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied.
The claim holds either way: the observable distinctness of wanting, direction, success, and will is present in awareness regardless of what explains it.

items.title: These definitions are too narrow — common usage gives richer meanings to purpose, success, failure, desire, and will.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: In everyday language, purpose implies deliberate planning, success implies intentional effort, failure implies having tried and fallen short, and desire covers any strong want. These minimal definitions strip the terms of their meaningful connotations and create confusion with ordinary usage.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Definitions should capture the ordinary meaning of the terms they define.
Stripping terms of their common connotations creates confusion between the technical definition and everyday usage.
A minimal definition that departs from common usage is incomplete, not foundational.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Each definition captures the most basic experiential observation — the foundation on which richer meanings build. The richer connotations (deliberation, effort, intensity) require concepts like intention, planning, and consciousness that are not yet defined at this level. These are starting points, not endpoints.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Richer notions build on these foundations as more vocabulary becomes available.
The definitions are minimal by design — capturing what is directly observed before adding layers that require further grounding. The broader everyday senses remain available through the parent terms.

items.title: Willful phenomena presuppose a self or agent — wanting, endorsing, and willing require someone who wants, endorses, and wills.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Philosophy of mind and common sense both presuppose a subject behind wanting and willing. 'Wanting' without a wanter is incoherent. Hard determinism further argues that the feeling of willing is a post-hoc narrative imposed on causally determined behavior — endorsement is an illusion.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Wanting, endorsing, and willing are acts that require a subject — an agent who performs them.
Without a self or agent, 'wanting' is a free-floating property with no bearer — which is incoherent.
The feeling of willing may be a post-hoc narrative imposed on causally determined behavior, not a genuine observation.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: These nodes identify what occurs in awareness — a want directed at food, a want directed at another want — without claiming who or what does the wanting. Whether or not these structures require a self, are causally determined, or involve an agent is a question these nodes do not address.
Two wants in a specific relationship are observable regardless of what produces them.

subSections.label: Correction
items: These nodes observe that wants occur and have structure — direction, success, failure, endorsement. whether or not this structure requires a self or agent is a question that arrives at (1.3.7).
The observation that wants occur does not presuppose an answer about what produces or anchors them.

nodes.claim: Intensities occur.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the entire domain of felt degree — that phenomena are not just present or absent but occur more or less strongly. Sensation, perception, satisfaction, and frustration all build on this.
nodes.search: intensity sensation perception satisfaction frustration degree strong weak dim vivid loud quiet feeling sense

sections.title: Observations
items: Dim red, vivid red. Quiet hum, loud crash. Faint ache, sharp pain.
The warmth of sunlight, felt strongly. The loudness of a crash, intense.
Hunger wanting food, and the taste arriving. Thirst wanting water, and dryness persisting.

items.text: Intensities occur.
items: "Intensity" (1.2.5.2.1) is the degree to which a phenomenon occurs — how dim or vivid, quiet or loud. Intensity that is not wanting is "sensation" (1.2.5.2.2) — a distinct quality from wanting, like loud and red.

The event of a sensation occurring is "perception" (1.2.5.2.3). When a wanted sensation occurs, that is "satisfaction" (1.2.5.2.4). When a wanted sensation does not occur, that is "frustration" (1.2.5.2.5).

items.title: No phenomenon ever occurs with degree
items.detail: Without intensity, phenomena are either present or absent with nothing in between. Dim and vivid are indistinguishable. The sensory dimension of experience collapses — warmth, loudness, and color have no felt degree. Sensation, perception, satisfaction, and frustration have nothing to stand on, and the felt difference between getting what was wanted sensorily and not getting it disappears.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The intensity vocabulary built across this section's five nodes.
items: "Intensity" — the degree to which a phenomenon occurs (1.2.5.2.1). "Sensation" / "feeling" — intensity that is not wanting (1.2.5.2.2). "Perception" / "perceive" — the occurrence of a sensation (1.2.5.2.3). "Satisfaction" — when a wanted sensation occurs (1.2.5.2.4). "Frustration" — when a wanted sensation does not occur (1.2.5.2.5).
Plus connector vocabulary grounded along the way: strong, weak, dim, vivid, loud, quiet, faint, more, less, sensory, see, hear, taste, smell, feel, gratification, fulfilled, frustrated, deprived.
The next steps: phenomena that depend on intensity and wanting together — temporal phenomena (1.2.5.3), physical phenomena (1.2.5.4), emotional phenomena (1.2.5.5).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: No phenomenon has degree — everything occurs at a single undifferentiated level.
Intensity and wanting are the same quality — there is no distinction between felt degree and felt directedness.
The sensory dimension of success and failure has no basis — getting and not getting what was wanted feel the same.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not intensity is continuous or occurs in discrete steps — deferred to later nodes.
What determines the intensity of phenomena — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not sensation and wanting are always separable in practice — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Intensity and perception are physical or cognitive processes, not experiential qualities.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Intensity is measured in decibels and wavelengths; perception involves interpretation, categorization, and top-down processing. These are not simple experiential qualities but complex processes that require scientific explanation, not experiential labeling.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Intensity and perception are physical or cognitive processes, not experiential qualities.
What appears as 'felt degree' is really a measurable physical quantity (decibels, wavelength).
Starting from experiential descriptions rather than physical mechanisms gets the explanation backwards.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: These nodes identify what occurs in awareness — felt degree and sensory events — without claiming what produces them. The physical and cognitive accounts address mechanism; the nodes address what is experienced. A dim red and a vivid red differ in felt degree regardless of whether or not that degree corresponds to a measurable amplitude.

Commitment #3 (scientific explanation replaces phenomenological description) is self-undermining in a way the objector rarely notices. Scientific practice *depends on* phenomenological observation: the scientist reads an instrument (a phenomenological act), observes a data pattern (a phenomenological act), and forms a conclusion (a phenomenological act). If phenomenological description is replaced by mechanism, the scientist's own experience of conducting the experiment has no standing — it is 'just mechanism' too. The objector needs phenomenological observation to be legitimate in order to do the science that they claim replaces phenomenological observation. Consistently applied, commitment #3 doesn't just eliminate the experiential description of intensity — it eliminates the experiential basis of the science invoked against it.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not intensity is explained by physical amplitude or perception involves cognitive processing is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied.
The claim holds either way: the felt difference in degree and the event of a sensation occurring are observable regardless of what produces them.

items.title: Sensation and wanting are inseparable — all experience has valence.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Hedonic traditions in psychology and phenomenology argue that every experience carries preference or aversion. Every warmth has a slight pull, every loudness a mild push. Truly neutral sensation — intensity without any wanting — may be an abstraction that never actually occurs.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Every experience carries preference or aversion — there is no neutral sensation.
If sensation and wanting always co-occur, distinguishing them is drawing an artificial line.
Inseparability in occurrence means inseparability in identity — always appearing together means being the same thing.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 is doing all the work, and it's false. The warmth of sunlight and the pull toward warmth are two different qualities, even when they co-occur — like loud and red can co-occur in a siren without being the same quality.
Two phenomena can always appear together and still be observably distinct. The question of whether or not they *always* co-occur is separate from whether or not they are the *same thing*.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Even if every sensation always co-occurs with some wanting, the sensation and the wanting are still different qualities. Sensation (1.2.5.2.2) names the intensity dimension; wanting (1.2.5.1.1) names the directedness.
They may always appear together, and this claim's observation — that they are different qualities — still stands.

items.title: These definitions are too narrow — common usage gives richer meanings to sensation, perception, satisfaction, and frustration.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: In everyday language, perception involves interpretation, satisfaction involves contentment and pleasure, frustration involves agitation and anger. These minimal definitions strip the terms of the connotations that make them meaningful and create confusion with ordinary usage.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Definitions should capture the ordinary meaning of the terms they define.
Stripping terms of their common connotations (contentment, agitation, interpretive richness) creates confusion between the technical definition and everyday usage.
A minimal definition that departs from common usage is incomplete, not foundational.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Each definition captures the most basic experiential observation — the foundation on which richer meanings build. The richer connotations require concepts like temporal persistence, emotional phenomena (1.2.5.5), and cognitive processing that are not yet defined at this level. These are starting points, not endpoints.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not these phenomena involve richer emotional or cognitive layers is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. The claim holds either way: felt degree, sensory events, and wanted sensations occurring or not are observable regardless of what additional layers accompany them.
The richer everyday senses build on these foundations once more vocabulary is available.

nodes.claim: Temporal phenomena occur.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the entire temporal dimension of experience — that awareness has a 'now,' a 'before,' memories, succession, change, and events. Mental phenomena like imagination and thought depend on this vocabulary.
nodes.search: temporal time present past memory recognition new sequence step change event now before after

sections.title: Observations
items: A sharp pain right now. The same pain from earlier, no longer felt but still in awareness. Tasting a strawberry and the taste matching something from before. Tasting an unknown fruit, nothing matching.
Lightning, then thunder. One note, then the next.
Red shifting to orange. A sound beginning from silence.

items.text: Temporal phenomena occur.
items: Temporal phenomena — those with the quality of sequence, present-ness, and past-ness — occur. These are not additional sensations or wants; they are qualities of when and in what order phenomena occur.

Some phenomena carry the quality of 'having occurred' — past (1.2.5.3.3). Present information about past phenomena is memory (1.2.5.3.4). Matching a present phenomenon to a memory is recognition (1.2.5.3.5). Occurring without recognition is newness (1.2.5.3.6).
Each occurrence within the sequence is a step (1.2.5.3.7). Qualities differing across steps is change (1.2.5.3.8). The transition from not-occurring to occurring is an event (1.2.5.3.9).

items.title: No temporal quality characterizes experience
items.detail: Without temporal phenomena, awareness has no 'now,' no 'before,' no memory, no recognition, no novelty, no succession, no change, and no events. Experience is a static, orderless array of qualities with no dimension of time. Mental phenomena that depend on temporal vocabulary — imagination, thought, possibility, the future — have nothing to stand on.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The temporal vocabulary built across this section's nine nodes.
items: "Present" / "now" — the quality of occurring immediately (1.2.5.3.1). "Sequence" / "sequential" — phenomena occurring in order (1.2.5.3.2).

"Past" / "before" — having occurred before the present (1.2.5.3.3). "Memory" / "remember" — present information about a past phenomenon (1.2.5.3.4). "Recognition" / "familiar" — a present phenomenon that is like a memory (1.2.5.3.5). "New" / "novel" — a phenomenon without recognition (1.2.5.3.6).
"Step" — a phenomenon in a sequence (1.2.5.3.7). "Change" — quality difference across steps (1.2.5.3.8). "Event" — the transition from not-occurring to occurring (1.2.5.3.9).

Plus connector vocabulary grounded along the way: immediate, current, before, after, then, precedes, preceding, follows, next, previous, succession, was, ago, prior, earlier, no longer, formerly, shift, transition, become, begin, start, appear, arise, happen, onset.
The next step: phenomena that depend on temporal vocabulary — mental phenomena like imagination and thought (1.2.5.6).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: No temporal quality characterizes experience — everything occurs simultaneously with no ordering, no memory, and no change.
Memory, recognition, and change have no experiential basis — they are constructs imposed on a timeless present.
Events never begin — phenomena are always occurring or never occurring, with no transition between the two.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not temporal experience corresponds to an objective temporal order — ontological question deferred to (1.3).
How precise temporal distinctions are (how fine-grained is 'now'?) — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not memory is always accurate — requires truth vocabulary not yet built.

items.title: These temporal concepts are too minimal — they miss the richness of how time is experienced.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The phenomenology of time is rich — duration (durée), time-consciousness, the specious present, subjective time distortion. These minimal definitions strip temporality of its most interesting features and seem to flatten what is actually a complex, layered experience.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: The phenomenology of time is rich — duration, time-consciousness, the specious present — and these minimal definitions miss that richness.
Definitions of temporal concepts should capture how time is actually experienced, not strip it to a skeleton.
A minimal definition that ignores the most distinctive features of temporal experience is incomplete.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Each definition captures the most basic experiential observation — the foundation on which richer accounts build. Duration, time-consciousness, and temporal distortion require concepts like attention, expectation, and cognitive processing that are not yet defined at this level. These are starting points, not endpoints.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not temporal experience involves richer structures is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied.
The claim holds either way: presentness, pastness, memory, recognition, sequence, change, and events are observable regardless of what additional layers accompany them.

items.title: Defining time requires already understanding time — this is circular.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Defining "present," "past," and "sequence" seems to require already understanding temporal concepts. This is circular — the definitions use what they are trying to establish.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Temporal concepts are bootstrapping — you can't define "present" without already understanding temporal ordering.
Circular definitions are epistemically worthless — they ground nothing.
An external (non-temporal) standpoint is needed to define temporal concepts non-circularly.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 is the key assumption, and it fails for the same reason it would fail for *any* foundational concept. You can't define "existence" without using existence. You can't define "occurrence" without something occurring.

The nodes do not define time from outside time — they identify qualities the reader already experiences from within temporal awareness: the felt quality of "now," the quality of "having occurred," the felt ordering of one phenomenon following another.
These are observations within temporal experience, not attempts to define time from a timeless perspective.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Your awareness of presentness, pastness, and succession is what any theory of time is built from. You do not need the theory to have the awareness. The nodes name what the reader already experiences — no external standpoint is assumed.

items.title: These are physical and cognitive processes, not experiential qualities — temporal phenomena are produced, not observed.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Your brain produces temporal ordering through neural processing. Memory works through strengthening connections between neurons. Change detection works through sensory adaptation.
These are physical processes, not experiential qualities. Starting from experience rather than mechanism gets the explanation backwards.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Temporal ordering, memory, and change are products of neural processing, not experiential givens.
Starting from experiential descriptions rather than physical mechanisms gets the explanation backwards.
If temporal phenomena are produced by the brain, they are not observed — they are generated.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: These nodes identify what occurs in awareness — presentness, memory, sequence, change — without claiming what produces them. The physical and cognitive accounts address mechanism; the nodes address what is experienced.
The felt quality of 'now,' the retained information about the past, and the ordering of phenomena are observable regardless of what explains them.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not temporal phenomena are explained by physical mechanisms is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied.
The claim holds either way: the temporal dimension of experience — presentness, memory, succession, change, events — is observable regardless of what produces it.

nodes.claim: Physical phenomena occur.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the spatial dimension of experience — location, extension, and arrangement. Body, objects, and spatial structure all build on this.
nodes.search: physical spatial location position shape extension arrangement body space where here there near far

sections.title: Observations
items: Colors arranged left, right, near, far in a visual field.
Pressure at a spot on the back.
A sound from the left.
The position of a limb, felt without looking.
Roughness under fingertips, spread across a surface.

items.text: Physical phenomena occur.
items: A "physical phenomenon" is a type of phenomenon (1.2.5) with spatial quality — location, extension, and arrangement. The visual field displays spatial arrangement. Pressure has location. Roughness has extent.
What distinguishes physical phenomena: wanting has direction but no location. Intensity has degree but no extent. Physical phenomena have a "where" and a "how spread out."

items.title: No phenomenon has spatial quality
items.detail: Without physical phenomena, there is no "where" in experience. Colors occur without arrangement. Pressure occurs without location. Roughness has no extent. The spatial structure that distinguishes one arrangement from another — this from that, here from there — is absent, and any concept that depends on spatial identity has nothing to stand on.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Physical" / "spatial" — a type of phenomenon with location, extension, and arrangement.
Also grounded: "location," "position," "where," "here," "there," "near," "far," "left," "right," "shape," "extent," "spread," "arrangement."
The next step: mental phenomena construct new information from memory, including spatial information (1.2.5.6).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: No phenomenon has spatial quality — experience consists only of intensities with degree, wantings with direction, and temporal sequences.
Location and extension are not features of experience — they are imposed by interpretation rather than observed.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not physical phenomena correspond to anything independent from awareness — deferred to ontological grounding (1.3).
Whether or not spatial qualities are fundamental or derived from other qualities.

items.title: Spatial qualities are constructed by the brain, not experienced directly.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Your brain constructs spatial perception from sensory inputs. What you experience as 'left' or 'near' is an output of neural computation, not a raw given.
If spatial qualities are constructed by the brain, they are not observed — they are generated.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Spatial perception is the product of neural computation — the brain constructs location from sensory inputs.
What is experienced as 'left' or 'near' is an output of processing, not a raw experiential given.
If spatial qualities are constructed, they are not observed — they are generated by the brain.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: This identifies spatial quality as it occurs in awareness — the experienced "where" of things. The question is not whether or not computation produces spatial experience — it is whether or not spatial experience occurs. That occurrence is what the node identifies, regardless of its mechanism.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not spatial qualities are neurally constructed is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. The claim holds either way: the quality of location, extension, and arrangement occurs in awareness regardless of what produces it.

items.title: What justifies calling any experience 'physical' without an external world?

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Phenomenology brackets the external world — you start from experience and build outward. But calling a subset of experience 'physical' reverses this: 'physical' already means 'of the external, material world.'

By sorting some phenomena as physical, you've smuggled the external world back in through vocabulary. The idealist (Berkeley, later Husserl) would say: all you have are experiences with spatial qualities. Calling them 'physical' is a theoretical commitment to an external world that hasn't been established at this level.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 'Physical' is an ontological category that presupposes the existence of a mind-independent material world.
Using the word 'physical' to describe experiences imports this ontological commitment even if the definition tries to bracket it.
Defining "physical" in experiential terms contradicts ordinary usage, which presupposes mind-independence.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 is the load-bearer, and it identifies a genuine tension. 'Physical' does carry connotations of the external world in ordinary usage. But the node doesn't use 'physical' to mean 'belonging to the external world.' It uses 'physical' to name a specific experiential type: phenomena whose distinguishing quality is spatial arrangement rather than intensity, direction, or temporal ordering.
The word is applied to the *experience* of extension, location, and spatial structure — not to a theoretical claim about what exists beyond experience.

Commitment #3 proposes an alternative (use 'spatial' instead of 'physical'), which has merit as a terminological preference — but the substantive question is whether or not the *phenomenon* exists, not what to call it. And the phenomenon does: some experiences have arrangement-qualities (the felt spatiality of a room, the extension of a visual field) that are structurally distinct from intensity or wanting.

subSections.label: Correction
items: 'Physical' here names the experiential type characterized by spatial arrangement — location, extension, shape as they appear in awareness. The node doesn't claim these experiences are *caused by* or *correspond to* an external world.

It observes that arrangement-qualities are a distinct experiential type, alongside intensity, direction, and temporal ordering. The ontological question (do these experiences track a mind-independent world?) requires later vocabulary.

nodes.claim: Emotional phenomena occur.
nodes.soWhat: Names the unified experience of wanting-and-sensation combined. Recognizes that anger, joy, fear, and sadness are a distinct type — not just wanting plus feeling side by side.
nodes.search: emotion emotional anger joy fear sadness excitement feeling mood affect

sections.title: Observations
items: A hot tightness fused with pushing-against, at an injustice.
A warm lightness pulling toward good news.
A cold sharpness pulling away from a sudden sound.
Heavy slowness and an ache, wanting what is gone.
A buzzing intensity leaning forward before an event.

items.text: Emotional phenomena occur.
items: An "emotion" is a quality that combines wanting (1.2.5.1.1) and sensation (1.2.5.2.2) as a unified experience. Anger, joy, fear, sadness, disgust — each has both direction (wanting) and sensory character (sensation), experienced as one thing.

What makes emotions distinct: wanting alone is direction without a specific sensory character. Sensation alone is sensory character without direction. An emotion has both — anger is not just a push-against, and not just a hot tightness, but both as a single experience.

items.title: Wanting-sensation combinations are invisible as a type
items.detail: Without recognizing emotions, the hot tightness that fuses with pushing-against has no identity apart from its pieces. Anger is just "a wanting alongside a sensation." But the reader already knows anger is not two things — it is one thing. Without naming this unity, every emotional state must be described from scratch each time, and the patterns between them (anger and fear are both aversive; joy and excitement are both approach-directed) have no common ground to stand on. Later, when evaluating whether or not a method of reasoning is influenced by wanting (1.6), the unified force of an emotion — not wanting alone, not sensation alone, but their fusion — is what actually biases reasoning. Without the type, that bias has no name.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Emotion" / "emotional" — a quality that combines wanting and sensation as a unified experience.
Also grounded: "angry," "joyful," "afraid," "sad," "excited" — specific emotions named by their characteristic wanting-sensation combination.
The next step: mental phenomena construct new information from memory (1.2.5.6).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Wanting and sensation never form a unified quality — they are always experienced as two separate things side by side.
Emotions are reducible to pure wanting or pure sensation without remainder.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not emotions correspond to specific physical processes — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not some emotions are more basic than others — deferred to later analysis.
The specific taxonomy of emotions — this node establishes the type, not a catalog.

items.title: Emotions are just bodily sensations — the James-Lange theory.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: William James's radical claim was not that emotions *cause* bodily changes, but that emotions *are* bodily changes. You don't tremble because you're afraid — you're afraid because you tremble.

The strongest modern version (Damasio's somatic marker hypothesis) goes further: the entire bodily configuration — including approach/withdrawal motor patterns, visceral states, and postural readiness — constitutes the emotion.

The 'directedness' this node claims distinguishes emotion from sensation is itself a bodily state: fight-or-flight posture IS the toward-or-away-from quality. There's no separate 'wanting' component — the body's orientation is doing all the work.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: The directedness (wanting component) of emotions is not a separate experiential layer — it is part of the bodily configuration.
Approach/withdrawal motor patterns are sensations (felt bodily states), not a different kind of phenomenon.
If directedness reduces to bodily sensation, the distinction between emotional and sensory phenomena collapses — emotions are just complex sensations.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 is where the objection breaks. Consider: trembling is a sensation. Pulling-away-from is also a sensation (you feel your body orienting). But pulling-away-from *includes a direction* — it is not just a state of the body, it is a state of the body *relative to something*.

The trembling has no built-in 'about' — it is simply occurring. The pulling-away has a built-in 'about' — it is away from *this*. The objector can verify the difference: trembling from cold and trembling from fear feel different, and the difference is that fear-trembling is directed (away from the threat) while cold-trembling is not directed at anything.

Commitment #1 correctly notes that the directedness is felt bodily — but 'felt bodily' and 'a sensation' are not the same. A sensation is intensity without wanting (the node's own definition). The bodily feeling of pulling-away *includes* wanting (the away-from). The body can carry directedness; that doesn't make directedness a sensation.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The James-Lange theory is right that emotions are felt bodily. It is wrong that all felt bodily states are the same kind of thing.

Trembling-without-direction is a sensation. Trembling-with-direction (toward or away from something) is an emotion. The body carries both — but the directedness is a structural feature that sensation alone does not have, and it is observable in the difference between shivering from cold and shivering from fear.

items.title: Emotions are socially constructed labels.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Cross-cultural research shows that emotion categories vary — some cultures recognize emotions that others lack. If emotions were a natural type, all cultures would recognize the same ones. This suggests "emotional phenomena" is an imposed category, not an observed type.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Cross-cultural variation in emotion categories shows emotions are not natural kinds.
If the categories are cultural, there is no natural type "emotional phenomena."
Variation in labeling implies variation in the underlying experience.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 is the key assumption: the objector moves from "cultures label emotions differently" to "the underlying experiences differ." But this claims that phenomena combining wanting and sensation into a unified quality occur — not that everyone labels them the same way.

whether or not anger is recognized as a single emotion or divided into subtypes varies; that anger-like experiences — a hot tightness fused with pushing-against, as in the observations — occur does not.

Commitment #1 also undermines the objector's own position. 'Social construction' is itself a category that varies across academic cultures — some traditions recognize it, others don't. If cultural variation in categories means the categories don't track real phenomena, then 'social construction' doesn't track a real phenomenon. The constructionist's own analytical category fails their own test. The principle (variable categorization = no real phenomenon) cannot be applied without dissolving the tool used to apply it.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The unified experience of wanting-and-sensation-combined occurs regardless of what it is called. Cultural variation in labeling is real but targets how experiences are categorized, not whether or not they occur.

nodes.claim: Mental phenomena occur.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the entire dimension of experience that constructs new information from memory — imagination, visualization, thought, possibility, and the future. Concepts, statements, arguments, and reasoning all build on these.
nodes.search: mental mind imagination thought possibility future visualization think imagine construct

sections.title: Observations
items: Picturing something not currently present.
An inner monologue about what to do next.
Wondering what happens when a ball reaches the edge.
Evaluating whether or not an idea fits with what is known.
Combining separate memories into something never experienced.

items.text: Mental phenomena occur.
items: A "mental phenomenon" is a type of phenomenon (1.2.5) that constructs information from memory. Imagination, visualization, thought, possibility, and the future are all mental phenomena — each builds on memory to produce something that was not directly experienced as a whole.

What distinguishes mental from other types: willful phenomena have direction. Intensities have degree. Temporal phenomena have sequence. Physical phenomena have spatial quality. Emotional phenomena combine wanting and sensation. Mental phenomena construct new information from what is remembered.

items.title: No new information is ever constructed from memory
items.detail: Without mental phenomena, awareness contains only present experience — current wants, current sensations, current perceptions, remembered past. There is no picturing what is not present, no evaluating whether or not an idea fits recognized patterns, no imagining what comes next. Concepts, statements, arguments, and reasoning — all of which depend on mental construction — have nothing to work with.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node and its children.
items: "Mental" / "mind" — phenomena that construct information from memory.

"Imagination" (1.2.5.6.1) — information from different memories. "Visualization" (1.2.5.6.2) — the sensation of an imagination. "Thought" (1.2.5.6.3) — a set of imaginations and their associations. "Possibility" (1.2.5.6.4) — a thought that matches recognized patterns. "Future" (1.2.5.6.5) — a possibility of what occurs after the present.
The next step: how phenomena relate to each other across experience — correlation, independence, consistency, and causation (1.2.5.7).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Experience contains no constructed content — everything in awareness is either directly perceived or directly remembered, with nothing new assembled from existing information.
There is no difference between imagining and remembering, between a thought and a single imagination, or between a possibility and an idle fantasy.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not mental phenomena correspond to physical processes — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not mental construction requires deliberate effort or occurs involuntarily.
The reliability of mental content — whether or not thoughts and possibilities are accurate — deferred to truth (1.4.1.2) and verification (1.5.5).

items.title: Mental phenomena are just complex memories — no new type exists.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Memory already covers the presence of past information. What is called "imagination" is just recombination of memories; "thought" is just structured memory associations; "possibility" is just memory-based pattern matching. No new type needs to be recognized.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: If mental phenomena are built from memories, they reduce to memories — no new type is needed.
Recombination of existing elements doesn't produce a genuinely new kind of thing.
Novelty of combination is not novelty of type.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 is the load-bearer. Memory (1.2.5.3) is present information about a single past phenomenon. Mental phenomena construct *new* information from multiple memories. The pink elephant is not a memory — nothing pink-and-elephant was ever experienced.
The construction of new information from existing information is a genuine new phenomenon.

By the logic of commitment #2, water (novel combination of hydrogen and oxygen) would "just be" hydrogen and oxygen — but water has properties (wetness, fluidity) that neither hydrogen nor oxygen has alone. Combination can produce genuinely new phenomena with properties not present in any component.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The result of constructing information from different memories (1.2.5.6.1) is itself a distinct type of phenomenon. The pink elephant was not in any single memory.
Assembling information across memory (1.2.5.3) boundaries produces something new — and that newness is what this names.

items.title: Mental content is private and unverifiable — it cannot ground objective claims.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Sensations are pointed at directly ("this redness"). Memories are corroborated by others. But mental constructions — imagined pink elephants, thoughts about the future — are entirely internal. Using them as a foundational type gives unverifiable content the same status as verifiable observation.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Sensations and memories can be pointed at or corroborated; mental constructions cannot.
Unverifiable content should not have the same foundational status as verifiable observation.
If mental content cannot be checked against anything external, claims about it are private and ungeneralizable.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: This identifies mental phenomena as they occur in awareness — the experience of imagining, thinking, evaluating possibility. These experiences are as observable (to the one experiencing them) as any sensation. whether or not their content corresponds to anything external is a separate question about truth, not about whether or not the phenomenon occurs.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not mental content corresponds to external reality is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. The claim holds either way: the experience of constructing information from memory (1.2.5.3) occurs.
Imagination, thought, and possibility are observable phenomena regardless of whether or not their content is true.

Your own acceptance of "only public evidence counts" was itself a private judgment you found compelling — showing that private reasoning is already doing foundational work, even in frameworks that claim to reject it.

nodes.claim: Relational phenomena occur.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the experience that phenomena do not just occur in isolation — they connect, disconnect, persist, and vary in relation to each other. Inference, objecthood, and later the structure of reality all depend on recognizing these relations.
nodes.search: relational phenomena relation connection between correlation independence consistency cause effect fundamental superficial expectation hope

sections.title: Observations
items: Some things tend to follow other things — clouds and rain, wanting to move and the arm moving.
Some things vary without any connection to each other — the flavor of food and the sound of traffic.
Some features persist across encounters while others change — sweetness stays, shade varies.
Some possibilities arise from what has been recognized, others from what is wanted.

items.text: Relational phenomena occur.
items: "Relational" phenomena are those that describe how phenomena connect, disconnect, persist, or vary in relation to each other. They are not additional sensations or wants — they are recognized structures across phenomena already occurring.

Examples: one event often following another (correlation). A persistent feature that does not vary (fundamental). Variation within a fundamental feature (superficial). The full vocabulary is in Unlocks.

items.title: Phenomena occur in isolation with no recognizable structure between them
items.detail: Without relational phenomena, every occurrence is disconnected from every other. Lightning followed by thunder is just two events with no recognized connection. Wanting to move an arm and the arm moving have no special relationship. Features that persist and features that vary have the same standing. Experience becomes a stream of isolated occurrences with no structure — and inference, objecthood, and any grasp of how things relate to each other become impossible.

children.title: No anticipation is possible
children.detail: Without correlation and expectation, recognized patterns generate no forward-facing thought. What has tended to happen has no bearing on what comes next.

children.title: Agency is indistinguishable from coincidence
children.detail: Without cause and effect, wanting something and it happening has the same standing as any other event pairing. The experience of making something happen has no label and no basis.

children.title: Nothing can be characterized as reliable or incidental
children.detail: Without consistency, fundamental, and superficial, there is no basis for distinguishing what something reliably is from how it happens to appear on one occasion.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The relational vocabulary built across this section's nine nodes.
items: "Correlation" (1.2.5.7.1), "expectation" (1.2.5.7.2), "hope" (1.2.5.7.3) — how phenomena connect across a sequence, and the possibilities that arise from those connections.
"Independence" (1.2.5.7.4) — how phenomena vary without connection.
"Consistency" (1.2.5.7.5), "fundamental" (1.2.5.7.6), "superficial" (1.2.5.7.7) — how features persist or vary across a sequence.
"Cause" (1.2.5.7.8), "effect" (1.2.5.7.9) — how wants connect to events.

Plus connector vocabulary grounded along the way: tends to, regularly, associated, anticipate, predict, likely, wish, long for, unrelated, separate, irrelevant, stable, steady, unchanged, persists, remains, essential, core, defining, incidental, surface-level, make happen, bring about, produce, action, result, consequence.
With willful, intensity, temporal, physical, emotional, mental, and relational phenomena all grounded, the full phenomenological type vocabulary for 1.2.5 is established.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Phenomena occur only in isolation — there are no recognizable structures between occurrences.
Relations between phenomena require a theory or framework to be noticed — they are not directly experienced.
All connections between phenomena are of the same type — there is no basis for distinguishing correlation from independence, or consistency from variation.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not relational phenomena exhaustively categorize all relations — other types of relation may exist beyond those named here.
Whether or not relations between phenomena reflect structures in reality or only patterns in experience — the ontological status of relations is deferred to later analysis (1.3).
Whether or not cause and effect extend beyond want-event correlations to physical or external causation — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: These are all just pattern recognition applied in different ways — no distinct 'relational' type is needed.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Correlation is a pattern across events. Consistency is a pattern across steps. Independence is the absence of a pattern. Fundamental and superficial are stable versus unstable patterns. Every relational concept reduces to pattern recognition. Calling them a separate type of phenomenon is misleading — they are just applications of an already-established capacity.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Every relational concept is an application of pattern recognition to different contexts.
2. If all relational concepts reduce to pattern recognition, they do not constitute a distinct type of phenomenon.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 is largely correct — relational phenomena do involve pattern recognition. But commitment #2 does not follow. Temporal phenomena also build on prior vocabulary (quality, sequence, change), and emotional phenomena build on wanting and sensation. Each type names a distinct domain of experience, not a wholly new capacity.

What makes relational phenomena distinct is what they are about: not the occurrence of qualities, not the experience of wanting or sensing, but the structures *between* occurrences. Correlation, independence, consistency, cause — these describe how phenomena relate to each other, which is recognizably different from the phenomena themselves.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Relational phenomena build on prior vocabulary — as every type does. Their distinctiveness is in what they describe: not the occurrence of qualities, wants, or sensations, but the structures between occurrences. This is a recognizably distinct domain of experience.

items.title: Relations are imposed by the mind, not found in experience — this smuggles in structure that isn't there.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Maybe the mind projects connections onto experience that are not actually there. Hume argued that causation is a mental habit, not something observed. If relations are mental impositions rather than experienced phenomena, calling them "relational phenomena" gives them an unearned experiential status.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Relations between phenomena are projected by the mind, not present in experience itself.
2. If relations are mental projections, they should not be treated as phenomena on the same level as sensations or wants.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 assumes a distinction between what is "in experience" and what the mind "adds to" experience — but at this level, that distinction is not yet available. What is available: the observations. Some things tend to follow other things. Some things vary without connection. Some features persist. These are recognized, just as colors and sounds are recognized.

Whether or not these recognitions reflect mind-independent structures or mental projections is an ontological question — deferred to later analysis (1.3). The node names what is experienced, not what underlies the experience.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not relations are mind-independent or mentally projected is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. The node names what is experienced: recurring sequences, disconnected variations, persistent features, want-event pairings. These are recognized in experience — the question of their deeper status is deferred.

nodes.claim: A type is a set of phenomena that share a fundamental feature.
nodes.soWhat: Names the experience of recognizing that phenomena belong together — 'these are the same kind of thing.' Grouping, classification, and the recognition that experience has distinct domains all depend on this.
nodes.search: type kind category grouping classification sort class share fundamental feature common character

sections.title: Observations
items: Wanting, craving, resisting, and endorsing all share something — a directedness that seeing and hearing lack.
Seeing, hearing, tasting, and touching all share something — an intensity that wanting and imagining lack.
Remembering, imagining, and planning all share something — a constructive character that raw sensation lacks.
Correlation, independence, and consistency all share something — they describe connections between phenomena rather than the phenomena themselves.

items.text: A type is a set of phenomena that share a fundamental feature.
items: A "type" is a set of phenomena that share a fundamental feature (1.2.5.7.6). Wanting, craving, resisting, and endorsing are the same type because they consistently share directedness — a fundamental feature present in each. Seeing, hearing, and tasting are the same type because they consistently share sensory intensity.

What makes a type distinct from any set: any phenomena can be grouped together arbitrarily. A type is a grouping based on a shared *fundamental* feature — one that is consistent across the members. The grouping reflects what the phenomena recognizably have in common, not an arbitrary selection.

items.title: Phenomena that share a fundamental character cannot be grouped
items.detail: Without recognizing type, there is no way to group phenomena by shared fundamental features. Wanting and craving share directedness, but this shared character has no label. Seeing and hearing share sensory intensity, but there is no basis for recognizing them as the same kind of thing. Classification — distinguishing one domain of experience from another — becomes impossible.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Type" / "kind" — a set of phenomena that share a fundamental feature.
Also grounded: "category," "class," "sort" (in the sense of a grouping based on shared fundamental character).
With type established, the parent claim — that phenomena are associated in distinct types (1.2.5) — is fully grounded.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: All groupings of phenomena are equally arbitrary — there is no principled basis for treating some groupings as natural and others as artificial.
Types require a theory or framework external to experience — grouping phenomena by shared character is not something recognized directly.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not types have sharp boundaries — whether or not a phenomenon can belong to more than one type. Not addressed here.
Whether or not types recognized in experience correspond to real divisions in what exists — the ontological status of types is deferred to later analysis (1.3).

items.title: This is just pattern recognition applied to phenomena — no new concept is needed.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Recognizing that wanting and craving share directedness is just recognizing a pattern — sameness across features. Pattern and sameness are already established. "Type" adds a label to the result of pattern recognition but no new experiential content.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Pattern recognition already captures the experience of grouping phenomena by shared features.
2. If the components fully account for the experience, a new label adds no conceptual value.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 overlooks what the specific combination names. Pattern names similarity across features. Fundamental names consistency. Type names the result of both: a *grouping* based on shared fundamental character. The experience of recognizing that wanting and craving are *the same kind of thing* is what type captures — not just that they share a feature, but that this shared feature makes them a coherent group.

Without type, classification and the recognition of distinct domains of experience — willful, sensory, temporal, mental, relational — cannot be expressed. Each domain is a type; the concept is what makes the grouping referrable.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Type names the specific result of recognizing shared fundamental features across phenomena — a coherent grouping. The components are prior, but the grouping itself is what allows classification and the recognition of distinct experiential domains.

items.title: Types are imposed by the observer's interests, not found in experience — a chef and a chemist type the same substances differently.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: What counts as a type depends on what features the observer treats as fundamental. A chef groups foods by flavor; a chemist groups them by molecular structure. If types depend on which features are attended to, they are not in experience itself — they are projections of the observer's framework.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Which features are treated as fundamental varies by observer.
2. If type-membership depends on the observer's attention, types are not features of experience but products of perspective.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 is partially correct — which features are recognized as fundamental can differ. But commitment #2 does not follow. Type names a structural relationship: a grouping of phenomena by shared fundamental features. The structure holds regardless of which features fill the role.

The chef and chemist recognize different fundamental features and arrive at different types. In both cases, the *experience* is the same: recognizing that these phenomena share a consistent character that those do not. The concept names that experience, not any particular grouping.

subSections.label: Correction
items: "Type" names the structural experience of recognizing a shared fundamental character across phenomena. Which features are treated as fundamental can differ, but the experience of grouping by shared character is the same in every case.

nodes.claim: A question is a want for specific information.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the experience of seeking information — the directedness that drives inquiry and makes knowledge or ignorance possible.
nodes.search: question inquiry wondering seeking information want direction asking curiosity

sections.title: Observations
items: A strange taste — and a pull toward what it is.
A loud sound in the dark — wanting directed at where it came from.
An unfamiliar face — wanting the features that identify it.
A feeling of being lost — wanting directed at which direction to go.
An unexpected ache — wanting directed at what is occurring.
A half-remembered melody — wanting the information that completes it.

items.text: A question is a want for specific information.
items: A "question" is a wanting (1.2.5.1.1) whose direction (1.2.5.1.2) is specific information (1.2.1.1). The pull toward what a taste is, the wanting directed at where a sound came from — each is a question.

The "specific" information is what distinguishes one question from another: wanting to identify a taste is a different question from wanting to identify a sound, because the direction of the wanting is different.

items.title: No basis for distinguishing inquiry from other kinds of wanting
items.detail: Without recognizing questions, wanting directed at information has no distinct label. Wanting food and wanting to identify a taste become structurally identical — both are just "wanting." Knowledge and ignorance cannot be built, because they depend on whether or not a question's specific direction is met or not.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The vocabulary of "question" — a want for specific information.
items: "Question" — a want for specific information. Synonyms: inquiry, wondering.
Also grounded: "ask" (to direct a question), "seek" (wanting directed at information not yet occurring).
The next step: what happens when the wanted information occurs — or does not (1.2.6.2 — answers).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: All wanting is structurally identical — no distinction between wanting food and wanting information about food.
Inquiry has no experiential structure of its own — it is just generic wanting that happens to involve information.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not the wanted information occurs — addressed next (1.2.6.2 — answers).
What states result from a question being met or unmet — addressed later (1.2.6.3 — knowledge, 1.2.6.4 — ignorance).
Whether or not questions require language — this defines the experiential structure, not its mode of expression.

items.title: Questions require language — without words, there is no questioning.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Questions are linguistic acts. "What is that?" requires words, grammar, and the capacity to formulate a sentence.
If questioning requires language, then defining a question as a "want for information" is too broad — it includes pre-linguistic states that aren't really questions.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Questions are necessarily linguistic — without language, there is no structural difference between wanting food and wanting to identify a taste.
The experience of "wanting information" in a pre-linguistic creature is not a question but something simpler — mere curiosity or exploration.
The definition smuggles in linguistic capacity by treating any want-for-information as a question.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 conflates the expression of a question with the experience of questioning. The observations — a pull toward what a taste is, wanting directed at where a sound came from — describe an experiential structure: wanting whose direction is specific information. This structure occurs whether or not it is expressed in words.

The objector needs commitment #2 to hold: that without language, the experience of wanting-directed-at-information is structurally identical to wanting-directed-at-food. But consider the difference between hunger (wanting food) and the pull toward identifying a strange taste. The direction of the wanting is different in kind: one is directed at a sensation, the other at information about a sensation.
Commitment #3 has the dependency backwards. The definition identifies the experiential structure. Language is one way that structure gets expressed — not a requirement for the structure to occur.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The linguistic form "what is that?" is one way a question occurs, but the underlying structure — wanting directed at specific information — occurs with or without language. The definition identifies the experiential structure, not the mode of expression.

items.title: Wanting information is just wanting — it doesn't need its own label.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: All wanting has direction (1.2.5.1.2). A question is just a want whose direction happens to be information. No new phenomenon is observed — only a special case of what is already established.
If every special case of wanting gets its own label, the vocabulary multiplies without limit.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Since direction already covers what a want is aimed at, specifying "information" as the target adds nothing structurally new.
Labels should only be introduced when a genuinely new phenomenon is observed, not for every combination of existing terms.
Questions are fully reducible to wanting-plus-information-as-direction, which is already described.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 is correct that questions are composed of prior vocabulary — this is a labeling node. But commitment #1 misses why the label matters: wanting directed at information produces a structurally distinct kind of outcome.

The success of wanting food is the occurrence of food. The success of wanting to identify a taste is the occurrence of an identification. The outcomes differ: one changes what is experienced, the other changes what information is present. Without naming the want that produces this distinct outcome, knowledge and ignorance have no anchor.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This is a labeling node, and the objector is right that questions are composed of prior vocabulary. The label is needed because wanting-directed-at-information produces distinct outcomes — knowledge or ignorance — that cannot be described without first recognizing the distinct kind of want that produces them.

nodes.claim: An answer is the occurrence of a question's wanted information.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the moment when a question's direction is met — the event that distinguishes knowledge from ignorance.
nodes.search: answer response result information occurrence question satisfied met found

sections.title: Observations
items: A strange taste — then recognition: chocolate. The wanted information occurs.
A loud sound — then turning and seeing a cat. The information of the source occurs.
An unfamiliar melody — then hearing its title. The wanted identification occurs.
Being lost — then seeing a landmark. The information of the direction occurs.
An unexpected ache — then noticing a bruise. The information of what is occurring arrives.

items.text: An answer is the occurrence of a question's wanted information.
items: An "answer" is when the specific information that a question (1.2.6.1) is directed at actually occurs. The question "what is that taste?" is answered when the identification "chocolate" occurs.
An answer is the success (1.2.5.1.3) of a question — the occurrence of what the question wanted.

items.title: No distinction between information that meets a question and information that does not
items.detail: Without recognizing answers, the occurrence of a question's wanted information is indistinguishable from any other occurrence of information. There is no basis for saying a question has been "met" — and therefore no basis for knowledge (having an answer) or ignorance (lacking one).

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The vocabulary of "answer" — the occurrence of a question's wanted information.
items: "Answer" — the occurrence of a question's wanted information. Synonyms: response, finding.
Also grounded: "found" (the wanted information has occurred), "resolved" (the question's direction is met).
The next step: labeling the states that result — knowledge when an answer occurs (1.2.6.3), ignorance when it does not (1.2.6.4).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: The occurrence of a question's wanted information is no different from any other information occurring — no structural distinction between "finding out" and "just experiencing."
Questions can be directed at information but can never be met — the concept of a question being satisfied has no ground.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not an answer corresponds to what is actually the case — the distinction between correct and incorrect answers requires ontological vocabulary not yet built (1.3).
What state results from having an answer versus lacking one — addressed next (1.2.6.3 — knowledge, 1.2.6.4 — ignorance).

items.title: Wrong answers are still answers — this definition only covers correct ones.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: If someone asks "what is that taste?" and thinks "vanilla" when it is actually chocolate, an answer occurred — just a wrong one.

The definition says an answer is the occurrence of the question's wanted information. But "vanilla" is not the correct information, yet it still feels like an answer. The definition seems to exclude wrong answers.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: "Wrong answer" is a coherent category: information can occur in response to a question and still be incorrect.
The definition requires that the *correct* wanted information occur, thereby excluding wrong answers from counting as answers at all.
A definition of "answer" that cannot accommodate error is too narrow.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 reads the definition as requiring correctness, but the definition says "the occurrence of a question's wanted information" — not "the occurrence of the correct information." The question "what is that taste?" wants an identification. When "vanilla" occurs as an identification, the question's direction has been met: wanted information has occurred.

Whether or not that identification corresponds to what is actually the case is a separate question — one that requires the distinction between what occurs and what is real (1.3). At this level, an answer is the occurrence of information that meets a question's direction, whether or not that information is later found to be wrong.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The definition covers any occurrence of information that meets a question's direction — including cases where that information later turns out not to correspond with what is actually the case. The distinction between correct and incorrect answers requires ontological vocabulary not yet available.

items.title: Information often occurs without any question preceding it — seeing red doesn't answer anything.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Information occurs constantly — sensations, recognitions, identifications — without any preceding question. Seeing red, feeling warmth, recognizing a face: these are all occurrences of information, but none of them are answers.
If answers are just "occurrences of information," then everything is an answer, and the concept is vacuous.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: The definition fails to distinguish answers from ordinary occurrences of information.
Information that occurs without a preceding question is structurally identical to information that occurs with one.
If the distinction depends entirely on whether or not a question was active, then "answer" is just a relational label with no experiential content.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 misses the structural difference. When a question is active, the occurrence of its wanted information meets the wanting — the direction is satisfied and the pull subsides. When no question is active, the same information occurs but without satisfying any wanting. Seeing red without a question is perception (1.2.5.2.3). Seeing red when the question "what color is that?" is active is an answer.

Commitment #3 is half right: an answer IS relational — it depends on a question. But "relational" does not mean "no experiential content." The experience of a question being met — the pull subsiding, the direction satisfied — is itself a distinct quality. It differs from information merely occurring.

subSections.label: Correction
items: An answer is specifically the occurrence of information that meets a question's direction. Information that occurs without a preceding question is not an answer — it is perception, recognition, or identification. The distinction is structural: an answer satisfies a wanting that was directed at specific information.

nodes.claim: Knowledge is when an answer occurs.
nodes.soWhat: Names the state of having an answer — the basis for distinguishing what is known from what is not.
nodes.search: knowledge knowing awareness information answer known understanding epistemic

sections.title: Observations
items: The taste is chocolate — the identification is present, not sought.
Two plus two is four — the information is there, stable, available.
North is that direction — the information holds without effort.
The smell is smoke — the identification persists.
A face is a friend's — the recognition remains.

items.text: Knowledge is when an answer occurs.
items: "Knowledge" is the state in which a question's wanted information has occurred — the answer (1.2.6.2) is present. The taste has been identified as chocolate; that information is now present rather than sought.
Knowledge is to questions what success (1.2.5.1.3) is to wanting: the occurrence of what was directed at.

items.title: No distinction between having an answer and still seeking one
items.detail: Without recognizing knowledge, the state of having an answer is indistinguishable from still seeking one. There is no difference between "the taste has been identified" and "the taste has not been identified" — and therefore no basis for learning (changing from not having an answer to having one) or forgetting (the reverse).

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The vocabulary of "knowledge" — when an answer occurs.
items: "Knowledge" — the state in which a question's wanted information has occurred. Synonyms: knowing, awareness-of-an-answer.
Also grounded: "known" (information that has occurred as an answer), "understand" (having the answer to a question about how something works).
The next step: labeling the opposite state — when an answer does not occur (1.2.6.4 — ignorance) — and the transitions between them (1.2.6.5 — learning, 1.2.6.6 — forgetting).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Having an answer and not having one are the same state — there is no structural difference between knowing and not knowing.
Knowledge is inaccessible or unachievable — questions can be asked but never meaningfully resolved.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not knowledge corresponds to what is actually the case — the distinction between knowledge and correct knowledge requires ontological vocabulary not yet built (1.3).
Whether or not knowledge can be certain or only approximate — addressed at a later level.
What happens when knowledge is lost — addressed later (1.2.6.6 — forgetting).

items.title: Knowledge requires justification, not just having an answer — this is too thin.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Since Plato, knowledge has been understood as more than just having information. The standard account requires justified true belief: not just that an answer occurred, but that it is true and that there are good reasons for holding it.
Defining knowledge as merely "when an answer occurs" strips away everything that makes knowledge different from lucky guessing.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Knowledge is not merely having an answer but having a *justified true* answer — the justification and truth conditions are part of what "knowledge" means.
Without justification and truth, the definition cannot distinguish between knowing something and merely believing it.
The justification condition must be present at the definitional level, not deferred to later vocabulary.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 demands that justification and truth be captured here, at the point where knowledge is first identified. But both "justification" (reasoning about whether or not an answer is well-supported) and "truth" (correspondence with what is actually the case) require vocabulary not yet available — reasoning is addressed at 1.5, and correspondence with reality at 1.3.

Commitment #2 is the real concern: without justification and truth, can this definition distinguish knowing from guessing? At this level, yes — but only partially. Knowledge here is the state of having an answer; guessing is a possibility (1.2.5.6.4) or a hope (1.2.5.7.3) — a thought based on a want, not the occurrence of a question's wanted information. The distinction is experiential: the information has occurred versus the information has not occurred.

The JTB account adds conditions that refine this initial distinction. It does not replace it — it builds on it. Even justified true belief requires that the believer *have* the information in question. This node identifies that foundational state.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This identifies the foundational state that all accounts of knowledge share: the wanted information has occurred. Justification and truth-correspondence are refinements that require vocabulary not yet built — they do not replace the basic experiential state of having an answer but add conditions to it.

items.title: Knowledge should be stable and enduring — but answers can be fleeting.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: If an answer occurs and is immediately forgotten, was that knowledge? A taste identified for a split second and then gone doesn't seem like "knowing."
Knowledge implies a durable state — information that is retained, available, and accessible — not a momentary flash.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Knowledge requires persistence — information that occurs and immediately vanishes is not knowledge.
The definition fails to capture the durability that distinguishes knowledge from a fleeting impression.
Duration is a necessary condition of knowledge, not a refinement to be added later.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 introduces a threshold: how long must information persist to count as knowledge? One second? One hour? Permanently? The objector needs to specify where the threshold falls, and any specific threshold will be arbitrary.

Consider the observations: "the taste is chocolate" — that information is present right now. Whether or not it persists for an hour or is forgotten in the next moment does not change the fact that, right now, an answer has occurred. If it is later forgotten, that transition has its own label: forgetting (1.2.6.6). But the forgetting presupposes that knowledge existed — otherwise there is nothing to lose.

Commitment #3 conflates knowledge with memory (1.2.5.3.4). That knowledge often persists as memory is an observation about how knowledge commonly occurs — not a definitional requirement. The definition identifies the state; persistence describes one way that state continues.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Knowledge is the state of having an answer — whether or not that state lasts a moment or a lifetime. If it fades, that is forgetting (1.2.6.6), which presupposes knowledge existed. Duration describes how knowledge persists, not what knowledge is.

nodes.claim: Ignorance is when an answer does not occur.
nodes.soWhat: Names the state of not having an answer — the complement of knowledge, and one of the two possible outcomes of a question.
nodes.search: ignorance not knowing unknown unanswered lacking information gap

sections.title: Observations
items: A strange taste — and the identification does not come. The pull persists.
A sound in the dark — and the source remains absent. The wanting continues.
