Calling them "independent from want" sneaks in the suggestion that they stand in some opposition or relation to want — as if they register it and resist it. That is a projection error: wanting is a mental phenomenon, and inanimate things cannot be independent-of-something they have no access to.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Walls, feathers, and other phenomena have no mental states.
2. Saying a phenomenon is "independent from want" attributes a relationship-to-want to the phenomenon itself.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 misreads what the independence is between. The claim does not place wanting into the wall. It names two observed occurrences — a want (wanting the wall to yield) and a phenomenon (the wall remaining) — and says they do not correlate (1.2.5.7.1).

The independence holds between observed occurrences, not within the wall. The observations make this visible: wanting an object to be a different shape and the shape being what it is are two separate occurrences, not a property of the object's inner life.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names a relationship between observed occurrences, not a property of things. Whether or not any phenomenon has an intrinsic mental quality is not addressed here — the claim only tracks the non-correlation between the want and the phenomenon's occurrence. The label "limit" belongs to the phenomenon as encountered, not to any attributed inner state.

items.title: What is called a limit is often just current ignorance — aircraft overcame flight, medicine overcame illness, so limits dissolve with enough effort.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Many of what previous eras called limits — flight, communication across distance, disease — became routine in later ones. Treating independence-from-want as a stable structure misses that it is a moving boundary shifted by want's accumulating capacity. What seems independent today is only what has not yet been overcome.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Many historical limits have been overcome through technology, practice, or knowledge.
2. If limits can be overcome, they are not truly independent of want — only temporarily resistant.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 conflates overcoming with dissolving. A successful flight in an aircraft still requires conformity to what is independent of want — the aircraft's weight, the atmosphere, the structural tolerances, gravity. The feather rising when lifted did not undo its weight; it proceeded by way of its weight.

What changes across history is the specific configuration under which an outcome is achieved. What does not change is that each step of the way proceeds by conformity to limits not given by wanting. The shape of a held object is unchanged by wanting it different, even when the holding succeeds.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the phenomenon of independence from want — not a permanent prohibition on specific outcomes. Whether or not a given limit can be worked around by finding routes that conform to other limits is a separate question, and those workarounds proceed by way of limits, not against them.

nodes.claim: An object is a structure with nature.
nodes.soWhat: Names the unit encountered in experience — a set of limits cohering into one whole with features of its own. Without it, reality is a field of loose features; with it, the stone, the hand, the tree, the room are each a unit with a character, available for existence and observation to attach to.

sections.title: Observations
items: A stone held in the hand, its weight and coldness and rough surface all at once.
A hand held up, fingers and palm and thumb as one shape.
A room walked through, floor and walls and ceiling as one enclosure.
An apple bitten, its roundness and firmness and sweetness all of one fruit.

items.text: An object is a structure with nature.
items: An "object" is a structure (1.3.3) whose limits together have a nature (1.3.2) — a set of features belonging to the whole. The stone, the hand, the tree, the room — each a set of limits cohering into one unit with its own features.

Features of the whole are distinct from features of the parts. Each brick in a wall is {hard, rectangular}; the wall itself is {vertical, enclosing, blocking}. Each finger has its own nature; the hand has its own — jointed, grasping, warm.

Not every set of limits forms an object. A ceiling beam, a shoe, and a cloud outside are three limits but are not encountered as one unit. The label marks the subset of structures whose limits cohere into one whole with features of its own.

items.title: Limits stay loose — no unit for what coheres into a whole.
items.detail: Without recognizing object, heavy-cold-rough is one bundle and jointed-reaching-warm is another, but neither is the stone or the hand. Nothing ties a set of limits into a single encountered unit. Existence has no foothold, observation has no target, and reality as a population of units loses its ground.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Object" — a structure with nature. The stone, the hand, the tree, the room, the cup — each a set of limits cohering into a unit with features of its own.

Also grounded: "entity," "item," "body" (in the sense of a structured unit with its own features), "unit" (in the sense of a coherent structured whole), "whole" (in the sense of an object as distinct from its parts).

The next steps: what it is for an object to occur (existence, 1.3.4.2), how objects enter experience through the senses (observation, 1.3.4.3), and from there the features of objects that make ontological grounding possible.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Only features exist — the wholes called objects are just convenient labels for groupings of limits, with nothing extra.
Every set of limits is an object — the label adds nothing beyond "structure" (1.3.3).
Objects are mental constructions imposed on an undifferentiated field — their unity is added, not encountered.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not objects exist independently of being encountered is not addressed here — this names the structure-with-nature pattern, not its mode of occurrence (that is taken up at 1.3.4.2 and 1.3.4.6).

Whether or not the boundaries of an object can be drawn in multiple ways — where the hand ends and the arm begins, where one tree ends and the forest begins — is not addressed here. The claim names the pattern of unit-with-features, not a rule for every edge case.

Whether or not objects can contain other objects as parts — a wall of bricks, a body of limbs, a forest of trees — is not addressed here. Both levels can fit the same pattern without this claim ranking which is more fundamental.

items.title: The "nature" of the whole is just the union of the natures of the parts — objects are structures, and the label adds nothing.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Nature (1.3.2) attaches to limits individually. A structure (1.3.3) is a set of limits. Each limit has its own nature. The "nature" of the whole structure is just the union of its limits' natures — so calling an object "a structure with nature" labels something every structure already is. No new pattern is named; a new word for the same phenomenon is introduced.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. The nature of a structure is the union of the natures of its component limits.
2. If #1, then "object" names nothing beyond what "structure" already names.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 overlooks features that belong to the whole but not to any part. A brick is {hard, rectangular}; the wall made of bricks is {vertical, enclosing, blocking}. Enclosing is not a feature of any single brick — it occurs at the whole. A finger flexes; the hand grasps, and grasping is not a feature of any finger alone.

The observations make this visible: a room walked through is encountered as an enclosure — a feature of the room, not of each wall; an apple bitten is encountered as round-and-firm-and-sweet all at once — features of one fruit, not of any sub-part. The whole has features the parts individually do not.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the pattern where a structure's limits together produce features belonging to the whole — features not attributable to any part alone. Whether or not such whole-features could in principle be further decomposed into features of smaller limits is a separate question, not addressed here. The label picks out the phenomenon at the level of encounter: the hand grasps, the room encloses, even though no single finger grasps and no single wall encloses.

items.title: The unity of an object is added in how features are organized — the whole is not in what is encountered, only in the sorting of it.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: What is actually given in experience is a stream of features — colors, pressures, temperatures, shapes. These features get grouped into "the hand" or "the cup," but the grouping is an operation performed on what arrives, not part of what arrives. Calling the grouped result "a structure with nature" smuggles unity into the given where it actually belongs to the operation.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. What is directly given is a stream of separate features.
2. Unity of features into a whole is added later, by how they are put together.
3. Therefore, the "object" label treats the unity as given when it is in fact contributed afterward.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 is not supported by the observations. When a hand closes on a stone, its weight and coldness and rough surface do not arrive as three separate pieces awaiting unification — they arrive as one encounter. There is no prior stage of "bare feature arrival" before unity is applied.

The observations make this visible: a stone held all-at-once, a hand as one shape, a room as one enclosure, an apple as one fruit. The unity is part of how the limits occur, not a later operation performed on them.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the phenomenon of limits occurring together as a unit with features of its own. Whether or not any further organizing also runs alongside the occurrence is not addressed here. The claim concerns the pattern of unity as it arrives; it does not pronounce on what may or may not happen to it afterward.

nodes.claim: Existence is the occurrence of an object.
nodes.soWhat: Gives "existence" a precise meaning — not any kind of occurrence, but specifically the occurrence of an object. Makes "what is there?" answerable by pointing at what occurs as a structure-with-nature, rather than at every phenomenon that happens in experience.

sections.title: Observations
items: A cup resting on the table right now.
A tree standing in the yard.
A stone on the path, underfoot.
A person breathing in the next room.

items.text: Existence is the occurrence of an object.
items: "Existence" is when an object (1.3.4.1) occurs — a structure-with-nature occurring as a phenomenon. To exist is to be there as a unit with features of its own.

This narrows the word from any kind of occurrence to the specific case where what occurs is an object. Wants occur; imaginings occur; thoughts occur. "Exists" specifically names the occurrence of objects — cups, trees, stones, hands, rooms.

The distinction makes "does X exist?" answerable. The question asks whether X is an object that occurs. Not every phenomenon is something that exists in this sense — but every object that occurs is something that exists.

items.title: "Exists" collapses into "occurs" — no distinction between a stone and a want.
items.detail: Without recognizing existence as the occurrence of an object, everything that occurs "exists" equally — wants, imaginings, thoughts, and stones all on the same footing. The distinction between what is there as a unit (a stone, handed to someone) and what is merely had (a fantasy that cannot be handed over) dissolves. Reality as a population of objects loses its footing.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Existence" / "exists" / "exist" — the occurrence of an object. The cup exists; the tree exists; the stone exists.
Also grounded: "there is" / "there are" (in the sense of an object occurring), "being" (in the sense of an object's occurrence), "is" (in the predicative sense of an object occurring).
The next steps: how objects enter experience through the senses (observation, 1.3.4.3), and from there the features of objects that make ontological grounding possible.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Everything that occurs exists in the same sense — there is no distinction between the occurrence of a stone and the occurrence of a want.
Existence applies to phenomena in general, not specifically to objects.
Nothing exists — only isolated features or fleeting occurrences do, and "existence" names nothing distinct.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not anything exists beyond what is currently encountered is not addressed here — this names what existence consists in, not which objects do or do not occur.

Whether or not abstract entities (numbers, possibilities, fictional characters) count as objects that exist is not addressed here — the label marks the occurrence of objects, and whether abstractions fit the structure-with-nature pattern is a separate application.
Whether or not existence admits of degrees — more fully existent versus less so — is not addressed here. The claim marks the occurrence of objects without ranking how fully they occur.

items.title: Pains, emotions, and other inner phenomena exist too — restricting "existence" to objects is artificially narrow.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: In ordinary speech, a pain exists while it is felt, anger exists when it grips someone, grief exists while mourned. Reserving "exists" for cups, stones, and trees ignores inner phenomena that are clearly there in experience. The narrowing is arbitrary and at odds with how the word is actually used.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Inner phenomena (pains, emotions, felt states) are commonly and correctly said to exist.
2. A definition that contradicts common usage fails to describe rather than clarifying.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 assumes the claim excludes inner phenomena from existence — but it does not necessarily. A felt pain has features (sharp, located, intense) that may cohere as a unit with its own nature; if so, the pain-as-encountered fits the structure-with-nature pattern, and the pain exists in the narrow sense of the claim.

The observations make this visible: a cup on the table, a tree in the yard — clear cases of object-occurrence. Whether a felt pain or a felt grief also fits the pattern is a case-by-case application of the same test, not a blanket exclusion.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the occurrence of objects as what "exists" picks out. Whether or not a given inner phenomenon counts as an object in this sense is a matter of whether it fits the structure-with-nature pattern — not addressed here. The label does not deny that inner phenomena can exist; it restricts "exists" to the occurrence of objects wherever they occur.

items.title: Existence isn't the same as present occurrence — the cup existed before anyone saw it and will exist after it is forgotten.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Objects exist whether or not they are presently being encountered. A cup left in a closed drawer still exists. A stone on the far side of a mountain exists without being seen. Defining existence as "the occurrence of an object" ties existence to present happening — falsely making unobserved objects not exist.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Objects can exist without being presently perceived or attended to.
2. "Occurrence" implies a phenomenon currently present to awareness.
3. Therefore, defining existence as occurrence-of-an-object makes awareness a condition of existence.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 imports a narrow reading of "occurrence" not required by prior grounding. A phenomenon (1.1.1) is anything that occurs; occurrence does not imply present attention. The cup in the drawer occurs as a cup — being there with its features — whether or not attention is currently on it.

The observations make this visible: returning to a cup left on the table to find it still there; coming back to a stone on the path still lying in the same spot. The cup's being-there does not start when it is first noticed or stop when it stops being attended to.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the occurrence of objects as what existence consists in. Whether or not an object must be presently attended to in order to occur is a separate question — the relationship between observation and occurrence is taken up directly at 1.3.4.6 and 1.3.4.7. The label "exists" covers the occurrence of objects, whether or not currently in view.

nodes.claim: An observation is the perception of an object.
nodes.soWhat: Names the act of taking in an object through the senses. Seeing a cup, feeling a stone, hearing a voice from across the room — each an encounter with an object, distinct from sensations (a diffuse warmth, a faint buzz) that are not directed at objects.

sections.title: Observations
items: Seeing a cup on the table.
Feeling a stone's weight in the hand.
Hearing a voice from across the room.
Smelling bread coming from the oven.

items.text: An observation is the perception of an object.
items: An "observation" is a perception (1.2.5.2.3) whose content is an object (1.3.4.1) — a sensation that takes in a structure-with-nature. Seeing a cup, feeling a stone's weight, hearing a voice, smelling bread — each an observation.

Observation is the mode through which an object enters experience. A cup's shape, color, weight, and temperature are taken in through seeing, holding, weighing, feeling. Its features are what is perceived when it is met as an object.
The label connects two things already in place: what is encountered (an object) and how it is encountered (perception). Observation names the meeting of the two.

items.title: Perception and object-encounter blur — no unit for meeting an object.
items.detail: Without recognizing observation, any sensation counts as perception — a toothache, a seen cup, a vague warmth, all the same. The act of encountering an object through the senses has no specific name. That objects can be newly met, that they hold their character across meetings, that they continue when unmet — none of these has the unit that observation provides.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Observation" / "observe" — the perception of an object. Seeing a cup, feeling a stone, hearing a voice, smelling bread — all observations.
Also grounded: "witness," "note," "take in" (in the sense of perceiving an object), "encounter" (in the sense of an object meeting the senses).

The next steps: that objects can appear as newly observed (1.3.4.4), that an object's nature holds steady across observations (1.3.4.5), and that the nature of an object is independent of its being observed (1.3.4.6).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: All perception is observation — the distinction between perceiving an object and perceiving a non-object sensation is empty.
Observation is a purely internal mental act — the object observed is incidental to what counts as observation.
Observation is a specifically scientific or theoretical activity — everyday seeing, holding, and hearing do not count.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not an observation accurately reports the object's full nature is not addressed here — the claim names the act of perceiving an object, not the reliability of what is perceived.

Whether or not objects can be known through routes other than direct perception (inference, language, memory of past encounters) is not addressed here — the claim names direct observation, not knowledge in general.

Whether or not some apparent observations are illusory — seeming to encounter an object where none is — is not addressed here. The label marks the pattern of perceiving an object; cases of error are taken up separately.

items.title: Observation is just perception — the label adds nothing new.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Every perception has content. Perceiving something is always perceiving some thing. Splitting off a subset called "observation" where the content is specifically an object labels what is already labeled — no new phenomenon is named, only a rebranded version of perception.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. All perception has some content.
2. If all perception has content, narrowing to a subset where the content is an object names nothing not already named by "perception."

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 overlooks that perception (1.2.5.2.3) covers any sensation's occurrence — including sensations whose content is not an object. The buzz of tinnitus, a diffuse feeling of unease, a gentle warmth spread across the skin — each is a perception, but none has an object (a structure-with-nature) as its content.

The observations make this visible: seeing a cup, feeling a stone, hearing a voice, smelling bread — in each, what is perceived is an object. The label marks what the other cases lack, not what they already share.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the subset of perceptions whose content is an object. The term is more specific than "perception" — that is the point. Observation picks out encounters with structures-with-nature, distinct from perceptions (buzzes, warmths, diffuse unease) where nothing object-like is the content.

items.title: What is called observation involves inference beyond bare perception — seeing a cup requires memory and categorization, not direct encounter.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Recognizing a cup requires memory, expectation, and category-matching. What is strictly perceived is patches of color and shape; the "cup" is built up from them. So calling observation "the perception of an object" smuggles inference into what is presented as simple perception.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Bare perception delivers only sensory features (color, shape, pressure), not objects.
2. Recognizing any object requires inferential steps beyond raw perception.
3. Therefore, "perception of an object" is not bare perception but perception plus inference.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 does not match the observations. When a hand closes on a stone, its weight, shape, and coldness arrive as one occurrence — not as three separate sensations to be assembled later. The object is what is given in the perception, not a construction added after.

The observations make this visible: in seeing a cup, feeling a stone, hearing a voice, smelling bread, there is no prior stage of "feature-only perception" followed by "object inference." The object is what is there in the perception from the start.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the pattern of an object occurring in perception. Whether or not further operations — naming, recognition, memory matching — also run alongside is not addressed here. Splitting perception into "bare" and "inferential" layers would require vocabulary for cognitive steps not yet in place. The label here marks only the case where what is perceived is a structure-with-nature, as given.

nodes.claim: New objects appear in observation.
nodes.soWhat: Names the phenomenon of first encounters — that observation regularly delivers objects whose features match nothing in memory. Without it, observation is only re-presentation of what is already known; with it, experience has a way of meeting what is not already accounted for.

sections.title: Observations
items: Turning a corner and seeing a building not seen before.
Tasting a fruit, with nothing in memory to match its flavor.
A stranger entering the room, a face unfamiliar.
Opening a box, finding a tool whose shape is new.

items.text: New objects appear in observation.
items: Observation (1.3.4.3) regularly includes encounters with objects (1.3.4.1) that occur without recognition — new (1.2.5.3.6) objects. Turning a corner to see a building not seen before, tasting a fruit unlike anything tasted, meeting a stranger: each is an object whose features do not match anything in memory.
Observation is not only the re-encounter with objects already known. It regularly produces first encounters — objects whose content cannot be reconstructed from prior observations.
The pattern is recognizable in experience. Not every observation is of something remembered.

items.title: Observation is locked to memory — nothing encountered is ever really first.
items.detail: Without new objects appearing, every observation re-presents something already known. No first encounters, no discoveries, no foreign land. Learning about objects through observation becomes impossible, since every observation's content could be reconstructed from prior ones. The idea that observation puts one in touch with what is not already accounted for — that reality can surprise — collapses.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "New object" / "unfamiliar object" / "strange object" — an object that appears in observation without recognition.
Also grounded: "first encounter," "discovery" (in the sense of observation meeting an object not previously met), "novel" (applied to objects), "unknown" (applied to an object not yet observed).

The next steps: that an object's nature holds steady across observations (1.3.4.5), that the nature is independent of the observation itself (1.3.4.6), and that not all objects are currently observed (1.3.4.7).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Observation only recirculates what memory already contains — all observed objects are recognized.
What seem like new objects are only recombinations of features already known — no objects are genuinely new in content.
The sense of novelty in observation is a misperception — what seems new is always familiar once examined closely.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not the source of new objects is external to the observer is not addressed here — this names the pattern of first-encounter in observation, not the origin of the objects that appear.
Whether or not every apparent new object is truly new (rather than forgotten or only dimly remembered) is not addressed here — the claim names the recurring pattern of fresh encounters.
Whether or not a new object's appearance can be predicted or expected beforehand is not addressed here — the claim names that such appearances occur, not under what conditions.

items.title: What appears as a new object is just a novel combination of features already observed — nothing genuinely new.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Any apparently new object can be decomposed into features already known. A new fruit is a new combination of shape, color, taste — each element already experienced elsewhere. Imagination (1.2.5.6.1) is information drawn from different memories; new objects are just the real-world analog. Calling these "new" oversells what is happening: recombination, not novelty of content.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Every feature of an apparently new object has been observed in some prior object.
2. If #1, the new object is a recombination, not a genuine novelty.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 overstates the case. A tasted fruit can have a flavor that does not decompose into familiar tastes — not merely a rearrangement of known components. Colors of unfamiliar shade, textures of unfamiliar feel, timbres of unfamiliar sound all appear in observation as content, not as reshuffles.

The observations make this visible: turning a corner to see a building with shapes and proportions unmatched by any memory; tasting a fruit whose flavor does not resolve into components tasted before. The novelty is at the level of content, not only of arrangement.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the pattern of objects appearing in observation without matching memory. Whether or not some apparent new objects are recombinations of already-observed features is a separate case — recombination is one way objects can come to seem new. The claim covers the broader pattern: observation delivers encounters where no match is found, by content or by arrangement.

items.title: What seems new is really weakly recognized — the sense of novelty is partial recognition, not genuine first encounter.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Recognition (1.2.5.3.5) admits of degrees. What appears as a new object may be only dimly matched to something in memory — the match is weak, so it seems unfamiliar, but no object is ever truly new. Everything observed draws on what has been observed before, if only implicitly.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Every observed object has some prior analog in memory, however partial.
2. What seems new is really partially-recognized, not genuinely unrecognized.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 is not supported by the observations. A first taste of a fruit, with no prior taste to partially match, is a pure first-encounter — not a weak recognition. The infant's first encounter with any object is of this kind, and the pattern continues throughout life whenever observation delivers features falling outside any past observation.

The observations make this visible: tasting a fruit with nothing in memory to match its flavor; a stranger's face bearing no partial resemblance to any remembered face. Weak recognition would still be some match; in these cases there is none.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the pattern of observation producing objects without recognition (1.2.5.3.6). Whether or not some borderline cases are better described as "weak recognition" than as full novelty is a separate question; the claim addresses the clear cases where no match is available. The label covers first-encounters where memory offers nothing.

nodes.claim: An object's nature is consistent across observations.
nodes.soWhat: Names the pattern of object-identity — the same features found each time an object is observed. Without it, every look is at a potentially different object; with it, objects become returnable, studyable, the same thing found again.

sections.title: Observations
items: A cup on the table, its shape the same from across the room as from up close.
A stone in the hand, its weight the same each time it is lifted.
A voice recognized across a conversation, its timbre holding from one sentence to the next.
A chair seen from different sides, its shape the same from each.

items.text: An object's nature is consistent across observations.
items: An object (1.3.4.1) observed (1.3.4.3) more than once shows the same nature (1.3.2) across those observations — consistency (1.2.5.7.5) in its features. The cup's shape does not shift between looks; the stone's weight does not change between lifts; the voice's timbre holds across a conversation.

Variation across observations — of angle, lighting, distance — is in how the object is presented, not in its features. The cup looks smaller from across the room, but its shape, handle, rim, and color hold.
This is a recognizable pattern. Returning attention to an object finds its features as they were. Different observations of the same object match in what they present.

items.title: Objects have no stable identity across encounters.
items.detail: Without recognizing nature's consistency across observations, every new look is potentially at a different object. Nothing secures the cup-now as the same cup-later. Learning about objects through repeated observation fails, and the world becomes a sequence of flashes rather than a population of returnable things.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "The same object" / "this object" (across observations) — an object recognizable as the same by its nature holding across observations of it.

Also grounded: "stays the same," "still the same thing" (across observations), "object identity" (in the sense of nature holding across observations), "found as it was" (in the sense of return to an object with its features intact).
The next step: that an object's nature is not only consistent across observations, but independent of observation altogether (1.3.4.6), and that not all objects are currently observed (1.3.4.7).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Every observation is of a different object — no object survives a second look.
An object's nature varies with the conditions of observation — angle, lighting, or time produce different natures.
Consistency of nature is a habit of memory projecting sameness, not a pattern in what is observed.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not objects change their nature over longer spans of time — a tree growing, a stone eroding — is not addressed here. The claim names consistency across observations, leaving large-scale change (1.2.5.3.8) for separate treatment.
Whether or not an object's nature is exhaustively revealed by observation is not addressed here — the claim says the nature observed is consistent, not that all features are always in view.

Whether or not the observer's state affects what of the nature is noticed is not addressed here — variations in attention may change which features are attended to, without changing the features themselves.

items.title: Observations vary — a cup looks smaller from across the room than up close. The "same nature" is a projection of habit, not a fact of the object.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: When observations of what is called the same object are compared carefully, they differ — in visual size, in color under different lighting, in loudness from different distances. The feeling of sameness is memory smoothing over these differences. Calling the nature "consistent" treats a cognitive habit as if it were an observed pattern.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Observations of what is called the same object differ across conditions.
2. Differences across observations contradict consistency of nature.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 conflates variation in how an object is observed with variation in what is observed. A cup looks smaller from across the room — but smallness-at-a-distance is not a change in the cup's shape; it is a consequence of where the observation is made from, not of the cup.

The observations make this visible: a cup's shape staying the same from across the room as from up close. What holds is the cup's shape, not the visual size in the field of view. A stone's weight does not change between lifts; a voice's timbre holds across a conversation. The features hold as the observational circumstances change.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the pattern of an object's nature holding across observations. Whether or not observations themselves vary in how they present objects — smaller from afar, brighter in sunlight — is a separate matter. The nature is what holds across such variations; that it holds is an observed pattern, not a projection imposed on unrelated observations.

items.title: Everything changes — the stone weathers, the tree grows, no nature is ever truly consistent.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Nothing is stable on close enough inspection. The stone weathers, the tree grows, the cup's glaze dulls. Calling any nature "consistent" is at best an approximation that fails under sustained scrutiny. At no pair of moments is an object exactly the same as at any other.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. All objects undergo continuous change, however slow.
2. If change is continuous, consistency of nature is strictly false.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 sets too strict a standard. The claim addresses consistency across observations, not unchangeableness across all spans of time. Across the span of a conversation, a voice's timbre holds. Across a return-visit to a table, the cup's shape holds. These are the patterns that the claim names.

The observations make this visible: a voice's timbre steady across a conversation; a chair's shape the same from different sides. At the scale of observing and returning, the nature holds. Slower drift — growth, erosion — operates at a different grain.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the pattern of nature holding across observations. Whether or not, over longer spans, the nature drifts (growth, erosion, decay) is addressed at the level of temporal change (1.2.5.3.8), not at the level of observation-to-observation identity. The label picks out the scale at which observation finds the nature stable enough to return to.

nodes.claim: An object's nature is independent from its observation.
nodes.soWhat: Names the pivotal independence — an object's features do not depend on observation for their hold. The cup's shape is its shape watched or not; the stone's weight is its weight looked at or not. This is what makes objects something encountered rather than produced, and what lets reality surprise and correct.

sections.title: Observations
items: A cup on the table, its shape unchanged by looking away and looking back.
A stone left on the path, found unchanged when returned to.
A voice continuing from the next room when no one is attending.
A room returned to, the walls still where they were.

items.text: An object's nature is independent from its observation.
items: The nature (1.3.2) of an object (1.3.4.1) is independent (1.2.5.7.4) of its observation (1.3.4.3). Variations in observation — attending or not, from different angles, at different times, at different distances — do not produce corresponding variations in the object's features.

The cup's shape is its shape, watched or not. The stone's weight is its weight, looked at or not. Closing one's eyes does not change the weight of what is held; looking away does not alter the cup's shape; attending elsewhere does not dissolve the voice in the next room.

This is a stronger claim than that the same nature appears across multiple observations. It says: the nature holds whether or not any observation takes place at all. The features are not produced by the observing.

items.title: The object collapses into the observation of it.
items.detail: Without this independence, an object's features are only what is observed of it at that moment. Look away, the cup's shape is not. Stop listening, the voice is not. Objects become shadows of observations, with no independent ground. Reality as what is encountered rather than made — what one can be wrong about, what rewards return by being there regardless — loses its footing.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Independent nature" / "objective nature" — an object's features holding regardless of whether, how, or when it is observed.

Also grounded: "external" (in the sense of an object's nature not depending on being observed), "real" (in the sense of a nature holding whether observed or not), "objective" (in the sense of a feature holding across observers and times of observation), "out there" (in the sense of an object whose nature is not contributed by the observing of it).
The next step: that not all objects that exist are currently observed (1.3.4.7) — completing the bridge from experience to reality as a population of objects that hold on their own.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: An object is only what it is observed to be — an unobserved object has no nature.
Observation produces the observed object's features — without observation, the features are not there.
Every observational frame produces its own object-nature — there is no observer-independent nature to be had.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not the act of observation can causally alter the object in specialized physical setups — for example, interference at atomic scales — is not addressed here. The claim names the ordinary pattern at the scale of everyday objects.

Whether or not the full nature of an object can be grasped by any single observation is not addressed here — the claim says the nature does not depend on observation, not that it is exhaustively revealed to any one observation.

Whether or not there is any mode of access to objects apart from observation is not addressed here — the claim concerns the relationship between observation and nature, not other possible modes of access.

items.title: All evidence about an object comes from observation — claiming the nature holds beyond observation is speculation.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Every piece of evidence for an object's nature is an observation. The claim that its nature holds when unobserved is not itself an observation — it is an inference from within observation that goes beyond what observation can report. Strictly, one can say only: the nature shows up consistently when observed. The further step — that it holds when not observed — has no evidential ground.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. All evidence about an object's nature comes from observation.
2. A claim about nature-when-not-observed cannot be evidenced by observation.
3. Therefore, the independence claim goes beyond the evidence.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 treats "nature-when-not-observed" as requiring special evidence. But the claim can be tested in the ordinary way: look away and look back. The cup's shape is there — the same shape — after the break in observation. The inference is not from inside observation to outside it; it is from observations-with-gaps to the object's holding across those gaps.

The observations make this visible: the cup unchanged by looking away and looking back; the stone left on the path, found unchanged when returned to; the room returned to with the walls where they were. The pattern across gaps is itself observed.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the pattern of nature-continuity across gaps in observation — the object's features found in place each time attention returns. Whether such continuity counts as strict evidence for nature-when-never-observed-at-all is a separate metaphysical question, not addressed here. The label marks the observed pattern: the features hold across the gaps, whatever else may happen during them.

items.title: Observation shapes what is observed — the object's features take the form they do because of how observation structures them.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Every observation is conditioned by the observer's senses, angle, attention, and prior concepts. What is called the object's nature is never the object itself, but a presentation shaped by the act of observing. To claim the nature is independent of observation ignores that observation is the medium through which any nature appears at all.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Every observation is shaped by the conditions of observing.
2. What appears as an object's nature is always shaped by those conditions.
3. Therefore, nature cannot be separated from the observation that presents it.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 conflates two separable things: how an observation presents an object, and what the object's features are. Different observations of the same cup — from different angles, in different lighting — present it differently. But what the cup is, by its features, does not shift with these presentations; the shifts are in the presenting, not in the presented.

The observations make this visible: the cup's shape unchanged by looking away and looking back; the stone unchanged when returned to; the voice continuing from the next room when no one is attending. The conditions of observation change; the features of the object do not.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the pattern where an object's features do not co-vary with observation. Whether or not every observation is conditioned by the observer's circumstances is not denied — observations do differ in how they present. What "independent from observation" names here is the holding-across-presentations: the features are what they are across the various ways they come to be presented.

nodes.claim: Not all possible objects are currently observed.
nodes.soWhat: Names the incompleteness of present observation relative to the broader space of objects matching recognized patterns. Without it, observation exhausts what objects there could be; with it, the observed is a subset of the possible, and discovery of what was already consistent with patterns becomes intelligible.

sections.title: Observations
items: Opening a drawer and finding a pen not attended to before.
Turning around in a room and seeing a chair that was behind.
Walking into another room and finding furniture unchanged from the last visit.
Lifting a stone to find an insect underneath.

items.text: Not all possible objects are currently observed.
items: A possible (1.2.5.6.4) object (1.3.4.1) is one matching recognized patterns of objecthood — the pen matching the pattern of pens, the chair matching the pattern of chairs, the insect matching the pattern of insects. At any moment, observation (1.3.4.3) takes in some of these, not all.

The cup on the table is a possible object that is also currently observed. The pen in the closed drawer, the chair behind, the furniture in the other room, the insect under the stone — each is a possible object, matching recognized patterns of what objects are like, yet not currently observed.

Each discovery — opening the drawer, turning around, entering the other room, lifting the stone — is a possibility moving into observation. The scope of possible objects is larger than what is in observation at any one moment.

items.title: Possibility collapses into current observation.
items.detail: Without recognizing this scope-gap, every possible object is also a currently-observed one — nothing consistent with recognized patterns could fail to be in view right now. Discovery becomes impossible, since finding something would require it to be both possible and yet not currently observed. The sense of the world extending beyond the present scene, of things waiting to be found, of returning to what has stayed — all lose their ground.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Unobserved possible object" — a possible object that is not currently observed. The pen in the closed drawer, the chair behind, the furniture in the next room, the insect under the stone.

Also grounded: "elsewhere," "out of sight" (in the sense of a possible object not currently observed), "undiscovered" (in the sense of a possible object not yet observed), "could be there" (in the sense of an object matching recognized patterns without being currently in view).

The next step: with object, existence, observation, consistency, independence, and the scope-gap between possibility and observation all in place, the branch generalizes into the full ontological bridge (1.3.4). From there: the full population of objects is reality (1.3.5), and what holds between objects is relationship (1.3.6).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: The currently-observed scene is all the objects there could be — possibility extends no further than what is presently in view.
Objects come into being when observed — a possible object unobserved is no object at all.
Discovery is a kind of creation — what is found takes on its features in the finding, rather than being a possibility that moves into observation.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not every possible object also exists (1.3.4.2) is not addressed here — this names the scope-gap between possibility and current observation, not a commitment that every unobserved possibility also occurs as an object.
Whether or not the set of possible objects is finite or unlimited is not addressed here — the claim names that the possible exceeds the currently-observed, not how far it extends.
Whether or not any object fails to match any recognized pattern — and so falls outside the possible altogether — is not addressed here.

items.title: A possibility is just a thought (1.2.5.6.4) — treating a possible-but-unobserved object as "there" mistakes a thought for an object.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: A possibility is a thought matching recognized patterns — nothing more. A thought is not an object. Speaking of possible objects as if they were out there waiting to be observed conflates the realm of thinking with the realm of objects, and lends a possibility-thought ontological weight it does not carry.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Possibility is a thought; thoughts are not objects.
2. Therefore, a "possible but unobserved object" is at most a thought, not an object in any meaningful sense.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 overlooks what happens at discovery. When the drawer opens, the thought of a pen matching the recognized pattern of pens becomes matched by an observed object — a pen with its weight, shape, and features met directly. Before opening, the thought held its pattern-match without an observation; after opening, the observation arrives. The claim names this scope-gap and its closing, not an elevated status for thoughts.

The observations make this visible: the pen found on opening the drawer, the chair found on turning around, the insect found under the stone. In each, a possibility-thought and an observation meet; before the meeting, the possibility was not in view.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the scope-gap between possibility and currently-observed objects. Whether or not every possibility corresponds to an object that can be met by observation is a separate question, deferred. The label picks out the pattern that possible objects exceed the currently-observed set — a pattern recognizable each time discovery moves a possibility into observation.

items.title: The claim is trivial — of course thinking ranges wider than current observation. Nothing of substance is named.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Since a possibility is any thought matching recognized patterns, possible objects include everything one can idly think of — a cat across town, a book never read, a mountain never visited. Saying "not all possible objects are currently observed" only restates the obvious: one can think of more than one sees. True, but vacuous.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Possibility includes any thought matching recognized patterns, including idle ones.
2. If so, the claim only says one can think of more than one observes — a trivial truth.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 overlooks that some possibilities are tied to objects waiting to be met. The thought of a pen in the drawer is not idle — opening the drawer resolves it into observation. The thought of a chair behind is not idle — turning resolves it. The claim carries weight because some unobserved possibilities become observations through specific acts.

The observations make this visible: each is a possibility met by a discrete act — opening, turning, walking, lifting. The scope-gap is not only idle thinking; it names what discovery traverses when the drawer opens onto the pen that was there.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the scope-gap between possibility and current observation as what discovery traverses. Whether or not every unobserved possibility is equally discoverable, or some are merely idle, is a separate matter; the claim does not require every possibility to be resolvable. The label picks out the general pattern of observation-as-subset — the condition that makes discovery possible at all.

nodes.claim: "I" is the object that will is.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds "I" — the object will is. Every later self-referential phrase (my body, my thought, I wanted) and the vocabulary of selfhood rest on this. Without it, wanting has no subject.
nodes.search: I, self, selfhood, will, object, identity, subject, me, mine, first-person, ego

sections.title: Observations
items: Wanting to raise an arm, then wanting to lower it — both wants come from one and the same place.
Shifting from wanting food to wanting rest — the wants change, but something continuous is behind them.
Trying to will wanting away — the wanting keeps going regardless.
The will to finish a sentence at its first word, and the same will still present at its last word.

items.text: "I" is the object that will is.
items: Will (1.2.5.1.8) — a wanted want — has consistent features: it is always directed, always comes from a single continuous source, always persists despite any want to end it. These consistent features are its nature (1.3.2). Will — a structure of limits with a nature — is an object (1.3.4.1). "I" is the name for that object.

What makes this a proper object rather than a floating label: the features above are not variable particulars of individual wants. They are what is shared across every wanting. The specific target of a want (food, rest) is superficial variation (1.2.5.7.7); the fundamental features of will persist. That consistency is what makes "I" an object and not just a word.

items.title: Wanting floats without a subject
items.detail: Without recognizing "I" as the object will is, wants have no source to attach to. "My body," "my will," "my thought" — any phrase connecting a want to a persistent origin becomes impossible. Agency, self-reference, and the entire territory of personal identity have no grounding object.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "I" / "me" / "myself" — the object that will is.

Also grounded: "my" / "mine" (possessive — pertaining to the "I"), "self" (the "I" considered as object), first-person constructions ("I want," "I think," "I feel") — all referring to the object that will is.
The next step: the body — an object that my will affects (1.3.7.2).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: "I" names something other than the object of will — a non-willing entity like a pure consciousness, a soul, or a substrate distinct from willing.
"I" is a grammatical fiction with no corresponding object — nothing consistent across willings to which the term refers.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not "I" extends to phenomena other than will — whether perceptions, thoughts, and sensations also originate from the same object. Addressed piecemeal in later nodes.
Whether or not multiple "I"s exist — whether there are many will-objects or only one, and how their relations would work. Not addressed here.
Whether or not "I" has properties beyond will's features — qualities not captured by willing itself. Deferred.

items.title: "I" is prior to will — will is something the "I" has, not something the "I" is.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The standard view is that the "I" is a subject that has a will, not that the "I" IS a will. When wanting to raise an arm occurs, there is an "I" that wants — the wanting is its state or activity, not its identity. The "I" is what has the wants.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. "Having" a will requires a subject distinct from the will.
2. The "I" is that subject — ontologically prior to its wantings.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 imports vocabulary not yet grounded — "subject," "substratum," "ontological prior." The observations don't deliver an "I" separate from willing; they show the willing itself having consistent features. Wanting to raise an arm and wanting to lower it both come from one and the same place; the will to finish a sentence is continuous from its first word to its last.

What commitment #1 requires — a subject distinct from willing that "has" the will — is a theoretical posit. The experience delivers willing with consistent features. Whether or not there is a deeper "haver" behind the willing is a separate question, and the vocabulary for it is not yet grounded.

subSections.label: Correction
items: "I" is grounded here in what is experientially available — the object that will is. Whether or not there is a further "haver" behind willing is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. Naming what is present does not preclude deeper structures if they can later be grounded.

items.title: There is no "I" — only a stream of wantings with no unifying object.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Looking closely for an "I," one finds only a sequence of individual wantings, each arising and passing. Hume searched for the self and found only perceptions, never a self. Buddhist traditions reach the same conclusion. The sense of a continuous "I" is a story assembled after the fact; the wantings are all that is really there.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Looking inward reveals only individual wantings, not a unifying object.
2. The "I" is a fictional label applied to the stream.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 stops at the particular contents of individual wantings and misses the structural features shared across them. The observation "shifting from wanting food to wanting rest — the wants change, but something continuous is behind them" is precisely the feature this view overlooks. The claim is not that "I" is an extra thing beyond the willings; it is that the willing itself, with its consistent features, is what "I" names.

Commitment #2 assumes "I" must be an additional substance for it not to be a fiction. But object (1.3.4.1) means structure with nature — not extra substance. The features consistent across willings are the nature; the willing itself is the structure. No posit of an additional entity is needed.

subSections.label: Correction
items: "I" does not name an extra entity beyond willing. It names the consistent structural features willing itself exhibits. Rejecting those features — claiming no consistency across wantings — is a different objection that would have to be made against the observations themselves. Naming the object-features of will is compatible with the insight that no extra substance is found beyond the mental contents.

items.title: Will depends on a body — without the body, no willing occurs, so "I" can't be just will.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: With no body, there is no will — no wanting to raise an arm, no wanting to speak. Will is dependent on a biological substrate. So "I," if it exists, must be at least will-plus-body, not just will alone.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Will requires a body to occur.
2. Therefore, "I" must include the body, not only the will.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 imports vocabulary not yet grounded — "biological substrate," "physical dependence," "causal necessity between brain and mind." The observations — wanting to raise an arm, trying to will wanting away, the continuity of will across a sentence — show consistent features of willing. They don't deliver or depend on claims about what underlies willing.

Commitment #2 assumes that if A depends on B, then A must include B in its identity. This conflates dependence with identity. The willing observed has features that are its own — direction, persistence, continuity — regardless of what further conditions its occurrence.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names "I" in what is immediately available — the object that will is. Whether or not will further depends on a body is a separate question, addressed in the following nodes. Dependence is not identity: naming the features of willing does not require resolving what underlies willing.

nodes.claim: "My body is the object that my will affects."
nodes.soWhat: Names "my body" — the one object whose events my will can cause. Unlike every other object, the body responds to willing. Without this, the body is no different from a distant stone; the unique responsiveness of the body to will has no label.
nodes.search: body, my body, will, affects, voluntary, effect, cause, object, mine

sections.title: Observations
items: Willing to raise my arm — the arm raises.
Willing to speak a word — sound comes from my mouth.
Willing to walk forward — my legs move me forward.
Willing to clench a fist — my hand closes.

items.text: "My body" is the object that my will affects.
items: "My body" is the object (1.3.4.1) that my will (1.2.5.1.8) affects — the object whose events my will causes (1.2.5.7.8). Willing to raise an arm, and the arm raising: that body event is caused by my will. Willing to speak, and sound coming from the mouth: that event is caused by my will.

What makes this object distinct from others: most objects do not correlate with my will's direction. Willing a distant stone to move produces nothing; willing a cloud to part produces nothing. Only one object reliably responds to willing. "My body" names that object.

items.title: The uniquely will-responsive object has no name
items.detail: Without recognizing "my body" as the object my will affects, the one object that reliably responds to willing has no label. The distinction between what I can directly will — raising an arm, speaking, walking — and what I cannot — moving a distant stone, stopping rain — collapses. Every will-to-event correlation has equal standing, and the special responsiveness of the body to will becomes invisible.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "My body" / "the body" — the object that my will affects.
Also grounded: "limb," "hand," "arm," "leg" (common English terms for parts of the object my will affects); "move" (in the bodily sense — a body event caused by my will).
The next step: some body events occur without being caused by my will (1.3.7.3).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: All objects respond equally to my will — the body is not uniquely responsive to willing.
No object responds to my will — willing has no correlation with any event in any object, ruling out agency entirely.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not "my body" is identical to "I" — this is the opposite question, addressed at (1.3.7.5).
How my will produces effects in the body — the mechanism of volition (nerves, muscles, signals) is not addressed here.

Where the precise boundary of the body falls — edge cases like prosthetics, tools, or internal organs the will never reaches directly. The concept is grounded by the correlation; precise edges are worked out by application.

items.title: Will doesn't really cause body events — neural processes do. "My body" is folk-psychology.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Body movements are caused by neural signals, not by "will" as a phenomenon. What feels like will-causing-body-events is really neural-activity-causing-body-events with a post-hoc sense of willing. So "my body is the object my will affects" is a folk-psychological story that contemporary science has displaced.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. The true cause of body events is at the neural level, not the will level.
2. The experience of willing-causes-body is illusory — the actual cause is neural.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 requires vocabulary not yet grounded — "neural processes," "biological causation," "substrate." What is available is the experience the observations record: willing to raise an arm, and the arm raising; willing to speak, and sound coming from the mouth. This correlation is what cause (1.2.5.7.8) names.

Commitment #2 does not eliminate the correlation; it claims a deeper explanation for it. Whether the correlation is grounded in something further is a separate question. The phenomenon being named — will's direction correlating with body events — is present in the observations regardless of what further mechanism might underlie it.

subSections.label: Correction
items: "My body" is named from the observed correlation between will's direction and body events. Whether or not a deeper process is what actually produces the correlation is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. Naming the correlation does not preclude later explanation of it.

items.title: Many body events don't follow will — so "my body is what my will affects" is only partially true.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The heart beats without any will directing it. Digestion proceeds without willing. Hair grows and wounds heal, all without willing. If "my body is the object my will affects," what about the many body events that my will does not affect?

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. For "my body is the object my will affects" to be true, all body events must be effects of will.
2. Many body events are not effects of will.
3. Therefore, the claim is false.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 misreads the claim. The claim identifies the body as the object in which will reliably produces effects — the object whose events can be willed. It does not say every event of that object is willed.

The observations here are of voluntary body events — raising an arm, speaking, walking, clenching a fist. They record the correlation that picks out the body as will-affected. Events that do not correlate with will — heartbeat, digestion — are a separate question, addressed next. That some body events don't follow will is not in tension with naming the body as the one object many of whose events do.

subSections.label: Correction
items: What this names is the object where will reliably produces effects — the only object where this consistently happens. That the same object also has events that don't follow will is compatible with the naming here, and is addressed directly next.

items.title: "My body" has a vague boundary — what about prosthetics, tools, or a transplanted limb?

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: If a prosthetic leg is willed and walks, is it "my body"? If a saw held in hand extends the arm's reach, is the saw part of the body when willing to cut? The boundary of "my body" is not obvious — which makes "the object my will affects" ambiguous.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. The boundary between "my body" and "not my body" must be specified in advance for the concept to be meaningful.
2. Prosthetics, tools, and partial-extensions blur the boundary.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 imports a requirement the claim does not make. The claim names the object traced by the correlation: whatever consistently responds to will is part of the object my will affects. The boundary is whatever boundary the correlation traces, not a fixed prior line.

The observations — willing to raise an arm and the arm raising, willing to clench a fist and the hand closing — show the correlation in central cases. Edge cases like a prosthetic limb are resolved by applying the same criterion: if willing consistently produces effects in it, it falls within "my body" in this sense.

subSections.label: Correction
items: "My body" is named by the correlation between will's direction and events. Whatever consistently responds is part of the object. Edge cases are resolved by the same criterion. The precise extent of the boundary is not addressed here — it is traced by application, not fixed in advance.

nodes.claim: "Not all of my body's events are caused by my will."
nodes.soWhat: The body is not exhaustively willed. Many of its events — heartbeat, digestion, healing — occur with no correlation to will. Grounds the distinction between voluntary and involuntary, and sets up the next step: the body can itself be a limit to will.
nodes.search: body, involuntary, voluntary, will, cause, heartbeat, reflex, autonomic, unwilled

sections.title: Observations
items: My heart beating continuously, without any wanting it to.
Digestion proceeding after a meal, not initiated or directed by my will.
My hair growing steadily over time — never willed.
A cut on my skin healing on its own.

items.text: Not all of my body's events are caused by my will.
items: My body (1.3.7.2) is the object my will (1.2.5.1.8) affects. But many events in my body occur without correlating with my will's direction — the heartbeat, digestion, hair growth, healing. These events are not effects of my will. My will does not cause (1.2.5.7.8) them.

What this distinguishes: body events split into two kinds — those caused by my will (voluntary) and those not (involuntary). The body is an object that contains both. My will reaches only part of the events in the object it affects.

items.title: The body would be entirely voluntary
items.detail: Without recognizing that not all body events are caused by my will, every heartbeat, digestive wave, and hair's growth would have to be an effect of willing. The distinction between voluntary action and involuntary process vanishes.

children.title: Involuntary categories lose their standing
children.detail: Sleep, reflex, autonomic function, illness — all would have to be willed. There is no vocabulary for something occurring in the body without being willed.

children.title: The body cannot stand in tension with will
children.detail: If every body event were willed, the body could not resist or constrain will. The possibility that will meets limits within its own body becomes invisible.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Voluntary" — a body event that is an effect of my will.
"Involuntary" — a body event that is not an effect of my will.
Also grounded: "reflex," "automatic" (in the sense of involuntary body events), "autonomic" (involuntary in the physiological sense).
The next step: the body does not just contain unwilled events — it constrains my will (1.3.7.4).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: All body events are caused by my will — the body is entirely voluntary.
No body events are caused by my will — the body is entirely involuntary, contradicting the prior correlation between willing and body events.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: The full catalog of which events are voluntary and which are involuntary — the specific list is not enumerated here.
Whether or not involuntary events can become voluntary through training, meditation, or biofeedback — not addressed.
Whether or not involuntary body events have some other cause — a source beyond my will. Whether such a source exists, and what it would be, is not addressed here.

items.title: Involuntary events are still caused by me — by a subconscious will beneath awareness.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The heartbeat, digestion, and breath are caused by an unconscious will — a subconscious drive. So "not caused by my will" is wrong; they are caused by my will, just not the conscious part. Everything in the body is ultimately caused by some layer of me.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. There is a "subconscious will" distinct from conscious will.
2. This subconscious will causes involuntary body events.
3. Therefore, all body events are caused by my will (conscious or subconscious).

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 imports vocabulary not yet grounded — "subconscious," "unconscious drive," "hidden agent." The observations record an absence of correlation between will's direction and certain body events: the heart beating continuously without any wanting it to; hair growing steadily, never willed. No want with those directions has been present.

"My will" was grounded (1.3.7.1) as the willing I am the object of — willing whose consistent features are available to me. Relabeling what causes the heartbeat as a "subconscious will" either names something that is by definition not my will (since it isn't the willing I am) — in which case the claim stands — or is just a renaming of what is here called involuntary.

subSections.label: Correction
items: What is named here is the absence of correlation between my will's direction and certain body events. Whether or not some further source causes those events is a separate question using vocabulary not yet grounded. The observed phenomenon — that the heartbeat does not respond to willing — is what grounds the claim.

items.title: With enough training, any body event can become willed — the line is not principled, just practical.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Yogis can slow their heart rate. Meditators can influence autonomic functions. Biofeedback can bring involuntary events under voluntary control. The distinction between voluntary and involuntary is a matter of current skill, not a principled split. With enough training, the line moves.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Training can bring some involuntary events under voluntary control.
2. Therefore, the involuntary/voluntary split is contingent — in principle, all body events could be voluntary.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 moves from a particular fact to a universal claim without warrant. That some involuntary events can become voluntary through training is not yet that all can.

The observations here — a cut on the skin healing, hair growing steadily — record events that remain outside any reported training's reach. Cell division, bone remodeling, and wound closure are not willed, even by trained practitioners. And the claim only requires that some body events are not caused by my will, which is true regardless of what training expands.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The claim is that, as will functions, not all body events correlate with its direction. Whether some scope can be expanded through training does not eliminate the current gap. Even maximally expanded, some body events remain outside will's reach. The distinction holds.

items.title: This confuses "not caused by my will" with "not mine" — the body's activity is still mine whether I will it or not.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Saying the heartbeat is "not caused by my will" suggests it isn't "mine." But ownership of body events doesn't require will-causation. My hair growing is still my hair growing. The claim, while narrowly true, seems to miss what matters about the body being mine.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. "Mine" does not require "caused by my will."
2. The claim implicitly displaces ownership of involuntary events.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 is a misreading. The claim does not say those events are not mine. It says they are not caused by my will. The body remains "mine" in the sense grounded at the prior node — the object my will affects. The observations show a distinction within body events — some follow will, many do not — not a displacement of ownership.

"Mine" is not weakened by distinguishing voluntary from involuntary. The body being mine is consistent with parts of its activity being outside will's direction. That is precisely what the claim distinguishes.

subSections.label: Correction
items: What is named is a distinction within body events between those caused by my will and those not. Both sets are events of my body. The claim does not displace ownership — it distinguishes which events are willed effects.

nodes.claim: "My body limits my will."
nodes.soWhat: My body is not just an object my will acts through — it resists my will. It ages, it tires, it refuses. Grounds the recognition that the body itself meets my will as a limit, setting up the distinction between "I" and "my body."
nodes.search: body, limit, will, counter-will, resistance, fatigue, pain, aging, my body limits

sections.title: Observations
items: Willing my arm to lift a weight heavier than it can — the arm gives out.
Willing to stay awake longer — sleep takes over regardless.
Willing pain away — the pain stays.
Willing to run faster — the legs slow, lungs burn, and the pace drops.

items.text: My body limits my will.
items: A limit (1.3.1.4) is what is independent (1.2.5.7.4) from want. My body (1.3.7.2) has features that do not correlate with my will's direction — fatigue, pain, the ceiling of what the arm can lift, the onset of sleep. Willing these away produces no change in them. My body is therefore a limit to my will.

What makes this distinct from the prior node: 1.3.7.3 noted that some body events occur without being caused by my will. Here, the stronger relation: some body events actively resist willing. Willing the arm to hold the weight, willing the pain gone, willing sleep off — these wants meet the body as counter-will.

items.title: The body cannot oppose me
items.detail: Without recognizing that my body limits my will, the body is an unlimited instrument — everything willed of it must be possible, and any failure to act must be a failure of will, not a limit of the body. Fatigue, pain, illness, and the body's finite capacities have no standing as constraints.

children.title: The distinction between "I" and "my body" cannot be made
children.detail: If my body cannot stand in tension with my will, then nothing within the object my will affects is independent of my will. The separation of "I" (the will-object) from "my body" (the will-affected-object) needs at least this tension to be visible.

children.title: The body cannot be a thing I inhabit rather than am
children.detail: An unlimited instrument is not distinct from the one using it. Only a body that resists, tires, and fails becomes recognizable as an object I encounter rather than simply an extension of willing.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "My body limits my will" — the body as a specific limit to willing.

Also grounded: "fatigue," "exhaustion" (the body limiting sustained will), "pain" in the resistance sense (a body event that will cannot remove), "capacity" / "limitation" (of the body — the range within which willing succeeds).
The next step: the object that will is (I) and the object will affects and is limited by (my body) are not the same (1.3.7.5).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: My body has no limits with respect to my will — any failure to act reflects weak willing, not bodily constraint.
My body's apparent resistance is an illusion — sufficient willing would always overcome it.
My body and my will are fully aligned — there is never tension between what I will and what the body permits.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: The full extent of the body's limits on my will — which limits are fixed and which can be stretched by training, adaptation, or age.
Whether or not all bodily limits are ultimately physical — whether some limits reflect psychological rather than bodily constraint. Not addressed.

Whether or not the body's limits are shared with other objects — the branch has established that most objects are independent of will; what is distinctive about the body's independence is not fully resolved here.

items.title: With enough will — discipline, courage, belief — no bodily limit is final. Pain can be ignored, sleep resisted, fatigue pushed through.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
