items: Athletes break what seemed impossible. Meditators override pain. People stay awake for days. What looks like bodily resistance is really weak will, and strengthened will meets no bodily limit it cannot cross. "My body limits my will" mistakes weakness for constraint.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Every bodily resistance can in principle be overcome by stronger will.
2. What presents as a limit is only unrefined willing.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 takes partial expansion as total eliminability without warrant. That some bodily resistances yield to training is not that all do. The observations record cases where willing does not produce the effect: willing the arm to lift a weight heavier than it can, and the arm gives out; willing pain away, and the pain stays.

Even the most trained athletes encounter limits — the arm that gives out, the heart that cannot pump faster, the aging that cannot be willed undone. Some limits stretch; others do not. Even if every individual limit could be pushed, the body at any given moment exhibits limits where willing does not correlate with outcome — which is what the claim requires.

subSections.label: Correction
items: What is named is that the body presents, at any given moment, resistances that willing does not remove. Whether training expands some of those resistances is consistent with this — training changes where the line is, not whether there is one. At every moment, willing meets the body as a limit somewhere.

items.title: This isn't the body limiting the will — it's just the outside world felt through the body. The body is just a mediator.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: When I try to lift a weight too heavy, what limits me isn't my body — it's gravity, the mass of the weight, the outside world. The body is a conduit, and calling it "the limit" is mislocating the real source. The body doesn't resist me; the world resists me through the body.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. The real source of bodily limit is outside the body.
2. Labeling the body as the limit mislocates the constraint.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 generalizes from one case (external load) to all cases. But many of the observations cannot be traced outside the body. Willing sleep off does not meet the outside world — it meets the body's sleep cycle. Willing pain away does not confront an external object — it confronts a body event. Willing to run faster meets legs that slow, lungs that burn — the body's capacities, not external obstacles.

Even the external-load case is still traced by what the body can and cannot do — what this body, with its current strength, can handle. The external and the internal resistance are both registered at the body. Calling the body the limit doesn't deny that outside objects also limit — it names where willing concretely meets resistance.

subSections.label: Correction
items: What is named here is the body as a place where willing meets resistance independent of will's direction. Whether some of that resistance originates in objects outside the body is a further question — one for which the relationship between body and other objects would need to be grounded. Naming the body as a limit does not foreclose it.

items.title: If the body limits me, then "I" am something separate from my body — but that's a dualism that isn't earned here.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Saying "my body limits my will" presupposes an "I" that can be limited by the body — as if the self is something other than the body. But this smuggles in a dualism between mind and body, which is a strong metaphysical claim that hasn't been established.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. For the body to limit me, I must be distinct from the body.
2. Claiming this distinction commits to mind-body dualism.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 imports vocabulary — "mind," "dualism," "substance" — that goes beyond what the claim requires. The claim follows from two grounded points: "I" was grounded at 1.3.7.1 as the object that will is; limit was grounded at 1.3.1.4 as what is independent from want. If the body has features independent from will's direction, it fits the definition of a limit to will. That inference alone is what the claim rests on.
The relationship between "I" and "my body" is the subject of the next node, not a presupposition of this one. What is established here is just that the body fits the definition of a limit to my will.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The claim only applies the branch's own definition of "limit" to the body. Whether or not this commits to a dualism between mind and body is a distinct question addressed in the next node — and it is settled by the specific observation of 1.3.7.1 and 1.3.7.2, not by importing a metaphysical framework.

nodes.claim: "I am not my body."
nodes.soWhat: The object will is and the object will affects are not the same. Will persists where the body does not reach; the body persists where will does not direct it. Grounds the recognition that "I am an object in reality" without reducing "I" to the body.
nodes.search: I am not my body, self, body, distinction, will, mind, identity, dualism

sections.title: Observations
items: Willing continues while a limb is numb — the leg cannot be felt, yet the will to move it is present.
A body part (a tooth, a nail, a strand of hair) ends up detached, and willing still feels whole.
The body ages visibly year by year, while the felt source of willing stays the same.
Willing to raise an arm, and at the same moment noticing the arm as something encountered — two distinct things present at once.

items.text: I am not my body.
items: "I" (1.3.7.1) is the object that will is — traced by the consistent features of willing itself. "My body" (1.3.7.2) is the object my will affects — traced by the correlation between willing and body events, and including events that limit willing (1.3.7.4). These two objects are traced by different phenomena and have different natures (1.3.2). They are not the same object.

What this claims, and what it does not claim: it claims the two objects are distinguishable. It does not claim they are unrelated, that they can exist apart, or that "I" exists somewhere other than where my body is. It claims only that what "I" names and what "my body" names are not the same thing.

items.title: "I" collapses into the body, or vice versa
items.detail: Without distinguishing "I" from my body, the two objects merge. Either "I" is nothing beyond the body (and the consistent features of willing become features of the body), or the body is nothing beyond "I" (and the object willing affects is the object willing is).

children.title: The tension between will and body has no subject
children.detail: "My body limits my will" requires that what is limited and what limits it be distinguishable. If "I" and my body are the same object, the prior node says an object limits itself — which no longer names the tension observed when willing meets fatigue, pain, or an arm that gives out.

children.title: Later distinctions — persons, other selves, the relation of mind to world — have no starting point
children.detail: Recognizing that I am one object in a reality of objects requires recognizing which object I am. Without this distinction, "I am an object in reality" means only "my body is in reality" — which fails to capture what the question of selfhood is asking.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: The distinction grounded by this node.
items: "I am not my body" — the object that will is and the object will affects are distinct objects.
Also grounded: "embodied" ("I" as the object whose will affects a particular body), "inhabit" (in the sense of "I" being present with a body without being reducible to it).
With "I" and my body distinguished, the full content of the parent node (1.3.7) is available — I am an object in reality, distinct from the body but standing in a specific relation to it.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: "I" just is the body — the object that will is and the object will affects are one and the same, with no distinguishing phenomena.
The body just is "I" — the body has no features independent of what "I" am; my body is me viewed from outside.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not "I" can exist without a body — whether separation is only conceptual or could also occur. Not addressed.
Whether or not "I" is a physical object, a non-physical object, or something that does not fit either category — the ontological type of the "I" is not addressed here.
How "I" and my body are related given that they are distinct — whether causally, constitutively, or in some other relation. Not resolved here.
Whether or not other "I"s exist and whether they stand in similar relations to their bodies — deferred.

items.title: "I" just is the body — will is a body process, and distinguishing them imports a non-physical ghost.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Will is a brain process. What is called "I" is the body — specifically, one organ of it. Distinguishing "I" from "my body" posits something over and above the body, which is a non-physical ghost — unjustified by the observations and contrary to everything known about biology.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Will is identical to a body process.
2. Therefore, the object will is and the object the body is must be the same object.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 imports vocabulary not yet grounded — "brain process," "neural substrate," "identical to." What the observations deliver is different: will persists when a limb is numb; a tooth or nail can detach and willing still feels whole; the body visibly ages while the source of willing stays the same. These are what trace the two objects and distinguish them.

Commitment #2 assumes that if X is realized by Y, X and Y must be the same object. That is a strong claim — the observations don't support it. Two things traced by different phenomena, with different natures, are distinguishable as objects by this branch's own definition (1.3.4.1), regardless of whether one is further realized by the other.

subSections.label: Correction
items: What is named here is the distinction traced by the observations — two objects with different natures. Whether or not "I" is realized by, identical to, or separate from some bodily structure is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. Naming two objects as distinct does not commit to any particular account of their further relation.

items.title: These observations can be read the other way — the body persists through willing's interruptions (sleep, anesthesia, coma). So the body is more fundamental than "I."

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The observations for distinguishing "I" from the body appeal to continuities of willing while the body changes. But willing is far more interrupted than the body — sleep, anesthesia, unconsciousness all stop willing while the body goes on. If anything, the body is the persistent thing, and "I" is the intermittent one. So the reduction should run the other way: the body is what's real, and "I" is a derivative appearance.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Interruptibility is evidence against being an object in its own right.
2. The body's greater continuity shows it is what's basic; "I" is a derivative appearance.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 misapplies what an object requires. Object (1.3.4.1) is structure with nature — a set of limits with consistent features. It does not require uninterrupted occurrence. Sensations, wants, and perceptions are all interrupted; they remain genuine phenomena when they occur. The question for "I" is not whether it occurs continuously, but whether willing has consistent features when it does occur — which the observations support.

Commitment #2 misses that the claim is a distinction, not a ranking. The claim is that the two objects are not the same — not that one is more fundamental than the other. Whether the body is more continuous than "I," or vice versa, is consistent with the two being distinct objects. The direction-of-reduction question is a separate one this node does not take up.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the distinction between two objects, not a ranking of which is more basic. Whether one is more continuous than the other, or whether either reduces to the other, is a separate question. The distinction itself is traced by the observations and requires no claim about priority.

items.title: "I" and "my body" are the same object described two ways — not two objects. Saying otherwise is a category error.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: A person and their body are one thing. Describing the thing through its willing (as "I") and through its physical events (as "my body") doesn't make two objects — it makes one object under two descriptions. Treating two ways of describing as two objects confuses vocabulary with ontology.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Different descriptions of the same thing do not create multiple objects.
2. "I" and "my body" are two descriptions of one object.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 is correct as a principle. Commitment #2 is what requires showing — and the observations tell against it. The features that trace "I" (consistency of willing, persistence through numbness, continuity across bodily change) are not features of the body as an object (which ages, loses parts, numbs). The features that trace "my body" (voluntary response to will, but also fatigue, pain, aging) are not features of will itself. The two objects have different natures.

Different descriptions pick out the same object only when they refer by features that track the same object. But the features tracking "I" and the features tracking "my body" come apart in the observations — the arm that cannot be felt is still willed; the tooth that detaches leaves willing unchanged. This is not two descriptions of one object; it is two objects, one of which can change while the other is unaffected.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Two descriptions of one object would have to track that object by its features. Here, the features come apart — what is true of the object will is and what is true of the object will affects differ systematically. That is what makes them two objects, not one under two names.

Descriptions are either true or false.
A statement is a description about reality.
Evidence is an observation that matches or mismatches what a statement describes.
A belief is a statement thought to be true.
An assumption is a belief without evidence.
A judgment is a belief with evidence.
A concept is a set of definitions.
Compatibility is when imagining a concept's definitions results in a visualization.
A contradiction is when imagining a concept's definitions does not result in a visualization.
A concept is rational when its definitions are compatible.
A concept is comprehensible when imagining its object results in a visualization.
A concept is either rational or irrational.
A concept is either comprehensible or incomprehensible.
A concept's rationality is independent from its comprehensibility.
Some concepts are rational and comprehensible.
Some concepts are irrational yet comprehensible.
Some concepts are rational yet incomprehensible.
Some concepts are irrational and incomprehensible.
Truth corresponds with rationality, not comprehensibility.
A possible statement is one that does not contradict what is known.
An impossible statement is one that contradicts what is known.
A dependency is when one statement's truth or falsehood contradicts another's.
A statement is necessary for another when its falsehood contradicts the other's truth.
A statement is sufficient for another when its truth contradicts the other's falsehood.
A condition is a statement that is necessary or sufficient for another.
An implication is the relationship between a sufficient statement and what it is sufficient for.
A premise is a statement from which an implication follows.
A conclusion is a statement that an implication leads to.
An argument is a set of premises and their conclusion.
An argument is valid when its premises are sufficient for its conclusion.
A derivation is the conclusion of a valid argument.

Unobserved derivations occur from valid arguments.
Wantings occur.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the everyday experience of wanting something. Direction, success, failure, desire, and will all build on this.
nodes.search: wanting want desire urge hunger thirst pull toward

sections.title: Observations
items: Hunger.
Wanting a loud sound to stop.
Wanting to know the answer to a question.
Wanting to understand how something works.
A craving for a cigarette.
Wanting to refuse a request.

items.text: Wantings occur.
items: A "wanting" is a distinct type of phenomenon (1.2.5). Hunger, thirst, the urge to move — all share this quality.
What makes wanting distinct from qualities like redness or loudness: it has a felt direction — hunger is toward food, thirst is toward water. This directedness is named at (1.2.5.1.2).

items.title: No phenomena have a quality of directedness
items.detail: Without wanting, every phenomenon just occurs without being toward or away from anything. Hunger is indistinguishable from a stomach sensation, thirst from dryness. There is no pull, no urge, no directedness — just occurrences.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Wanting" / "want" — a phenomenon with felt directedness.
Also grounded: "urge," "pull" (in the wanting sense).
The next steps: what wanting is directed toward (direction, 1.2.5.1.2) and wants about wants (1.2.5.1.6).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: No phenomena have a quality of directedness — everything occurs without being toward anything.
Hunger, thirst, and urges are indistinguishable from sensations like redness or loudness — there is no distinct quality that wanting adds.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: What wanting is directed toward — addressed by direction (1.2.5.1.2).
Whether or not wanting is reducible to physical processes — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not some wants occur outside awareness — deferred to later nodes with more vocabulary.

items.title: Wanting is not a separate phenomenon — it is just a complex arrangement of sensations.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Maybe wanting is just a label for a complex arrangement of sensations.
Hunger is stomach contractions plus low blood sugar — no separate quality of 'wanting' exists beyond the physical sensations.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Wanting is a label for a complex arrangement of sensations — no separate quality of 'wanting' exists.
Hunger is stomach contractions plus low blood sugar — the 'pull toward food' is just a description of these sensations.
If wanting can be fully described in terms of non-willful sensations, it is not a separate phenomenon.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: The objection claims wanting reduces to sensations. But consider the observations: hunger is not just stomach contractions — it includes a pull toward food. Wanting to know the answer to a question has no bodily sensation at all, yet the wanting is unmistakable. The question is whether or not directedness — the quality of being 'toward something' — is itself a sensation or something distinct.
Hunger includes a pull toward food; the objection needs to show that this pull is fully captured by the non-directional sensations it reduces to.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not wanting is reducible to physical sensations is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. The claim holds either way: the observable quality of directedness in hunger, thirst, and craving is present in awareness regardless of what explains it.

items.title: Some wants are unconscious — wanting does not always occur in awareness.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Some desires operate outside awareness — unconscious wants influence your behavior without being experienced.
If wanting can be unconscious, then defining it as something that 'occurs in awareness' is too narrow.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Some wants operate outside awareness — unconscious desires influence behavior without being experienced.
If wanting can be unconscious, defining it as something that 'occurs in awareness' is too narrow.
A foundational account of wanting must accommodate both conscious and unconscious instances.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 is the load-bearer, and it proves more than the objector intends. If a phenomenological definition that excludes unconscious instances is incomplete, then every phenomenological definition faces the same charge. Perception (1.2.5.2.3) describes what appears in awareness — but subliminal perception exists. Memory (1.2.5.3.4) describes present information about the past — but implicit memory (procedural, priming) operates outside awareness. Thought (1.2.5.6.3) describes structured imagination — but unconscious inference is well-documented.

The objection applies identically to all of these. The objector almost certainly accepts some of these definitions without complaint — few people object that the tree's definition of perception 'misses' subliminal perception. If they accept phenomenological scoping for perception, they cannot consistently reject it for wanting.
The objection, taken seriously, is not an objection to this node — it is an objection to the entire phenomenological approach. And the objector probably doesn't hold that.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The node defines wanting as it appears in awareness. Unconscious wants are real and important — and they require vocabulary about mechanisms, processing, and inference that is built later.

The phenomenological scope is the same scope used throughout the tree: perception, memory, and thought are all defined by what shows up in awareness, not by what operates beneath it. Rejecting the scope here means rejecting it everywhere.

nodes.claim: Direction is the wanted information.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds what wanting is toward — the 'food' in hunger, the 'water' in thirst. Success and failure both depend on having a direction.
nodes.search: direction target aim purpose toward goal for

sections.title: Observations
items: In hunger, the food. In thirst, the water.
In the urge to move an arm, the movement.
In wanting a sound to stop — the silence is the wanted information.

items.text: Direction is the wanted information.
items: "Direction" is the information (1.2.1.1) that a wanting (1.2.5.1.1) is toward. In hunger, the direction is food; in thirst, the direction is water.
Direction is what makes each wanting specific — two wantings with different directions are different wantings.

items.title: Wanting exists but has no identifiable target
items.detail: Without recognizing direction, wanting is a directionless quality — hunger wants but is not toward anything. There is no way to distinguish one wanting from another, and nothing can succeed or fail.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Direction" — the wanted information. What the wanting is toward.
Also grounded: "target," "aim," "purpose," "toward," "for," "goal."
The next steps: what happens when direction is achieved (success, 1.2.5.1.3) or not achieved (failure, 1.2.5.1.4).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Wanting has no identifiable target — it is a directionless quality with nothing to distinguish one wanting from another.
Purpose requires something beyond what wanting is toward — an external authority, cosmic design, or deeper meaning.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: What happens when what is wanted occurs — addressed by success (1.2.5.1.3).
What happens when what is wanted does not occur — addressed by failure (1.2.5.1.4).
Whether or not direction requires deliberate planning or consciousness — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Direction requires deliberate purpose — a stomach growling toward food is not purposive.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Direction implies purpose, and purpose implies deliberation. A stomach doesn't 'aim' at food — it just produces sensations. Calling the content of a want its 'direction' smuggles intentionality into what might be mere sensation.
Real direction requires a plan, a goal, and some awareness of the gap between where you are and where you want to be. Without those, 'direction' is a metaphor, not an observation.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Direction is intelligible only as a feature of deliberate, plan-governed action.
Non-deliberate toward-ness (hunger 'toward' food) is metaphorical, not literal — the sensation doesn't literally point.
The gap between sensation and intentional aiming is a difference of kind, not degree.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 is where the objection breaks. Consider hunger: it does not merely produce a neutral sensation — it produces a sensation *of something missing*, and the missing thing has specific character (food, not music). That specificity is the direction. The objector can verify this directly: hunger feels different from loneliness, and the difference is not just in the sensation's intensity or location — it is in what each want is *about*.

Commitment #3 assumes that deliberate purpose and felt toward-ness are different kinds of thing. But deliberate purpose is built *from* felt toward-ness: you can only plan toward food because wanting food already has the character of being about food. The plan adds structure; it does not create the direction.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Direction here is not a plan — it is the specific content that a want is about. Hunger is about food. Loneliness is about connection. The aboutness is present in the wanting itself, prior to any deliberation.
Deliberate purpose is a later, more structured form of the same phenomenon.

nodes.claim: Success is the occurrence of what is wanted.
nodes.soWhat: Names when wanting is satisfied — when what was wanted occurs. Outcomes, satisfaction, and achievement all build on this.
nodes.search: success achieve satisfy get occur wanted resolution

sections.title: Observations
items: Hunger directed toward food, and food occurs. The pull ends.
Wanting an arm to move, and the arm moves.
Wanting a sound to stop, and silence arrives.
Wanting to recall a name, and the name coming to mind.

items.text: Success is the occurrence of what is wanted.
items: "Success" is when a wanting's direction (1.2.5.1.2) occurs. In hunger, the direction is food — when food occurs, that is success.
Success is identified when a wanting's direction occurs — not by whether or not the wanting itself ends. Hunger's direction is food; when food occurs, that is success, even if hunger persists.

items.title: Wanting has direction but nothing ever arrives
items.detail: Without recognizing success, wanting is permanently unsatisfied. Hunger is directed toward food, but no occurrence ever corresponds to that direction. The felt difference between hunger-before-eating and hunger-after-eating disappears — they are indistinguishable.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Success" — the occurrence of what is wanted.
Also grounded: "achieve," "satisfy" (in the wanting sense), "get" (as in getting what is wanted).
The next step: what happens when what is wanted does not occur (failure, 1.2.5.1.4).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: No wanting is ever satisfied — direction exists but nothing ever corresponds to it.
The felt difference between before and after getting what was wanted has no basis — hunger and satiation are indistinguishable.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: What determines whether or not success occurs — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not success requires awareness that the wanting was satisfied — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Success requires agency — accidental fulfillment is luck, not success.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: If I want water and it rains, the wanted thing occurred — but did I succeed? Ordinary language reserves 'success' for cases where the agent's effort contributed.
Nozick's experience machine poses a parallel challenge: if a machine gives you the experience of success without any real achievement, most people say that isn't real success.
Defining success as mere occurrence of what is wanted strips the concept of everything that makes it matter — effort, risk, agency, the possibility of failure.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Success requires a causal connection between the agent's action and the outcome — coincidence is not success.
The felt significance of success comes from the effort involved, not from the matching between wanting and occurring.
A definition that includes accidental fulfillment captures too much — it makes every lucky coincidence a success.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 imports a causal story that requires vocabulary not yet built (agency, effort, causal chains). But the experiential observation the node captures is prior to all of that: when what is wanted occurs, something specific happens in experience — the wanting resolves. This happens whether or not the occurrence was caused by the wanter or not.

The person who wanted water and got rained on *does* experience the wanting resolving. The fact that we also have a richer concept of success (earned, effortful) doesn't eliminate the simpler phenomenon.

Commitment #2 misidentifies the source of the felt difference: the difference between lucky fulfillment and earned fulfillment is real, but it's a difference in *how* the success occurred, not in *whether or not* something wanting-shaped resolved. The richer concept is built on top of this one.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Success here names the basic phenomenon: the wanted information occurs. The richer sense — earned, effortful, causally connected to the agent — is a specific *type* of success, not a correction of this definition.
You cannot distinguish earned success from lucky success without first having the concept of wanting-meeting-occurrence that both share.

The objector's concept of success — requiring agency and causal contribution — is a richer phenomenon. But it requires vocabulary not yet established (cause, agency). Call it "fulfillment" if "success" carries too much baggage — the observation is the same. Rejecting even this narrow phenomenon means no wanting ever reaches its direction.

items.title: Accidental fulfillment is not success — moral luck shows that outcome without agency is mere coincidence.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: You want water. Water appears — but through no action of yours, and for reasons completely unrelated to your wanting. Is this success?
The moral luck literature (Williams, Nagel) and Nozick's experience machine suggest that genuine success requires more than coincidence between wanting and occurring.

If success is just "what is wanted occurs," then a person in Nozick's experience machine succeeds at everything they desire, and a person whose wants are accidentally fulfilled is equally successful as one who worked for the outcome.
This strips "success" of the very thing that makes it meaningful — the relationship between the wanting and the occurring.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Success requires a causal or agentive connection between the wanting and the occurring — mere coincidence does not count.
Accidental fulfillment and earned fulfillment are different in kind, not just in how they feel.
A definition of success that cannot distinguish real achievement from lucky coincidence is too thin.

subSections.label: What's Missing

items.text: Commitment #1 imports a richer notion of success that requires agency, effort, or causal connection. But at this level, those concepts have not been built. This identifies the most minimal form of what "success" tracks: the wanted thing occurred.
items: Even in the accidental case, the wanting had a direction, and what occurred matched that direction. The match is what this identifies. whether or not the match was caused by the wanting (agency) or coincided with it (luck) is a further question requiring vocabulary for causation and action.
The distinction between accidental and earned success is real — but it is a distinction *within* success, not between success and something else.

Commitment #2 claims they differ "in kind," but the experiential core is the same: the wanted information occurs. What differs is the *story around* the occurrence — how it came about. That story is important, but it is downstream of the basic observation.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Success here names the minimal structure: what is wanted occurs.
The distinction between accidental success and earned success requires vocabulary for causation, effort, and agency — concepts built later.
This identifies the common core that all forms of success share: the direction of the wanting matched what occurred.

nodes.claim: Failure is the non-occurrence of what is wanted.
nodes.soWhat: Names when wanting goes unsatisfied — what was wanted does not occur. Outcomes, frustration, and the concept of limits all build on this.
nodes.search: failure fail miss not occur wanted unresolved

sections.title: Observations
items: Wanting to fly, and remaining on the ground.
Wanting to recall a name, and no name coming to mind.
Wanting a pain to stop, and the pain continuing.
Wanting to fall asleep, and wakefulness persisting.

items.text: Failure is the non-occurrence of what is wanted.
items: "Failure" is when a wanting's direction (1.2.5.1.2) does not occur. Wanting to fly, and flight not occurring — that is failure.

Failure is identified when a wanting's direction does not occur — not by whether or not the wanting persists. Wanting to fly, and flight not occurring — that is failure, whether or not the wanting continues or fades.

items.title: Wanting has direction but nothing ever goes unsatisfied
items.detail: Without recognizing failure, every wanting either succeeds or simply persists without status. Wanting to fly and remaining grounded is indistinguishable from waiting for flight — there is no recognized phenomenon of not-getting-what-is-wanted.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Failure" — the non-occurrence of what is wanted.
Also grounded: "fail," "miss" (as in missing what is wanted).
The next step: abstracting the general pattern from success and failure (outcome, 1.2.5.1.5).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: No wanting ever goes unsatisfied — every direction is always reached.
The felt difference between wanting something and not getting it versus still waiting for it has no basis.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: What determines whether or not failure occurs — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not failure is always recognized or sometimes goes unnoticed — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Failure requires an attempt — non-occurrence without effort is just absence.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Wanting something and not getting it isn't failure — it's just continued wanting. Failure requires that you tried and fell short.
A person who wants to fly but never attempts it has not failed to fly; they simply haven't flown.
If failure is just 'wanted thing didn't happen,' then every unfulfilled desire is a failure, which makes the concept trivially universal and therefore useless.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Failure is an achievement-category term: it presupposes an attempt that fell short.
Non-occurrence without attempt is mere absence — experientially inert, not a felt phenomenon.
If every unfulfilled want counts as failure, the concept loses its discriminating power.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 is false, and the objector can verify this directly. You want coffee. There is no coffee. The non-occurrence is not 'experientially inert' — it is felt as a specific lack, distinct from the absence of things you didn't want. The wanting *makes* the absence salient. You don't experience the absence of a meteor shower because you weren't wanting one.
This is the phenomenon the node names: the conjunction of wanting and non-occurring produces a specific experiential quality — not neutral absence, but absence-shaped-by-the-want.

Commitment #3 confuses universality with triviality. Every unfulfilled want *does* produce this specific quality of absence-shaped-by-wanting. That's not a defect of the definition — it's the observation. The richer sense (tried-and-fell-short) is a specific type of this phenomenon, not its replacement.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Failure here names the experience of wanting something that does not occur. The wanting is what makes the non-occurrence a felt phenomenon rather than neutral absence.
The richer sense — failure as falling short of an attempt — adds vocabulary about effort and agency that is built later. Both senses share the same experiential root: wanting meeting non-occurrence.

items.title: Non-occurrence is not detectable without expectation — you can only fail at what you anticipated.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Do you experience the non-occurrence of something you didn't know you wanted? If you have a vague, unarticulated desire and the desired thing fails to occur, is there a felt experience of failure, or just a continuation of the status quo?

Failure seems to require not just wanting-plus-non-occurrence, but awareness of the gap — an expectation against which the non-occurrence registers. Without expectation, non-occurrence is invisible. You cannot notice the absence of something you weren't looking for.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Failure requires awareness of the gap between what was wanted and what occurred — mere non-occurrence is not enough.
Expectation (not just wanting) is constitutive of failure — you must have anticipated the occurrence for its non-occurrence to register.
Wants that are too vague to generate expectations cannot produce failure, only continued wanting.

subSections.label: What's Missing

items.text: Commitment #2 is too strong. You can experience the non-occurrence of what is wanted without having explicitly anticipated the occurrence.
items: Commitment #3 is interesting but also too strong: even vague wanting has a direction, and the non-occurrence of anything along that direction is experienced as continued unfulfillment.

Hunger involves wanting (1.2.5.1.1) food; the continued absence of food is felt as failure (1.2.5.1.4) (the wanting is not fulfilled) even without a specific expectation that food would arrive. The wanting itself provides the contrast against which non-occurrence registers — no separate expectation is needed.

The deeper point: "expectation" is itself wanting (1.2.5.1.1)-with-temporal-content — the want for something to occur at a particular time. This describes the simpler case: wanting exists, what is wanted does not occur. Expectation adds temporal specificity to this structure but is not required for the structure itself to hold.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Failure does not require explicit anticipation. The wanting (1.2.5.1.1) itself provides the reference against which non-occurrence is felt.

Hunger is a want; continued absence of food is the non-occurrence of what is wanted — and this is experienced as failure (unfulfillment) without requiring the expectation "food will arrive at 6pm." Expectation is a temporally specific form of wanting, not a prerequisite for failure.
Expectation adds a temporal constraint — "I want X by time T." Remove the temporal constraint and you still have wanting without occurrence. That residual is what failure names.

nodes.claim: An outcome is a success or failure.
nodes.soWhat: Names the general pattern across success and failure — every wanting with a direction has a result.
nodes.search: outcome result success failure wanting resolution

sections.title: Observations
items: Hunger directed toward food, and food occurs.
Wanting to fly, and flight does not occur.
Wanting a pain to stop, and the pain stops. Wanting a pain to stop, and the pain continues.

items.text: An outcome is a success or failure.
items: An "outcome" is the general term for what results from a wanting having a direction — either a success (1.2.5.1.3) or a failure (1.2.5.1.4).

Every wanting with a direction has an outcome: what was wanted either occurs or does not. The wanted information either occurs or it does not — there is no state between occurrence and non-occurrence.

items.title: Success and failure have no common term
items.detail: Without recognizing outcome, there is no way to refer to what results from a wanting having a direction. Success and failure are disconnected observations with no shared identity — the general pattern that both name 'what happened with respect to what was wanted' goes unrecognized.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Outcome" — a success or failure. What results from a wanting having a direction.
Also grounded: "result" (as in the result of a wanting).
This completes the direction branch: wanting (1.2.5.1.1) → direction (1.2.5.1.2) → success / failure → outcome.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Success and failure are unrelated — there is no shared phenomenon that both name.
There is a third option beyond getting and not-getting what is wanted.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not outcomes are always observed — deferred to later nodes.
What patterns emerge across outcomes — deferred to relational phenomena (1.2.5.7).

items.title: Some outcomes feel neutral — neither success nor failure.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Sometimes a wanting has a direction and something happens, but the result feels neither like success nor failure — just a thing that happened. Wanting a meal and getting something edible but unremarkable. Wanting to move and the movement being slightly different from what was wanted. Not every outcome feels clearly sorted into success or failure.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Some outcomes feel neither like success nor failure — they feel neutral or indeterminate.
If neutral outcomes exist, the binary of success/failure does not exhaustively cover all outcomes of wanting.
A framework that forces every outcome into success or failure distorts the phenomenology.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: The feeling of neutrality comes from one of two things. Either the wanting (1.2.5.1.1) was weak enough that the outcome doesn't feel significant — but a mild success is still a success (1.2.5.1.3). Or the wanting's direction was vague — wanting 'a meal' rather than a specific dish — and the result partially matches.
In the second case, specifying the direction more precisely reveals specific successes and failures within the vague outcome: the food occurred (success), but the enjoyment didn't (failure).

subSections.label: Correction
items: The neutral feeling is real, but it is explained by weak wanting or vague direction — not by a third type of outcome. If a want is so weak that its outcome feels neutral, that is a case of either extremely mild success or extremely mild failure — not a third category. The binary is about the wanted information's occurrence, not about the intensity of the response.

items.title: Some outcomes involve both success and failure simultaneously — the binary is false.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: You get the job — but lose the free time. You solve the problem — but the solution is uglier than you hoped. Real outcomes regularly involve the fulfillment of one want and the non-fulfillment of another, simultaneously.
If an outcome is defined as "a success or failure," what do you call an outcome that is both? The binary excludes the most common case — mixed results where something is gained and something is lost.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Many real outcomes involve simultaneous success and failure — the binary is not exhaustive.
A definition that forces every outcome into "success" or "failure" distorts the phenomenology of mixed results.
Mixed outcomes are not just "success + failure side by side" — they have their own distinctive character (bittersweet, ambivalent).

subSections.label: What's Missing

items.text: Commitment #1 is correct that real outcomes are often mixed — but the mixture consists of *multiple* successes and failures occurring together. Getting the job is a success relative to the want for the job; losing free time is a failure relative to the want for free time. These are two outcomes (each binary), not one outcome that is neither.
items: Commitment #3 is the interesting challenge: the *felt quality* of ambivalence or bittersweetness may seem like a third category.
But that quality arises from holding two wants whose outcomes conflict — it is the co-occurrence of success and failure, not a separate kind of outcome.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Mixed results involve multiple wants with different outcomes, each of which is a success or failure relative to its own want's direction. The bittersweet quality of mixed outcomes is the experience of these co-occurring — not evidence of a third category beyond success and failure.
"Outcome" applies to each want separately; the felt mixture is the experience of multiple outcomes at once.

nodes.claim: Wants are themselves wanted or unwanted.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the observation that wants can be directed at other wants — the basis for distinguishing desire from will.
nodes.search: wanted unwanted want meta-want recursive endorsement resistance craving

sections.title: Observations
items: Craving a cigarette while wanting not to crave it.
Wanting to be hungry.
Curiosity about a puzzle, and a welcome of that curiosity.
An urge to hit something, and wanting that urge to go away.

items.text: Wants are themselves wanted or unwanted.
items: Wants are themselves subject to wanting. A craving occurs and is unwanted; curiosity occurs and is welcomed. Wanting is not only directed at things like food or silence — it is also directed at other wants.
This is not a separate type of phenomenon — it is the same wanting (1.2.5.1.1), but with another wanting as its direction rather than information like food or silence.

items.title: No want is ever itself wanted or unwanted
items.detail: Without this, every want simply occurs with no felt endorsement or resistance. Craving a cigarette and welcoming curiosity feel the same — both are just wants, with no quality of being toward or against the wanting itself. The difference between a craving that is resisted and one that is embraced disappears — and desire and will cannot be distinguished.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Wanted" / "unwanted" (applied to wants) — a want is wanted when another want is directed toward its occurrence; unwanted when no want brought it about.
"Endorse" — a want directed toward the occurrence of another want. The felt approval of a wanting.
"Resist" — a want directed against another want. The felt tension when two wants oppose each other.
The next steps: naming the two cases — an unwanted want (desire, 1.2.5.1.7) and a wanted want (will, 1.2.5.1.8).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: All wants are on equal footing — no want is ever endorsed, resisted, or evaluated by another want.
The difference between craving a cigarette and welcoming curiosity is just a difference in direction, with no layer of wanting about the wanting itself.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not wants about wants can stack further — wanting to want to want — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not all wants are themselves wanted or unwanted — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Wanting a want is just a more complex want — and the hierarchy regresses.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: If every want can itself be wanted or unwanted, then what about the want *about* the want? I want coffee. I don't want to want coffee. Do I want the not-wanting?
If the hierarchy continues, it never terminates — there's no final attitude that grounds the whole chain. Harry Frankfurt's higher-order desire theory ran into this exact regress.

Saying 'wants are themselves wanted or unwanted' opens a door that never closes: each new attitude toward a want generates another want that must itself be wanted or unwanted. Without a stopping point, the observation is structurally unstable.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: A recursive structure without a termination condition is vicious — it explains nothing because every explanation requires a further explanation.
Frankfurt's framework collapsed under this regress, so any framework with the same structure inherits the same problem.
The node must provide a stopping point or accept that the hierarchy is infinite and therefore vacuous.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 assumes the recursion must resolve into a fixed foundation to be legitimate. But the node is not building a foundational hierarchy — it is making an observation: for any want you attend to, you can observe whether or not it is itself wanted or unwanted. This is a *repeatable observation*, not a chain that requires completing.
The regress is real but not vicious: it is like asking 'what is north of this point?' — the question always has an answer, but not answering every instance doesn't undermine the concept of north.

Commitment #2 misidentifies what Frankfurt's regress threatened. Frankfurt needed a *decisive* higher-order desire to ground autonomy — a desire that settled the matter. This node doesn't need that. It observes that the relationship exists (wants can be wanted or unwanted), and the specific vocabulary for will and desire follows from just the first level of that relationship.
The regress doesn't destabilize the observation because the observation doesn't depend on the hierarchy terminating.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The node observes that any attended-to want is experienced as wanted or unwanted. This observation holds at every level: you can want your wanting, and you can attend to *that* want too. The recursion is not a defect — it is a feature of self-reflective experience.
The definitions of will (wanted want) and desire (unwanted want) require only one level of this structure, not its completion.

Concretely: you can observe (1) a craving for cigarettes, and (2) wanting that craving to go away. You do not need to observe (3) a want about the want about the craving in order for (1) and (2) to be real. Each level is independently observable. The hierarchy does not need to terminate any more than a sequence needs a last step.

items.title: The hierarchy of wants about wants generates an infinite regress.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Harry Frankfurt's framework of higher-order desires faces a well-known regress: if a first-order desire can be wanted or unwanted by a second-order desire, the second-order desire can itself be wanted or unwanted by a third-order desire, and so on without limit. Where does the hierarchy stop?
Frankfurt himself appealed to "wholehearted identification" to block the regress, but this was widely criticized as ad hoc.

If this holds that every want is itself wanted or unwanted, it inherits the same regress: the want about the want is itself wanted or unwanted, and that meta-want is itself wanted or unwanted, generating an infinite stack with no natural stopping point.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: A hierarchy of evaluative attitudes (wants about wants about wants) requires a principled stopping point to be meaningful.

If every want generates the question "is this want itself wanted?", the structure is vicious — it cannot ground the distinction between desire and will because the grounding want is itself ungrounded.
Frankfurt's appeal to "wholehearted identification" was ad hoc, and any similar move here would be equally unprincipled.

subSections.label: What's Missing

items.text: The regress is real as a *logical possibility* but not as a *observation within experience*.
items: Commitment #1 assumes the hierarchy must be completed — that every want must have its meta-want resolved before any want counts as a desire or a will. But in actual experience, the hierarchy typically terminates within one or two levels: you want coffee, and you don't want to want coffee. The question "do you want to not-want-to-want coffee?" is intelligible but rarely *occurs*. This does not claim the hierarchy must complete — it claims that wherever a want is, it is either wanted or unwanted. This is a description of what is found at each level, not a requirement that all levels be traversed.
Commitment #2 assumes viciousness, but the regress is benign: each level is independently observable, and no level depends on the resolution of a higher level to have its character.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The regress is logically available but experientially finite. At any given moment, a want either is or isn't the direction of another want — and that observation holds at whatever level you find yourself.

The hierarchy does not need a principled stopping point because it is not generated top-down (from a final authority that endorses all the way down) but observed bottom-up (each want, as it occurs, either has or lacks another want directed at it).
Frankfurt needed a stopping point because he was trying to derive free will from the hierarchy.  This is not deriving anything — it is observing that the structure exists.

nodes.claim: A desire is an unwanted want.
nodes.soWhat: Names the specific case of a want that occurs despite being unwanted — cravings, temptations, involuntary pulls.
nodes.search: desire craving temptation unwanted want involuntary urge

sections.title: Observations
items: Craving a cigarette, unbidden.
Suddenly wanting to eat after smelling food.
An urge to hit something during an argument.
A pull toward checking a notification, uninvited.

items.text: A desire is an unwanted want.
items: A "desire" is a want whose occurrence is not itself wanted (1.2.5.1.6). The craving for a cigarette, the sudden hunger triggered by a smell — these are wants that arrived without being willed into existence.

"Unwanted" here does not mean disliked or resisted. It means the want's occurrence was not itself the direction of another want. A craving for food may be enjoyed — but it is still a desire because it was not itself wanted into existence. It just happened.

items.title: No want ever arrives unbidden
items.detail: Without distinguishing desire, every want that occurs was itself wanted — there is no such thing as a want that just shows up. A craving and a deliberate commitment are indistinguishable: both are simply wants with no distinction in how they arrived. The basis for later recognizing that some wants intrude while others are endorsed — and everything that distinction makes possible — has nothing to stand on.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Desire" — an unwanted want. A want whose occurrence was not itself wanted.
Also grounded: "craving" (a desire with strong intensity), "temptation" (a desire whose direction opposes a will).
The counterpart: a want that IS wanted — will (1.2.5.1.8).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: All wants are self-generated — no want ever just occurs without being willed.
There is no distinction between wants that arrived unbidden and wants that were endorsed into existence.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: What causes desires to occur — the mechanism behind uninvited wants is deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not a desire can become a will (or vice versa) — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not desires that are resisted differ in kind from desires that are welcomed — deferred; may involve compulsion/volition distinctions requiring more vocabulary.

items.title: Some desires are wanted — a craving for food can be enjoyed and welcomed.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: A craving for a favorite food can feel good and be welcomed. If the craving is welcome, then the want IS wanted — making it a will, not a desire. The definition "unwanted want" seems to exclude desires that are enjoyed.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Enjoying a desire means the desire is wanted, which reclassifies it as a will.
How a want is *received* (welcomed vs. resisted) is the same as how it *arrived* (willed vs. unbidden).
If a desire can be wanted after it occurs, the unwanted/wanted distinction collapses.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: The objection conflates two things: whether or not the desire was *willed into existence* and whether or not the desire was *liked after arriving*. A craving for food may be enjoyed after it arrives — but that enjoyment is a response to the craving, not the cause of it.

The craving itself showed up without being willed. Being glad that a desire occurred is a separate want (a want about the desire) — it does not change the fact that the desire's own occurrence was not itself wanted.
Commitment #2 is where the objection breaks: arrival and reception are different events.

subSections.label: Correction
items: "Unwanted" in this definition means the want's occurrence was not itself the direction of another want — not that the want is disliked.
A desire can be welcomed after it arrives and still be a desire, because welcoming it is a separate want that came after the desire's occurrence.
What makes it a desire is how it arrived, not how it was received.

items.title: In common English, 'desire' covers any strong want — this definition is too narrow.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: People say "I desire to succeed" or "I desire justice" — strong, deliberate wants that are clearly endorsed. Restricting "desire" to unwanted wants contradicts ordinary usage and creates confusion.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: A technical definition that diverges from ordinary usage creates more confusion than clarity.
The broader everyday meaning of "desire" (any strong want) is the correct or primary meaning.
Philosophical traditions use the term more broadly, so the narrow definition is out of step.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: This gives "desire" a precise definition to capture a real distinction: between wants that arrive unbidden and wants that are willed. Everyday language blurs this distinction, but the reader already recognizes it — the difference between a craving that just shows up and a commitment that is actively maintained.

Commitment #3 is actually false: major philosophical traditions — Schopenhauer's "will and desire," Buddhism's distinction between *tanha* (craving that arises unbidden) and deliberate intention (*cetana*), and the Stoic separation of involuntary impulse from rational assent — all isolate exactly this sense of "desire": the want that was not chosen.

subSections.label: Correction
items: "Desire" here names the specific case of a want whose occurrence was not itself wanted.  The broader everyday sense (any strong want) remains available through the parent term "wanting." The alternatives — "urge," "impulse," "craving" — each carry intensity or brevity connotations that are not part of the definition.

A mild, lingering, unbidden want is still a desire. "Desire" is the best available English word for the full range of wants that were not willed into existence, and the narrowing captures a distinction that both ordinary experience and major philosophical traditions already recognize.

nodes.claim: A will is a wanted want.
nodes.soWhat: Names the specific case of a want that is itself wanted — deliberate, endorsed wanting. The self is later identified through will.
nodes.search: will willing deliberate endorsed wanted want volition intention

sections.title: Observations
items: Wanting to eat, and that wanting being itself wanted. Not just hunger toward food, but the wanting itself endorsed.
Wanting to listen carefully, and that want being itself welcome.
Wanting to stay silent during an argument, and wanting to want that silence.
Wanting to keep running despite fatigue, and endorsing that want.

items.text: A will is a wanted want.
items: A "will" is a want whose occurrence is itself wanted (1.2.5.1.6). Wanting food and also wanting that wanting — the want occurs with endorsement from another want.

What makes will distinct from desire (1.2.5.1.7): a desire arrives without being wanted into existence; a will is a want whose occurrence is itself wanted. The difference is not in how the want feels, but in whether or not another want brought it about.

items.title: No want is ever endorsed
items.detail: Without distinguishing will, there is no wanting that is itself wanted — every want simply arrives, and none are endorsed into existence. The difference between a deliberate commitment and an unbidden craving disappears. A carefully maintained commitment and a sudden urge that showed up on its own are indistinguishable — both are just wants.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Will" — a wanted want. A want that is itself wanted.
Also grounded: "willing" (the occurrence of will), "deliberate" (in the sense of a wanted wanting).
This completes the wants-about-wants branch: wants are wanted or unwanted (1.2.5.1.6) → desire (unwanted want, 1.2.5.1.7) and will (wanted want, 1.2.5.1.8).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: All wants are equally unendorsed — there is no distinction between a deliberate wanting and an involuntary craving.
The concept of willpower has no experiential basis — there is no felt difference between wants that are endorsed and wants that are resisted.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Who or what wills — deferred to the self (1.3.7).
Whether or not will requires awareness of the endorsement — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not all wanted wants are equally strong — deferred to intensity (1.2.5.2).

items.title: Will requires a self or agent — a want cannot want itself.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Free will debates in philosophy presuppose an agent who does the willing. A 'wanted want' is incoherent without a subject — who is doing the endorsing? Without a self, 'wanted want' is a recursive loop with no ground.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Willing requires an agent — a subject who does the endorsing.
A 'wanted want' without a subject is a recursive structure with no ground — no one is doing the wanting.
Without a self, the hierarchy of wants has no anchor point.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: This does not claim that a want wants itself — it identifies that a want occurs and is itself the direction of another want. These are two distinct wants: one directed at food, and another directed at the first want. Whether or not this structure requires a self or agent is a question this does not address.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Will names the observation that two wants stand in a specific relationship — one is directed at the other. whether or not this structure requires a self or agent is a question that arrives later (1.3.7). The observation does not presuppose an answer.

items.title: Will is an illusion — all wants are determined by prior causes, not by other wants.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Maybe the feeling of willing is an after-the-fact story — your brain makes a decision, and then you experience it as a choice.
If so, the 'endorsement' of a want is itself caused by prior neural events, not by a genuine want about a want.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: The feeling of willing is a post-hoc narrative, not a genuine observation.
All wants — including 'wants about wants' — are causally determined by prior neural events.
If endorsement is itself determined, the relationship between the two wants is causal, not willful.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: This describes what is present in awareness, not what causes it. The experience of wanting a want is observable regardless of whether or not that experience is causally determined. Two phenomena can be determined by prior causes AND be observably distinct.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The node describes the felt quality of a wanted want. whether or not this quality is caused by prior physical events does not dissolve the quality, any more than the causal history of perception dissolves what is perceived.

The determinist's own activity — reasoning toward the conclusion that will is illusory — is itself a phenomenological quality (the felt quality of following an argument to a conclusion). If causal determination eliminates the phenomenological quality of willing, it equally eliminates the phenomenological quality of reasoning — and the determinist has undermined the very process by which they reached their conclusion.
Consistently applied, commitment #2 dissolves not just willing but every experiential distinction, including the distinction between 'I reasoned my way here' and 'I arbitrarily arrived here.'

nodes.claim: Phenomena occur with intensity.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the everyday experience of degree — that phenomena are not just present or absent but occur more or less strongly. Sensation, satisfaction, and frustration all build on this.
nodes.search: intensity degree strong weak dim vivid loud quiet more less magnitude

sections.title: Observations
items: A dim red and a vivid red, the same quality at different strengths.
A quiet hum and a loud crash.
A mild ache and a sharp pain.
A faint scent of coffee and an overpowering smell of smoke.

items.text: Phenomena occur with intensity.
items: "Intensity" is the degree to which a phenomenon occurs — how dim or vivid, how quiet or loud, how faint or strong.
The quality itself stays the same — red stays red, a sound stays a sound. What differs is how much of it there is.

items.title: No phenomenon is ever more or less than another
items.detail: Without intensity, no phenomenon is more or less than another — a whisper and a scream, a dim glow and a blinding flash, are indistinguishable in degree. Satisfaction and frustration (which depend on the match between wanted and actual intensity) become impossible.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Intensity" — the degree to which a phenomenon occurs.
Also grounded: "degree," "strong," "weak," "dim," "vivid," "loud," "quiet," "faint," "more," "less."
The next step: identifying intensity as a quality distinct from wanting (sensation, 1.2.5.2.2).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: No phenomenon has degree — everything occurs at a single undifferentiated level.
The felt difference between a whisper and a scream has no experiential basis.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not intensity is continuous or occurs in discrete steps — deferred to later nodes.
What determines the intensity of a phenomenon — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Intensity is just a different quality, not a dimension of the same quality.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: A loud sound and a quiet sound could be two different qualities, not one quality at different degrees. What is called 'intensity' might be distinct qualities mislabeled as the same thing at different levels.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: A loud sound and a quiet sound could be two different qualities rather than one quality at different degrees.
What is called 'intensity' might be distinct qualities mislabeled as a single quality varying in degree.
If the 'different degrees' are really different qualities, intensity is not a dimension but a confusion.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: A loud middle-C and a quiet middle-C share everything except how much of the quality is present. If they were different qualities entirely, there would be no shared character between them — but the reader recognizes them as the same sound at different levels.
Intensity is identified precisely by this: two instances share a quality while differing only in degree.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Two instances share a quality and differ only in degree. That difference in degree is intensity. The reader points at it directly — no separate qualities need to be posited.

items.title: Intensity is a physical measurement, not an experienced quality.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Intensity is a matter of measurable amplitude — decibels, wavelength, pressure.
What you experience as 'more or less' may not be a genuine experiential dimension but a byproduct of physical quantities.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Intensity is a physical measurement (decibels, wavelength), not an experiential quality.
What is experienced as 'more or less' is a byproduct of measurable physical quantities.
Starting from felt degree rather than physical measurement gets the explanation backwards.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: This describes what is present in awareness: two instances of a quality that differ in degree. Whether or not physical measurement explains the degree is a question about mechanism. The felt difference between a dim red and a vivid red is observable regardless of whether or not it corresponds to a measurable quantity.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not intensity is explained by physical amplitude is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. The claim holds either way: the felt difference between a dim red and a vivid red is observable regardless of what produces it.

nodes.claim: Sensation is intensity without wanting.
nodes.soWhat: Distinguishes the sensory dimension from wanting — they are different qualities, like loud and red. Perception, satisfaction, and frustration all build on this.
nodes.search: sensation feeling sense redness warmth loudness intensity without wanting neutral

sections.title: Observations
items: Redness, vivid or dim.
The warmth of sunlight on skin.
The loudness of a sound.
The brightness of a light.

items.text: Sensation is intensity without wanting.
items: A "sensation" is intensity (1.2.5.2.1) that is not wanting (1.2.5.1.1). The vividness of redness, the loudness of a sound, the warmth of sunlight — each is an intensity, and none of them are wantings.
Sensation is what remains of a phenomenon's intensity when wanting is absent. The loudness of a crash is a sensation — it has intensity but no direction.

items.title: Intensity and wanting are indistinguishable
items.detail: Without distinguishing sensation, there is no quality of intensity that is distinct from wanting. The vividness of red is indistinguishable from a pull toward something. The loudness of a sound is indistinguishable from wanting something about it. Every degree is a direction, with no distinction between the two — and perception, which depends on sensation, has nothing to stand on.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Sensation" / "feeling" — intensity that is not wanting. The degree-quality of a phenomenon, distinct from its directedness.
Also grounded: "sensory" (relating to sensation).
The next step: the event of a sensation occurring (perception, 1.2.5.2.3).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Intensity and wanting are the same quality — there is no distinction between felt degree and felt directedness.
Warmth and the pull toward warmth, loudness and the urge to respond to it, are a single quality — not two.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not sensation is always separable from wanting in practice — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not sensation requires awareness to occur — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: All sensations involve some wanting — pure sensation without wanting does not exist.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Some philosophers and psychologists (in the hedonic tradition) argue that all experience has an emotional pull (affective valence) — every redness has a slight preference or aversion, every sound is at least mildly pleasant or unpleasant. Truly neutral sensation may be an abstraction that never actually occurs.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: All experience has affective valence — every sensation comes with at least a mild preference or aversion.
Truly neutral sensation without any wanting is an abstraction that never actually occurs.
If wanting always accompanies sensation, isolating 'sensation without wanting' misrepresents the phenomenon.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: This does not claim that sensation occurs in isolation from wanting. It proposes that sensation and wanting are distinct qualities — as different as loud and red. The objection needs to show that this distinction fails: that the warmth of sunlight and the pull toward warmth are not merely co-occurring but genuinely indistinguishable.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not every sensation always co-occurs with some wanting is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. The claim holds either way: even if every warmth comes with a slight preference, the warmth and the preference are still distinct qualities.
Sensation names the intensity dimension; wanting (1.2.5.1.1) names the directedness. They may always appear together, and this claim's observation — that they are different qualities — still stands.

items.title: Sensation is just another word for quality — no new distinction is introduced.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Quality (1.1.3) already names any distinct phenomenon. Calling intensity-without-wanting a 'sensation' just relabels what quality already covers. Every red, every warmth, is already a quality — why add another term?

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Quality (1.1.3) already names any distinct phenomenon — sensation is just a relabeling.
Every red, every warmth is already a quality — adding 'sensation' introduces no new distinction.
A term that maps exactly onto an existing concept is redundant, not foundational.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Quality names any distinct phenomenon. Sensation names a specific case: a quality's intensity when wanting is absent. Not all qualities are sensations — wanting is a quality with direction, not a sensation. The distinction isolates the sensory dimension of experience from the motivational dimension.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Sensation narrows quality by identifying a specific kind: intensity that is not wanting. Not all qualities are sensations — wanting is a quality with direction, and direction is not a sensation.
This grounds a distinction the reader already recognizes — the warmth felt versus the pull toward warmth.

nodes.claim: Perception is the occurrence of a sensation.
nodes.soWhat: Names the event of sensing — seeing, hearing, tasting. Satisfaction and frustration both depend on whether or not a wanted perception occurs.
nodes.search: perception perceive sense see hear taste smell feel sensory event

sections.title: Observations
items: A color appearing, redness suddenly present.
A sound arriving, loudness filling the moment.
A taste on the tongue, sweetness occurring.
A smell encountered, the sharpness of smoke.

items.text: Perception is the occurrence of a sensation.
items: A "perception" is the event of a sensation (1.2.5.2.2) occurring. Seeing is the occurrence of a visual sensation; hearing is the occurrence of an auditory one.
Perception names the event from the sensation's side — not a separate process added on top of sensation, but sensation happening.

items.title: Sensory events have no name
items.detail: Without recognizing perception, sensations have intensity but there is no recognized event of experiencing them. The felt difference between a color appearing and a color being absent, between a sound arriving and silence, goes unnamed. Satisfaction and frustration — which depend on whether or not a wanted sensation occurs — have nothing to stand on.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Perception" / "perceive" — the occurrence of a sensation.
Also grounded: "sense" (as a verb — to perceive), "see," "hear," "taste," "smell," "feel" (as specific perceptions).
The next steps: what happens when a wanted sensation occurs (satisfaction, 1.2.5.2.4) and when it does not (frustration, 1.2.5.2.5).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Sensations never happen as events — intensity exists as a static quality with no experiential moment of arrival.
There is no distinction between a sensation occurring and a sensation not occurring — both are unnamed.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not perception requires attention or focus — deferred to later nodes.
What determines which sensations occur — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Perception requires interpretation — this definition captures stimulation, not perception.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Cognitive science's central finding is that perception is constructive. What appears in awareness is not raw sensory impact — it is a structured percept already shaped by categorization, expectation, and top-down processing.

The Müller-Lyer illusion, change blindness, and inattentional blindness all show that what you 'see' is not what hits the retina. The Bayesian brain hypothesis holds that perception is inference, not registration.
Defining perception as 'the occurrence of a sensation' captures the input to perceptual processing, not its output — and the output is what people mean by perception.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: There is a real and important difference between sensory stimulation (causal impact on receptors) and perception (the structured experience that results from processing that impact).
What appears in awareness is always already processed — there is no pre-interpretive sensory layer accessible to experience.
The node's definition captures stimulation, not perception — it names the wrong thing.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 actually supports the node rather than undermining it. If what appears in awareness is *already processed* — if you never experience the raw, pre-interpretive signal — then what you experience IS the final product. And the final product is a sensation occurring.
The Müller-Lyer lines *appear* unequal — that appearance is the sensation that occurs. The processing happened, but it happened behind the scenes; what shows up in awareness is the result.

Commitment #3 is where the objection breaks: it assumes the node is trying to describe the input (stimulation), but the node describes the output (what actually appears in awareness). If processing is invisible — if you never catch yourself mid-interpretation — then the occurrence of the sensation IS perception as experienced. The constructivist's own claim (you only ever access the processed result) is exactly what the node names.

subSections.label: Correction
