items: The processing the constructivist describes is real and important — but it is not experienced. What is experienced is its result: a sensation occurring. This node names that result.

The mechanism that produces the sensation (whether or not Bayesian inference, top-down prediction, or ecological pickup) is a separate question about what happens *before* the sensation appears. The node describes what arrives in awareness, not what produced it.

items.title: Even the simplest perception is already a construction — there is no bare 'occurrence of a sensation.'

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: From Helmholtz's 'unconscious inference' through modern Bayesian accounts, the consensus is that perception is never the bare occurrence of a sensation.
What appears in your awareness is already structured: edges sharpened, ambiguities resolved, context applied, predictions integrated.
What you 'perceive' is your brain's best guess — shaped as much by prior expectations as by sensory input.
Even Gibson's ecological approach, which rejects internal construction, holds that perception picks up relational, action-relevant information — not bare sensory events.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: What appears in awareness is already a structured, processed product — not a bare sensory event.
There is a real difference between stimulation (causal impact on sensory surfaces) and perception (what the organism experiences), and this claim's definition captures stimulation, not perception.
Even "direct" theories of perception (Gibson) hold that perception involves structured information (affordances), not raw sensation.

items.text: Commitment #2 is the strongest form of the objection, and it deserves direct engagement. The constructivist is right that what appears in awareness is structured.
items: But this is describing what appears *in awareness* — the final product, not the processing that produced it. The Bayesian brain's "best guess" is itself a phenomenon that occurs with specific sensory character.

The unconscious inference is, by definition, unconscious — it does not appear in awareness. What *does* appear — the structured percept — is itself a sensation (it has intensity, quality, spatial character). This defines perception at the level of the conscious result, not at the level of the processing pipeline.

items.text: Commitment #1 is true about the causal history of the percept, but this is not describing causal history — it is describing what shows up.
items: The Gibson point in commitment #3 actually clarifies this claim's position: affordances are features of the experienced environment, and experiencing them is itself a sensory event — you see the graspability of the cup, and that seeing has phenomenal character. whether or not you call the result "bare" or "structured," it is a sensation that occurs, and this names that occurrence "perception."

subSections.label: Correction
items: The constructivist is correct that the processing behind perception is complex.
But this describes what arrives in awareness after all that processing — the experienced result, not the mechanism.

whether or not the result was constructed by Bayesian inference, unconscious hypothesis-testing, or direct ecological pickup, it shows up as a sensation: something with intensity, quality, and specific character.
The construction is beneath perception; the occurrence of the constructed result IS perception.

nodes.claim: Satisfaction is when a wanted sensation occurs.
nodes.soWhat: Names the sensory dimension of fulfillment — not just that what was wanted occurred, but that the sensory quality itself arrived.
nodes.search: satisfaction gratification fulfillment sensory pleasure wanted sensation occurs

sections.title: Observations
items: Thirst directed toward water, and the cool taste of water arriving.
Hunger directed toward food, and the flavor of the first bite.
Wanting warmth in the cold, and the heat of sunlight on skin.
Wanting to hear a melody, and the melody sounding.

items.text: Satisfaction is when a wanted sensation occurs.
items: "Satisfaction" is the specific case of success (1.2.5.1.3) where the wanted direction is a sensation (1.2.5.2.2) and that sensation occurs (1.2.5.2.3). The cool taste arriving when thirst wanted water — that is satisfaction.

Satisfaction names what the reader already recognizes as distinct from abstract success: the sensory quality of getting what was wanted. A name coming to mind when wanted is success; a wanted flavor arriving is satisfaction.

items.title: The sensory quality of fulfillment goes unrecognized
items.detail: Without recognizing satisfaction, success is just an outcome — what was wanted occurs — but the felt quality of the sensation arriving has no name. The difference between getting what was wanted and tasting what was wanted, between an arm moving and the felt warmth of sunlight, disappears. Success is identified, but the experiential richness of the sensation arriving is indistinguishable from the abstract fact of the direction being achieved.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Satisfaction" — when a wanted sensation occurs.
Also grounded: "gratification" (satisfaction from a strong wanting), "fulfilled" (in the sensory sense).
The counterpart: what happens when a wanted sensation does not occur (frustration, 1.2.5.2.5).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Success has no sensory dimension — getting what is wanted and experiencing the sensation of getting it are indistinguishable.
The felt richness of a wanted taste, warmth, or sound arriving has no basis beyond abstract success.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not satisfaction requires awareness of the wanting — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not satisfaction differs in intensity based on the wanting's intensity — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Satisfaction is just success — adding 'sensation' does not create a new concept.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Success (1.2.5.1.3) already names the occurrence of what is wanted. Specifying that the wanted thing is a sensation does not introduce a new phenomenon — it is just success applied to a particular direction. Every concept could be split this way: 'success with food,' 'success with silence,' etc.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Satisfaction is just success (1.2.5.1.3) applied to a specific kind of direction (wanting a sensation).
Specifying the type of thing wanted does not create a new concept — it is just a special case.
Every concept could be split this way (success-with-food, success-with-silence) without producing genuinely new phenomena.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Satisfaction names something the reader experiences as distinct from abstract success (1.2.5.1.3). The taste of food arriving when hungry is not just 'what was wanted occurred' — it has a sensory quality that abstract success (like a name coming to mind) does not.
The reader recognizes this felt difference: the experiential richness of a wanted sensation arriving versus the recognition that a direction was achieved.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The reader already distinguishes between a name coming to mind (success) and a wanted flavor arriving (satisfaction). The sensory quality of fulfillment is not just success applied to a different direction — it is a recognizably different experience.

items.title: Satisfaction involves pleasure or contentment — stripping the emotion strips the phenomenon.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: When a wanted taste arrives, what you experience isn't just 'wanted sensation occurred' — it's *pleasure*, relief, a felt warmth of fulfillment.

Satisfaction without that emotional quality isn't satisfaction; it's a neutral event with a misleading label. The emotional dimension is what *constitutes* satisfaction — remove it, and you've removed the phenomenon you were trying to name.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: The emotional quality (pleasure, contentment) is constitutive of satisfaction — not an addition to it, but what makes it satisfaction.
A wanted sensation arriving without any felt quality of fulfillment is not satisfaction; it is merely a sensation arriving.
Stripping the emotional dimension doesn't produce a 'minimal' version of satisfaction — it produces a different phenomenon entirely.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: The objector is right that satisfaction *feels like something* beyond a neutral event. The question is what produces that feeling. Try this: you're thirsty. Water arrives. The wanting-for-water meets the sensation-of-water. Is the resulting experience neutral? No — it has a distinctive felt quality: the cessation of the wanting, the arrival of the wanted thing, the two meeting. That felt quality IS the satisfaction.
Now ask: where in this description did pleasure get 'stripped'? It didn't. The pleasure is *what the meeting of wanting and sensation feels like from inside*.

Commitment #3 assumes that the node removes the felt quality and keeps only the structure. But the structure IS felt. Wanting-meeting-its-object is not an abstract description of something that also happens to feel good — it is a description of *what feeling good in this specific way consists in*.

Commitment #1 treats pleasure as an additional ingredient. But try to describe the pleasure of quenched thirst without mentioning wanting and its resolution. You can't — the pleasure just IS the experience of the want being met. What the objector calls 'the emotional dimension' and what the node describes are the same phenomenon identified at different levels of specificity.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The node doesn't strip the pleasure — it identifies what the pleasure consists in. The felt warmth of a wanted sensation arriving is not an emotional layer added to a neutral event; it is what wanting-meeting-occurrence feels like.
The objector and the node are describing the same experience — the objector from the side of how it feels, the node from the side of what is happening when it feels that way.

nodes.claim: Frustration is when a wanted sensation does not occur.
nodes.soWhat: Names the sensory dimension of failure — not just that what was wanted did not occur, but that the felt absence of the sensation is itself experienced.
nodes.search: frustration frustrated deprivation sensory lack absence wanted sensation not occur

sections.title: Observations
items: Hunger directed toward food, and no taste arriving. Just emptiness.
Thirst wanting water, and dryness persisting.
Wanting warmth, and cold continuing.
Wanting to hear a voice, and silence remaining.

items.text: Frustration is when a wanted sensation does not occur.
items: "Frustration" is the specific case of failure (1.2.5.1.4) where the wanted direction is a sensation (1.2.5.2.2) and that sensation does not occur. Hunger wanting taste, and no taste arriving — that is frustration.

Frustration names what the reader already recognizes as distinct from abstract failure: the felt absence of a wanted sensation. A name not coming to mind is failure; the persistent dryness when water was wanted is frustration.

items.title: The sensory quality of deprivation goes unrecognized
items.detail: Without recognizing frustration, failure is just an outcome — what was wanted did not occur — but the felt quality of the sensory absence has no name. The specific sting of wanting a taste and getting emptiness, wanting warmth and feeling cold, is indistinguishable from the abstract fact that a direction was not achieved.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Frustration" — when a wanted sensation does not occur.
Also grounded: "frustrated" (experiencing frustration), "deprived" (in the sensory sense).
This completes the intensity branch: intensity (1.2.5.2.1) → sensation (1.2.5.2.2) → perception (1.2.5.2.3) → satisfaction (1.2.5.2.4) / frustration.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Failure has no sensory dimension — not getting what is wanted and feeling the absence of what was wanted are indistinguishable.
The felt sting of sensory deprivation has no basis beyond abstract failure.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not frustration always involves awareness of what is missing — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not frustration intensifies over time — deferred to later nodes with temporal vocabulary.

items.title: Frustration is just failure — adding 'sensation' does not create a new concept.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Failure (1.2.5.1.4) already names the non-occurrence of what is wanted. Specifying that the wanted thing is a sensation does not introduce a new phenomenon — it is just failure applied to a particular direction.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Frustration is just failure (1.2.5.1.4) applied to a specific kind of direction (wanting a sensation).
Specifying the type of thing wanted does not create a new concept — it is just a special case.
Every concept could be split this way (failure-with-food, failure-with-silence) without producing genuinely new phenomena.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Frustration names something the reader experiences as distinct from abstract failure (1.2.5.1.4). The persistent dryness when water was wanted is not just 'what was wanted did not occur' — it has a sensory quality that abstract failure (like a name not coming to mind) does not.
The reader recognizes this felt difference: the bodily sting of a wanted sensation not arriving versus the recognition that a direction was not achieved.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The reader already distinguishes between a name not coming to mind (failure) and the persistent dryness when water was wanted (frustration).
The sensory quality of deprivation is not just failure applied to a different direction — it is a recognizably different experience.

items.title: Frustration involves anger or agitation — stripping the emotion strips the phenomenon.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Frustration isn't just 'wanted sensation didn't arrive' — it's the grinding tension, the rising agitation, the felt pushback against the absence.

The emotional quality is what makes frustration frustration. A definition that strips the agitation produces a concept of mere non-arrival, which anyone can calmly note without experiencing what people mean by frustration.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: The agitation and tension are constitutive of frustration — not additions to it, but what makes it frustration.
A wanted sensation failing to arrive without any felt tension is not frustration; it is just an unfulfilled want.
The emotional dimension is what distinguishes frustration from neutral non-occurrence.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: The objector is right that frustration *feels like something* — grinding, tense, agitated. The question is what generates that feeling. Try this: you want cold water. None comes. Does the wanting sit calmly? No — the wanting is *for* something specific, and the absence is the absence *of that specific thing*. The wanting keeps pressing toward something that isn't there, and that pressing-against-nothing is the tension.
Now describe the agitation of frustration without mentioning what you wanted and its absence. You can't — the agitation just IS what wanting-against-absence feels like.

Commitment #3 assumes there is a 'neutral non-occurrence' that the emotion then gets added to. But there is no neutral version of wanted-sensation-not-arriving. The wanting guarantees that the absence is felt, and felt specifically as the absence of *this*. Remove the wanting, and you get neutral absence (no tension, no frustration — just nothing happening). Add the wanting, and the tension arrives with it. The tension is not a third ingredient; it is the felt character of the structure.

Commitment #1 treats agitation as the defining feature. But the agitation varies (mild annoyance to rage), while the structure (wanting + non-occurrence) is constant across all cases. What the objector recognizes as frustration across this entire range is the structure, not the intensity of agitation.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The node doesn't strip the agitation — it identifies what generates it. Wanting-pressing-against-absence is not a neutral structural description that also happens to feel tense; it IS the tension.

The agitation varies in intensity, but the structure that produces it is what the node names. Mild frustration and intense frustration share this structure; what varies is the strength of the wanting, not the type of phenomenon.

nodes.claim: Phenomena occur presently.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the quality of 'now' — that what occurs in awareness is immediate and happening. Past, memory, sequence, and all other temporal concepts build on this.
nodes.search: present now immediate happening current presently temporal time moment

sections.title: Observations
items: A sharp pain, right now.
Warmth on skin.
A loud crash.
Present hunger.
The taste of a strawberry, gone from the mouth, yet here now.

items.text: Phenomena occur presently.
items: "Presently" is the quality of occurring right now — the immediacy of what is happening in awareness. The pain, the warmth, the crash, the hunger — each occurs with this quality: it is present.
Everything in awareness shares this: whatever occurs, occurs now. This is not a claim about duration or brevity — it identifies the quality that all occurrences have in common.

items.title: No phenomenon has the quality of immediacy
items.detail: Without presentness, phenomena occur but without the quality of 'now.' There is no distinction between what is happening and what is no longer happening — and past and memory have no contrast to build on.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Presently" / "present" / "now" — the quality of occurring immediately in awareness.
Also grounded: "immediate," "current," "right now," "instant," "at this moment."
The next step: how phenomena follow one another (sequence, 1.2.5.3.2).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: No phenomenon has a quality of immediacy — everything occurs but nothing occurs 'now.'
Presentness is indistinguishable from mere occurrence — there is no temporal quality to experience.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not awareness is continuous or intermittent — requires more temporal vocabulary.
What determines the boundary of 'now' — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Presentness is just occurrence — this adds nothing beyond 'phenomena occur' (1.1.1).

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Everything in awareness already 'occurs.' If all experience is present, then 'presently' is just a synonym for 'occurring.' No new quality is being identified — it's a redundant restatement.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Everything in awareness already 'occurs' — so everything is already present.
If all experience is present, 'presentness' is just a synonym for 'occurring,' not a new quality.
Adding 'presently' to occurrence is a redundant modifier that introduces no new distinction.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Occurrence says something is happening. Presentness identifies the quality of HOW it is happening — with immediacy, with 'now-ness.' This quality is what allows the later contrast with past (what is no longer present). Without naming it, there is no anchor for the distinction between what is happening and what has happened.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This grounds the temporal quality of immediacy — the 'now-ness' that occurrence already has. Without this grounded, past and memory have no contrast to build on — 'no longer present' has no meaning if 'present' was never identified.

items.title: Physics shows 'now' is relative — presentness doesn't track anything real.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Special relativity eliminates a privileged 'now' — simultaneity is frame-dependent, and the block universe treats past, present, and future as equally real.

If physics doesn't privilege the present moment, the felt sense of 'now' is parochial — a feature of how brains work, not of how things are. Presentness is an indexical (like 'here'), not a quality of reality.
Building foundational vocabulary around it means building on something that physics has shown to be perspectival at best.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: If physics doesn't privilege 'now,' then the felt sense of presentness doesn't track anything real — it is a brain artifact.
Phenomenological observations must be ratifiable by physics to be legitimate foundational claims.
The block universe shows that 'now' is an indexical (like 'here') — it points to where the observer happens to be, not to a real feature of reality.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 is where the objection breaks, and the objector almost certainly doesn't hold it consistently. Physics also doesn't privilege 'here' — spatial location is relative in exactly the same way temporal location is. But nobody concludes that the experience of being *here* is an illusion or that spatial location in experience is a brain artifact not worth naming.

If the objector accepts that 'here' picks out a real feature of spatial experience despite being relative, they must accept that 'now' picks out a real feature of temporal experience on the same grounds.

Commitment #3 actually supports the node rather than threatening it: the observation that presentness is an indexical — a quality that points to the observer's location in time — is exactly what the node describes. An indexical is still a quality of experience. The block universe doesn't eliminate the *experience* of presentness; it eliminates the *metaphysical privilege* of the present — which the node never claimed.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The node describes the experiential quality of presentness, not a claim about time's metaphysical structure. Physics may show that 'now' is relative, just as 'here' is relative — but relativity doesn't eliminate the experience of being here or being now.
It shows that the experience is perspectival. The node names the perspective.

nodes.claim: Phenomena occur sequentially.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the experience of temporal ordering — that phenomena follow one another. Step, change, and event all build on this.
nodes.search: sequence sequential order succession follow follows after before then precedes preceding next previous temporal ordering

sections.title: Observations
items: A flash of lightning, then thunder.
One note, then the next in a melody.
Inhale, then exhale.
A door closing, then footsteps.

items.text: Phenomena occur sequentially.
items: Phenomena do not all occur at once — they follow one another. This ordering is "sequence."
Sequence is observable: lightning comes before thunder, one note follows another. The ordering is felt, not inferred.

items.title: No phenomenon ever follows another
items.detail: Without sequence, phenomena occur but without any ordering. Lightning and thunder have no 'before' and 'after.' Notes in a melody have no succession — they are simultaneous. Change, which depends on comparing qualities across a sequence, has nothing to stand on.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Sequentially" / "sequence" — phenomena occurring in an order, one following another.
Also grounded: "before," "follows," "after," "then," "precedes," "preceding," "succession," "order" (temporal), "next," "previous."
Two branches open from sequence: what is no longer present (past, 1.2.5.3.3) and naming individual phenomena within a sequence (step, 1.2.5.3.7).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: No phenomenon ever follows another — everything occurs simultaneously.
Temporal ordering is an illusion — phenomena have no felt succession.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not sequence is linear or branching — deferred to later nodes.
What determines the order of phenomena in a sequence — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Sequence is just how the brain processes information — not a feature of experience itself.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Your brain stamps events with order — temporal sequencing is a product of neural processing.
The felt sense of 'before and after' is constructed, not observed.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Temporal ordering is produced by neural processing — events are stamped with order by the brain.
The felt sense of 'before and after' is constructed by neural mechanisms, not directly observed.
If sequence is a product of processing, it is not a feature of experience but an artifact of how the brain organizes information.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: This describes what occurs in awareness — the felt quality of one phenomenon following another. Whether or not neural processing produces this quality is a question about mechanism. Lightning is experienced before thunder regardless of what produces the ordering.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not sequence is produced by neural processing is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. The claim holds either way: the felt ordering of phenomena — one following another — is observable regardless of what produces it.

items.title: Sequence presupposes an objective flow of time — this smuggles in metaphysical assumptions.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The existence of temporal sequence presupposes a temporal framework — an objective 'flow' of time in which events are ordered. Without such a framework, 'before' and 'after' have no meaning. Starting from sequence assumes what needs to be argued.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: The concepts 'before' and 'after' presuppose an objective temporal framework — a flow of time in which events are ordered.
Without an independently established temporal framework, sequence is undefined.
Starting from sequence assumes the very thing (time) that needs to be argued for.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: This identifies the felt quality of succession in awareness — the observable fact that phenomena follow one another. Whether or not this requires an objective temporal framework is a question about what ultimately exists. The ordering is experienced regardless of its metaphysical underpinning.

The objector's own argument demonstrates what it denies. Their objection proceeds in logical sequence: (1) sequence requires temporal flow, (2) temporal flow needs independent definition, (3) the node doesn't provide one, therefore (4) the node is circular. This is itself a sequence — an ordered series where each step depends on the one before it. If sequence cannot be self-grounding, logical sequence cannot be self-grounding either, and the objector's chain of reasoning (which IS a sequence) has no ground.
They need sequence to be legitimate in order to sequence their argument against sequence.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This identifies the felt quality of succession — one phenomenon following another. whether or not this requires an objective temporal framework is a question about what ultimately exists — one this does not address.
The experienced ordering is observable; its metaphysical underpinning is a separate matter.

nodes.claim: Past phenomena are those that occur before the present.
nodes.soWhat: Names the temporal contrast to the present — what was happening but is no longer. Memory depends on this distinction.
nodes.search: past earlier ago was prior no longer formerly temporal

sections.title: Observations
items: A pain that has stopped.
A sound from earlier.
A taste that has faded.
A hunger from this morning, no longer felt.

items.text: Past phenomena are those that occur before the present.
items: A "past" phenomenon is one that occurred but is no longer present (1.2.5.3.1). "Before" the present means: it was present, and now it is not.
Past is the temporal contrast to present — what was happening but is no longer happening.

items.title: No phenomenon ever ceases to be present
items.detail: Without recognizing the past, every phenomenon in awareness is either present or absent — but there is no quality of 'having been present.' Memory has no subject matter: there is nothing for present information to be about. The distinction between what is happening and what has happened disappears.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Past" — phenomena that occurred before the present. ("Before" is grounded by sequence, 1.2.5.3.2.)
Also grounded: "was," "ago," "prior," "earlier," "no longer," "formerly."
The next step: what retains information about the past (memory, 1.2.5.3.4).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: No phenomenon ever has the quality of 'having occurred' — everything is either present or absent with nothing in between.
Past is indistinguishable from absence — there is no temporal quality to what is gone.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: How much of the past is accessible — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not the past exists independently of present awareness — requires ontological vocabulary (1.3).

items.title: 'Past' is just 'absent' — no new quality is identified.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Once a phenomenon stops occurring, it is absent. "Past" adds nothing beyond "not present." Why introduce a new term for something already covered?

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Non-occurrence and having-occurred are not genuinely different — both mean "not here."
The quality of "having been present" is a memory artifact, not a feature of absence itself.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Absence says a phenomenon is not present. Past says a phenomenon WAS present and is no longer.

Commitment #1 collapses a real distinction: the absence of redness (redness is not occurring) versus the pastness of redness (redness occurred and stopped). Memory (1.2.5.3.4) depends on this distinction — it is information about what was, not about what merely isn't.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Past is not mere absence — it is absence with the quality of "having been present." Without this quality, memory has nothing to be about, and awareness contains no connection to what occurred before.

items.title: The past does not exist — only the present is real.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Presentism holds that only present entities exist; the past has no existence-status. If the past does not exist, it cannot be described as something that 'occurs.'

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Only present entities exist — the past has no existence-status (presentism).
If the past does not exist, it cannot be described as something that 'occurs' or has qualities.
Any claim about 'past phenomena' smuggles in a claim about what exists to the reality of the past.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 is where the objection breaks, and it breaks against the objector. The presentist claims that describing the past commits you to its existence. But the presentist's own central claim — 'the past does not exist' — refers to the past in order to deny it. If referring to something phenomenologically commits you to its existence, the presentist is committed to the past's existence by the very act of denying it.

The only way out is to accept that phenomenological description does not entail ontological commitment — that you can describe the quality of pastness without being committed to the past existing as a domain. But that is exactly what this node does. The presentist's own position requires the separation between phenomenological description and ontological commitment that they deny the node.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The node describes a present quality — the quality of 'having occurred' — not a metaphysical claim about a domain called 'the past.'
The presentist needs this separation (phenomenological description ≠ ontological commitment) to state their own position. The node is doing what the presentist's own framework requires.

nodes.claim: A memory is a present phenomenon about a past phenomenon.
nodes.soWhat: Names the bridge between past and present — how awareness retains information about what occurred. Recognition and newness both depend on this.
nodes.search: memory remember recall retain past present information about

sections.title: Observations
items: The taste of a strawberry from yesterday.
A melody heard this morning.
Words from an earlier conversation.
The character of a pain that is gone.

items.text: A memory is a present phenomenon about a past phenomenon.
items: A "memory" is information (1.2.1.1) that is currently present (1.2.5.3.1) and is about (1.2.1) a phenomenon that is past (1.2.5.3.3).
The original phenomenon is gone; what remains is present information about it. The taste is absent, but the information about the taste persists.

items.title: Present information is never about what has occurred
items.detail: Without recognizing memory, awareness contains present phenomena only — with no connection to what occurred before. The past is inaccessible from the present, and recognition (which depends on comparing present phenomena to memories) has nothing to compare against.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Memory" — a present phenomenon about a past phenomenon.
Also grounded: "remember," "recall," "retain" (in the memory sense).
The next step: when a present phenomenon resembles a memory (recognition, 1.2.5.3.5).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Awareness has no access to the past — present information is never about what occurred before.
Memory is a separate faculty rather than present information about past phenomena.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: How memories are formed or stored — mechanism deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not memories accurately represent what occurred — accuracy requires truth vocabulary not yet built.
How many memories awareness contains at once — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Memory requires a brain and storage mechanisms — this definition is too minimal.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Memory is defined by how it works — encoding, storage, and retrieval processes in the brain.
A definition that ignores the mechanism is incomplete. Without specifying how information is stored and retrieved, 'present information about the past' could refer to anything.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Memory is defined by its mechanism — encoding, storage, and retrieval processes.
A definition of memory that ignores mechanism is incomplete and potentially misleading.
Without specifying how information is stored and retrieved, 'present information about the past' could refer to anything.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: This identifies what memory (1.2.5.3) IS as experienced — present information about what occurred. Whether or not that information requires a brain, encoding, or storage is a question about mechanism, not about what is observed.
The phenomenon of having present information about a past taste, a past conversation, or a past pain is observable regardless of what produces or stores it.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not memory requires specific physical mechanisms is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. The claim holds either way: present information about past phenomena is observable regardless of what produces it.

items.title: False memories exist — memory is not always 'about' a past phenomenon that actually occurred.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Psychology has documented false memories, confabulation, and memory distortion. If a memory is defined as present information about a past phenomenon, false memories don't fit — they are present information about events that never occurred.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: If a memory can be about an event that never occurred, "about a past phenomenon" is inaccurate.
A definition of memory must account for the possibility of error.
"About" implies successful correspondence — and false memories don't correspond to anything real.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 is where the objection breaks. "About" here describes the *experiential direction* of the memory — it presents itself as being about the past — not a guarantee of accurate correspondence.

A false memory still has the quality of being about something past; it is the *accuracy* of that aboutness that fails. Accuracy and truth are downstream concepts that require comparison and verification vocabulary not yet built.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This defines memory as present information about a past phenomenon. whether or not that information accurately represents the past is a separate question.
A false memory (1.2.5.3) is still present information that carries the quality of being about something past — its error is in accuracy, not in experiential structure.

nodes.claim: Recognition is when a phenomenon is like a memory.
nodes.soWhat: Names the moment when a present phenomenon matches something from the past. The distinction between familiar and new depends on this.
nodes.search: recognition recognize familiar known seen before match memory like

sections.title: Observations
items: Tasting a strawberry, and the taste matching a memory.
A melody, heard before.
The smell of coffee, familiar.
A face that matches features from memory.

items.text: Recognition is when a phenomenon is like a memory.
items: "Recognition" is the awareness that a present phenomenon shares qualities with a memory (1.2.5.3.4) — it is like (1.1.4) something that occurred before.
The present phenomenon is matched against the memory: the taste of strawberry now is like the taste of strawberry in memory.

items.title: No present phenomenon is ever connected to what occurred before
items.detail: Without recognizing recognition, no present phenomenon is ever matched to a memory. Every experience occurs without connection to the past — there is no familiarity, no 'this is like what occurred before.' The distinction between what has been experienced before and what has not disappears.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Recognition" / "recognize" — when a present phenomenon is like a memory.
Also grounded: "familiar," "known" (in the recognition sense), "seen before."
The next step: what occurs when there is no recognition (newness, 1.2.5.3.6).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Present phenomena are never connected to past phenomena — every occurrence is isolated from what came before.
Familiarity has no experiential basis — no phenomenon ever matches a memory.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: How precise the similarity needs to be — whether or not approximate likeness counts as recognition — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not recognition is always conscious or noticed — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Recognition requires more than similarity — it involves judgment, categorization, and conceptual thought.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: There is a difference between simple pattern-matching and genuine recognition. Recognition involves categorization, semantic processing, and sometimes conscious judgment.
Saying a phenomenon is 'like' a memory undersells the cognitive complexity of what recognition actually involves.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Recognition involves judgment, categorization, and conceptual thought — not just similarity-detection.
Saying a phenomenon is 'like' a memory undersells the cognitive complexity of recognition.
A minimal definition that reduces recognition to similarity misses what makes recognition a distinct cognitive act.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: This identifies the experiential core of recognition — the moment when a present phenomenon matches a memory. Whether or not additional cognitive processes are involved is a question about mechanism. The phenomenon of 'this taste is like the strawberry from before' is observable regardless of how complex the underlying process is.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not recognition involves additional cognitive processes is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. The claim holds either way: the moment when a present phenomenon is like a memory (1.2.5.3) is observable regardless of what produces it.

items.title: Infants recognize faces without memories — recognition doesn't require memory.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Newborns prefer faces to scrambled face-patterns within hours of birth. They track face-like stimuli preferentially before they could have formed relevant memories.

Developmental psychologists call this recognition. If the definition requires memory and infants recognize without memory, either the definition is wrong or the word 'recognition' is being used in a way that excludes paradigm cases.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Innate face-preference in newborns is genuine recognition — it produces the same behavioral output (preferential tracking, differential response) as memory-based recognition.
A definition of recognition that excludes paradigm cases of recognition has failed to capture the phenomenon.
The behavioral criterion (differential response to familiar-type stimuli) is the correct criterion for recognition, not the experiential structure (matching to a memory).

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 uses 'recognition' to cover two different experiences and then objects that the definition only captures one. But the two are genuinely different from inside. Consider an adult case: you see someone on the street and your body responds — heartbeat quickens, attention sharpens — but you don't know why. Is that recognition? It has the behavioral signature (differential response), but it's missing something: the *familiarity*, the sense of 'I have encountered this before.'

Now you remember — it's a childhood friend. The familiarity arrives. Something changed between the differential response and the recognition, and what changed is the memory-connection. The newborn's face-preference is like the first moment (differential response without familiarity), not the second (recognition with memory-connection).

Commitment #3 defines recognition by its behavioral output. But the node is tracking a specific experiential quality — the quality of *encountering-again*, which requires having encountered before. The newborn has never encountered before. What the newborn does have is an innate response pattern, which is a real phenomenon (a pattern, 1.2.1.6, or an association, 1.1.4) — but it is a different phenomenon with a different experiential structure.
Calling both 'recognition' obscures the difference between reacting to something for the first time (however selectively) and re-encountering something familiar.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The definition identifies recognition by its experiential character: the quality of a present phenomenon being like a memory. Innate face-preference produces selective response without familiarity — it is a real phenomenon, but a different one.
The node doesn't deny that newborns respond selectively; it names the specific experience of encountering-again, which requires having encountered before.

nodes.claim: A phenomenon is new when it occurs without recognition.
nodes.soWhat: Names the experience of encountering something for the first time — when nothing in memory matches. Completes the memory chain: present, past, memory, recognition, new.
nodes.search: new novel unfamiliar first time unprecedented unknown fresh

sections.title: Observations
items: A fruit never tasted before.
An unfamiliar language.
An unusual color, unrecognized.
An unfamiliar place.

items.text: A phenomenon is new when it occurs without recognition.
items: A "new" phenomenon is one that occurs without matching any memory — recognition (1.2.5.3.5) does not happen.
Newness is the absence of recognition: the present phenomenon has no counterpart in memory.

items.title: No phenomenon is ever unfamiliar
items.detail: Without recognizing newness, every occurrence is either recognized or simply unclassified — but nothing ever has the quality of 'first time.' The difference between tasting a fruit for the hundredth time and tasting one never encountered before disappears. Surprise has no ground, and the impetus to explore what does not yet match any memory — which feeds imagination (1.2.5.6.1) and possibility (1.2.5.6.4) — has no starting point.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "New" / "novel" / "unfamiliar" — a phenomenon that occurs without recognition.
Also grounded: "novelty," "first time," "unprecedented."
This completes the memory chain. With presentness, pastness, memory, recognition, and newness, awareness has the basic vocabulary for how experience relates to what occurred before.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: No phenomenon is ever unfamiliar — everything that occurs is always recognized.
Newness requires something beyond the absence of recognition — a separate faculty of novelty-detection.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not newness is always noticed — deferred to later nodes.
What makes a phenomenon seem 'almost familiar' — borderline recognition deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Newness is just the absence of something — it is not a real phenomenon worth naming.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: If recognition does not happen, nothing new actually occurs — there is just an absence of recognition. Naming this absence 'new' treats a non-event as a concept. It adds nothing to the vocabulary.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: The absence of recognition is a non-event — nothing new actually happens when recognition fails to occur.
Naming an absence as if it were a positive phenomenon is a category error.
A vocabulary does not need a term for every absence — 'not recognized' suffices without coining 'new.'

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: The absence of recognition (1.2.5.3.5) IS something observable. Encountering something without any matching memory has a felt quality — unfamiliarity, the sense of 'never before.' This quality is observably distinct from the quality of recognition.
Downstream concepts that depend on novelty — such as learning and discovery — depend on this distinction being named.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not newness is 'merely' the absence of recognition or a positive quality in its own right is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied.

The claim holds either way: phenomena that occur without recognition (1.2.5.3.5) are observably distinct from phenomena that are recognized, and naming this distinction gives downstream concepts something to build on.

items.title: Absence is not a genuine quality — 'newness' as the absence of recognition is a category error.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The debate about negative facts in analytic philosophy (Russell, Molnar, Armstrong) raises a genuine question: is the absence of something a positive fact or merely the failure of a positive fact to obtain?
If newness is just "no recognition occurred," then naming it as a quality attributes positive character to a mere absence. This is like calling darkness a color or silence a sound.
The absence of recognition doesn't *add* anything to the phenomenon — it just means something (recognition) didn't happen. Treating non-recognition as a quality is a category error.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Absences are not positive properties — they are the failure of positive properties to be instantiated.
Naming an absence as if it were a quality (calling non-recognition "newness") is a category error.
The felt quality of unfamiliarity is not evidence of a positive property — it is the experiential artifact of searching for recognition and failing.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 is the strongest form and is worth taking seriously. The objector proposes that the feeling of newness is really the experience of failed recognition-search, not a positive quality.

But this reformulation still concedes the key point: there IS a felt quality — the quality of encountering something without recognition. whether or not that quality is "positively" present or "negatively" generated by a search-failure, it occurs in awareness with specific character.

Darkness IS experienced as a quality, whatever its physical status. Silence IS experienced as a quality when it follows noise. The category-error charge depends on commitment #1, which applies to ontology (what exists in the world) rather than phenomenology (what occurs in experience).
In experience, absences have character.

subSections.label: Correction
items: whether or not newness is a "genuine" property or the result of absent recognition (1.2.5.3.5) is a question about what ultimately exists. In experience, the encounter with something unrecognized has specific felt character — the quality of unfamiliarity — and that character is what this identifies.
Darkness is not a wavelength, but it is a visual quality. Newness may not be a "positive property" in the metaphysical sense, but it is a quality that occurs in awareness.

nodes.claim: A step is a phenomenon in a sequence.
nodes.soWhat: Names the individual unit within a sequence. Change depends on comparing steps.
nodes.search: step stage phase unit individual occurrence in sequence part

sections.title: Observations
items: A single note in a melody.
One inhale in a breathing cycle.
One footstep in a walk.
The flash of lightning in lightning-then-thunder.

items.text: A step is a phenomenon in a sequence.
items: A "step" is a single phenomenon considered as part of a sequence (1.2.5.3.2) — the individual occurrence within the flow of succession.
Each note is a step in the melody. Each breath is a step in the cycle. The step is the unit that change compares.

items.title: No individual phenomenon is identifiable within a sequence
items.detail: Without recognizing steps, sequences have no individual parts. Change, which requires comparing qualities at different points in a sequence, has no individual occurrences to compare.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Step" — a single phenomenon within a sequence.
Also grounded: "stage," "phase" (as synonyms for a unit in a sequence).
The next step: what happens between steps — change (1.2.5.3.8).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Sequences have no individual parts — the flow of succession is indivisible.
Individual phenomena exist but have no place within a sequence.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: How fine-grained steps are — deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not steps have fixed duration — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Isolating a phenomenon from its sequence changes what it is — temporal experience is holistic.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: You cannot extract a note from a melody without changing what it is. A note heard in context — preceded by the notes before it, anticipating the notes after — is a different experience from the same pitch heard in isolation.

Temporal experience is holistic: the meaning and character of each moment is constituted by its sequential context. Calling a phenomenon a 'step' suggests it can be cleanly identified within the sequence and then discussed independently.
But if the sequence constitutes the step's character, 'a phenomenon in a sequence' is an abstraction that doesn't match the actual experience.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: The sequential context is constitutive of a phenomenon's experiential character — the same content in a different position is a different experience.
Isolating a 'step' from its sequence is an analytic fiction — useful for description, but not matching how temporal experience actually works.
Phenomenological description should respect the holistic structure of temporal experience rather than decomposing it into atomic steps.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 is true — and the node accommodates it. A step is defined as 'a phenomenon IN a sequence,' not 'a phenomenon extracted FROM a sequence.' The 'in' is load-bearing: it identifies the phenomenon *as positioned*, not as abstracted from position.
The middle C that follows a B in a melody is identified as a step that includes its sequential context — the preceded-by-B quality is part of what makes this step this step.
Commitment #2 assumes the node strips context; it doesn't. It names the phenomenon-with-its-position, which is exactly the holistic unit the objector wants to preserve.
Commitment #3 demands what the node already provides: a vocabulary for phenomena as they occur within sequences, not apart from them.

subSections.label: Correction
items: A step is not a phenomenon *removed from* a sequence — it is a phenomenon *identified within* one. The sequential context (what came before, what follows) is part of the step's character.
The node names the unit of temporal experience that the holist rightly insists cannot be separated from its context — by defining it as always already in context.

nodes.claim: Change is the difference of a quality in a sequence.
nodes.soWhat: Names the phenomenon of qualities varying across steps in a sequence. Events — and eventually causation — build on this.
nodes.search: change shift transition vary become different alter transform sequence quality

sections.title: Observations
items: Red shifting to orange.
A loud sound fading to quiet.
Warmth cooling.
Sharp pain easing to a dull ache.

items.text: Change is the difference of a quality in a sequence.
items: "Change" is when a quality differs between steps (1.2.5.3.7) in a sequence (1.2.5.3.2). Red is followed by orange. Loud is followed by quiet. The quality varies across steps.
This combines distinction (1.1.2), quality (1.1.3), and sequence (1.2.5.3.2) to name a recognizable pattern.

items.title: No quality ever differs across a sequence
items.detail: Without recognizing change, qualities in a sequence are always the same — red stays red, loud stays loud, warm stays warm. Events, which depend on the specific change from not-occurring to occurring, have no basis.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Change" — the difference of a quality across steps in a sequence.
Also grounded: "shift," "transition" (in the general sense), "become," "turn into."
The next step: a specific kind of change — the appearance of a phenomenon (event, 1.2.5.3.9).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Qualities never differ across a sequence — everything in a sequence stays the same.
Change requires something beyond the difference of qualities in a sequence — an external force or causal mechanism.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: What produces change — mechanism deferred to later nodes.
Whether or not change is continuous or discrete — deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Change requires a theory of time — grounding change in sequence is circular.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Sequence is already a temporal concept — 'before and after' is what time *means*. If change is 'difference in a sequence,' and sequence is temporal ordering, then change is 'difference over time' — which requires an independently defined notion of time.

But the tree doesn't define time independently; it derives temporal concepts from experienced sequence. So the circle is: change depends on sequence, sequence depends on temporal ordering, temporal ordering is what change is. You haven't grounded change; you've restated it.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Sequence is a temporal concept — it means 'ordered in time.'
Defining a temporal concept (change) in terms of another temporal concept (sequence) is circular and therefore explanatorily empty.
Non-circular grounding of change requires an external (non-temporal) standpoint from which temporal concepts can be independently defined.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 is where the objection breaks. The demand for non-circular grounding of foundational concepts is a demand no foundation can satisfy. You cannot define 'existence' without using existence. You cannot define 'difference' without using difference. You cannot define temporal concepts from a non-temporal standpoint because temporal experience is the ground, not the thing being grounded.
The 'circle' the objector identifies is not a defect — it is what it looks like when a concept is genuinely foundational.

Commitment #2 conflates two kinds of circularity: *definitional* circularity (using a word in its own definition, which is vacuous) and *foundational* circularity (identifying a concept that cannot be reduced to something more basic, which is what foundations are). Sequence doesn't define change — it identifies the structure within which change is observable. The sequence is experienced directly; change is observed within it. That's not a circle — it's a dependency.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Change is observed within experienced sequence. The sequence is not itself derived from a theory of time — it is the felt ordering that any theory of time is built from.
The objector's demand (ground temporal concepts non-temporally) would eliminate the possibility of any foundational temporal concept. Sequence is the foundation; change is what you observe within it.

items.title: Nothing truly changes — what appears as change is a succession of distinct, momentary states.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Some philosophical traditions argue that change is illusory. What appears to change is really a succession of distinct, momentary states — not a single thing undergoing alteration.
If each state is separate and complete, the 'change' between them is something you add, not something that occurs.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: What appears as change is really a succession of distinct, momentary states — not a single thing undergoing alteration.
True change requires a persisting subject that undergoes alteration — without persistence, there is only replacement.
If each momentary state is distinct, the 'change' between them is an observer's construction, not a feature of the states themselves.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: This does not claim that a single underlying thing persists through change. It identifies a pattern in experience: a quality that differs across steps in a sequence. Whether or not this is 'true change' in the metaphysical sense — or a succession of distinct states — is a question about what ultimately exists.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not change involves a persisting subject or a succession of distinct states is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. The claim holds either way: the quality-difference across steps is observable regardless of what metaphysically explains it.

nodes.claim: An event is the transition from "not-occurring" to "occurring".
nodes.soWhat: Names the specific change where a phenomenon appears — the transition from absence to presence. Completes the sequence chain: sequence, step, change, event.
nodes.search: event begin start appear arise happen transition occurrence beginning onset

sections.title: Observations
items: A sound beginning: silence, then a note.
Pain appearing: comfort, then a sharp sting.
A light turning on: darkness, then brightness.
Hunger arising: no pull toward food, then a pull.

items.text: An event is the transition from "not-occurring" to "occurring."
items: An "event" is a specific kind of change (1.2.5.3.8): the quality changes from absent to present. A sound beginning, pain appearing, a light turning on — each is a transition from not-occurring to occurring.
This applies the vocabulary of change to the most basic shift: from absence (1.1) to presence (1.2.5.3.1).

items.title: No phenomenon ever begins
items.detail: Without recognizing events, phenomena change but never start. There is no 'beginning' — no transition from absence to presence. The appearance of anything in awareness has no name and no distinct identity.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Event" — the transition from not-occurring to occurring.
Also grounded: "begin," "start," "appear," "arise," "happen" (in the event sense), "onset."
This completes the sequence chain. With sequence, step, change, and event, the temporal vocabulary for ordering and transitions is established.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Phenomena never begin — everything either always occurs or never occurs.
The transition from absence to presence is indistinguishable from any other change.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not every phenomenon has a beginning — deferred to later nodes.
What the reverse transition is (from occurring to not-occurring) — cessation is deferred to later nodes.
What causes events — causation deferred to later nodes.

items.title: Events have sharp boundaries, but real phenomena don't — the onset problem.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Dawn doesn't start. Falling asleep doesn't begin at a moment. Pain fades in. The definition ('transition from not-occurring to occurring') implies a sharp boundary — a moment where the phenomenon crosses from absent to present.
But many phenomena have no such moment. The sorites paradox applies: add one photon of light at a time, and there is no single photon that makes it 'dawn.'
If the transition is gradual, there is no determinate point where 'not-occurring' becomes 'occurring,' and the definition fails for exactly the cases where events are most interesting.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 'Transition from not-occurring to occurring' implies a sharp, identifiable boundary between absence and presence.
Gradual-onset phenomena have no such boundary — the transition is continuous, not discrete.
A definition of 'event' that fails for gradual-onset cases fails for a large and important class of phenomena.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 imports a precision that the node doesn't require. 'Transition' does not mean 'instantaneous switch.' It means the region where not-occurring gives way to occurring. For sharp-onset phenomena (a clap, a flash), the region is narrow. For gradual-onset phenomena (dawn, falling asleep), the region is wide — but the transition still occurs.
There is a time when it is dark and a time when it is light; the transition between them is the event, however extended.

Commitment #2 is true (the transition is continuous) but doesn't threaten the definition — it shows that events can be temporally extended, not that they don't exist. The sorites paradox challenges the precision of the boundary, not the reality of the transition. Nobody doubts that dawn occurs; the difficulty is saying exactly when. That difficulty is about the *boundaries* of the event, not about whether or not the event is real.

subSections.label: Correction
items: An event is the transition from not-occurring to occurring — and transitions can be gradual. Dawn is an extended event, not a failed instantaneous one.
The sorites paradox shows that the boundaries of some events are vague, not that those events don't occur. Vagueness of boundary and reality of transition are compatible.

items.title: Gradual-onset phenomena have no sharp transition point — when does 'not-occurring' become 'occurring'?

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Dawn does not begin at a moment. Falling asleep has no sharp onset. A headache can intensify so gradually that there is no point at which you were clearly not-in-pain and then clearly in-pain.
The sorites paradox applies directly: if removing one grain doesn't destroy the heap, and you can remove any individual grain without effect, the heap never disappears — yet it does.

Similarly, if no single moment constitutes the transition from not-occurring to occurring, yet the transition happens, then "transition" is an unprincipled concept.  The definition requires a boundary it cannot locate, and an unlocatable boundary is no boundary at all.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: "Transition from not-occurring to occurring" requires a determinable boundary between the two states — without one, the definition is vacuous.
The sorites structure shows that vague boundaries are not merely imprecise but *incoherent*: if no individual moment constitutes the transition, no collection of moments does either.
Phenomenology that relies on vague predicates inherits the logical problems of vagueness — it cannot simply gesture at "you know it when you see it" without addressing why that isn't unprincipled.

subSections.label: What's Missing

items.text: Commitment #2 is the strongest form. The sorites reasoning shows that no *single step* in a gradual series is the decisive one.
items: But the conclusion — that therefore no transition occurs — contradicts what the sorites itself presupposes. The sorites argument *requires* that there is a heap at the beginning and no heap at the end; without the transition, the paradox cannot even be stated. The argument proves that the transition cannot be located at a precise point, not that no transition occurs.

items.text: This matters because commitment #3 assumes description of experience must meet the standards of predicate logic — that "transition" must be a sharp predicate with determinate extension.
items: If vague boundaries disqualified experiential concepts, then "present" would fail before "event" is even reached.  The sorites objector would have to reject the entire temporal branch of the tree, not just this — which is a far heavier commitment than objecting to "event."

But description of experience operates at the level of what is experienced, and what is experienced includes vague transitions. The specious present itself — the experienced "now" — has no sharp boundaries; it fades into just-past and about-to-be without a cutoff.

items.text: Commitment #1 demands a locatable boundary.
items: But this says "transition," not "moment of transition." A transition is a change in status — from absent to present — and the change is observable even when the change-point is not. You were awake; now you are asleep. The transition is real. The objector cannot deny this without denying the very data the sorites argument is built from (the heap existed and then didn't).

subSections.label: Correction
items: The sorites paradox shows that the *location* of the transition resists precise identification. It does not show that no transition occurs — in fact, it presupposes that one does (otherwise there is no paradox).

This defines an event as the transition itself, not as the precise moment of transition. Gradual-onset phenomena are events with vague boundaries, which is a description of the boundary's character, not evidence that the event didn't happen.
The objector's own paradox requires the transition it claims to undermine.

nodes.claim: Imagination is information from different memories.
nodes.soWhat: Names the experience of combining pieces from separate memories into something new. Visualization, thought, and possibility all build on this.
nodes.search: imagination imagine imaginary fictional hypothetical mental construct combine memories creative

sections.title: Observations
items: A pink elephant.
A horse with wings.
A familiar face in a place it has never been.
The sound of one voice speaking another person's words.

items.text: Imagination is information from different memories.
items: An "imagination" is information assembled from different memories (1.2.5.3.4). A pink elephant combines pinkness from one memory with elephant-shape from another. A winged horse combines features from separate past experiences into something that was never experienced as a whole.
Imagination differs from memory: a memory is a present phenomenon about a single past phenomenon. An imagination combines information from multiple distinct memories into something new.

items.title: Combining information from different memories has no name
items.detail: Without recognizing imagination, there is no label for the experience of assembling information from separate memories. The pink elephant, the winged horse — each is just "a memory" with no recognition that something new has been constructed from pieces. Visualization, thought, and possibility — which all build on imagination — have no foundation.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Imagination" / "imagine" / "imaginary" — information assembled from different memories.
Also grounded: "fictional" (imagined, not from a single memory), "construct" (in the mental sense — something built from pieces).
The next step: the sensory quality of imagination (visualization, 1.2.5.6.2) and the structure of connected imaginations (thought, 1.2.5.6.3).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Everything in awareness is a direct memory or current sensation — nothing is constructed from pieces of different memories.
There is no difference between remembering and imagining — both are the same type of experience.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not imagination requires deliberate effort or occurs involuntarily — deferred to later analysis.
What constrains which combinations of information are assembled — deferred to possibility (1.2.5.6.4).

items.title: Imagination contains genuinely novel elements untraceable to any memory.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Dreams contain entities, textures, and spatial configurations that the dreamer has never encountered. Psychedelic experiences produce geometries and colors with no apparent source in past experience.
Artists describe moments of genuine novelty — a shape or color combination that 'came from nowhere.'
If imagination is recombination of memories, these cases are counterexamples: the elements weren't in memory to begin with.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Some imagined content has no traceable source in any past experience — it is genuinely novel, not recombined.
The subjective sense of novelty ('I've never seen this before') is reliable evidence that the content is not memory-derived.
If even one element is genuinely novel (not from memory), the definition 'information from different memories' is incomplete.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 is where the objection breaks. The subjective sense of novelty is unreliable evidence for the *source* of the content, because the recombination can be unrecognizable even to the person doing it. A dream geometry that feels unprecedented may combine the spatial structure of a childhood room with the color palette of a sunset and the texture of tree bark — each element from memory, the combination novel.
The pink elephant has never been seen, but pink has and elephants have.

Commitment #1 faces a structural problem: for an element to appear in imagination with any character at all (color, shape, spatial structure, texture), it must have *some* quality — and that quality was encountered somewhere. An element with no connection to any past experience would have no character — it would be experientially empty.

Commitment #3 is valid in principle but hasn't been established: no one has demonstrated an imagined element that lacks all connection to prior experience, only elements whose connections are not obvious.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The novelty of imagination is in the combination, not in the elements. Every element that has character — color, shape, texture, spatial structure — draws that character from experience.

What imagination does is assemble these elements into configurations that were never experienced as a whole. The subjective feeling of 'I've never encountered this' accurately reports the novelty of the combination while being unreliable about the source of the components.

items.title: Definition too broad — ordinary associations also combine information from different memories.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Association (1.1.4) already describes the co-occurrence of qualities. When a smell triggers a visual memory, that combines information from different sources. The definition of imagination is so broad it includes ordinary associative recall.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: If a smell triggers a visual memory, that counts as combining information from different memories — which would qualify as imagination under this definition.
The definition doesn't distinguish creative construction from passive association.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: The distinction is in what is produced. Associations are qualities co-occurring — the smell and the visual memory each remain what they were. Imagination produces *new information* — a unified phenomenon drawn from multiple memories that was not present in any single memory.
The pink elephant is something never experienced; the smell-memory link recalls something that was. Commitment #1 confuses co-occurrence of existing information with construction of new information.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Imagination (1.2.5.6.1) produces new information — a unified phenomenon assembled from multiple memories (1.2.5.3). Association (1.1.4) is the co-occurrence of existing qualities. The pink elephant is new; the smell-memory link is not.

nodes.claim: A visualization is the sensation of an imagination.
nodes.soWhat: Names the sensory quality of imagining — the 'seeing' in the mind's eye, the 'hearing' of an imagined melody. Compatibility and contradiction later depend on this.
nodes.search: visualization visualize mental image mind's eye picture envision imagine sensation

sections.title: Observations
items: The color of an imagined red apple.
The sound of an imagined melody.
The felt weight of an imagined heavy stone.
The taste imagined when reading a menu.

items.text: A visualization is the sensation of an imagination.
items: A "visualization" is the felt, sensory quality (1.2.5.2.2) of an imagination (1.2.5.6.1). The imagined red apple has a sensory quality — dimmer than actual red, but recognizably red.
Visualization is to imagination what perception (1.2.5.2.3) is to observation: the sensory dimension of the experience.

items.title: Imagination has no sensory dimension
items.detail: Without recognizing visualization, imagining a pink elephant and merely thinking the words "pink elephant" are indistinguishable. But the reader already knows these are different experiences — one has sensory character, the other does not. Without naming this difference, compatibility and contradiction lose their experiential ground: they depend on imagining definitions together and checking whether or not a visualization results (1.4.2.2–1.4.2.3). If imagination has no sensory dimension, there is nothing to check — and the entire logical vocabulary from compatibility onward has no test the reader performs.

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Visualization" / "visualize" — the sensation of an imagination.
Also grounded: "mental image," "mind's eye," "picture" (as a verb — to visualize), "envision."

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Imagination has no sensory quality — all mental content is abstract, without any felt character.
Imagining a red apple and merely knowing the concept "red apple" are identical experiences.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not visualizations vary in vividness across individuals (e.g., aphantasia) — deferred to later analysis.
The relationship between visualization vividness and memory quality.

items.title: Some people cannot visualize — aphantasia shows this is not universal.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Research on aphantasia shows some people report having no mental imagery at all. They imagine without any visual, auditory, or tactile quality. If visualization is the sensation of imagination, either these individuals do not imagine (contradicted by evidence — they do) or the definition is wrong.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Aphantasia demonstrates that productive imagination occurs without any sensory quality whatsoever — not just without visual imagery, but without any phenomenal character.
The aphantasia research alone is sufficient to establish that imagination can be phenomenally empty.
If the definition doesn't accommodate aphantasia, it fails as a universal definition.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: The objection faces a dilemma it does not resolve. If aphantasic imagination has any experiential quality at all — however dim, however non-visual (spatial structure, verbal character, abstract felt-sense) — then that quality is what this calls visualization, and the definition holds.

If aphantasic imagination has zero experiential quality — truly nothing it is like to combine those memories — then in what sense is it imagination? The research cited says aphantasic people do imagine productively.

Commitment #2 is where the objection breaks: accepting productive imagination while insisting on zero phenomenal character commits the objector to a much heavier position — that genuinely contentful cognitive processes occur with no experiential quality whatsoever.
That is a localized form of the zombie hypothesis, and it is a far larger commitment than aphantasia research alone supports.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Either aphantasic imagination has some experiential quality (in which case the definition applies), or it has none (in which case the objector must defend the claim that productive cognition occurs with zero phenomenal character — a commitment that goes well beyond the aphantasia data).
Whether or not all individuals visualize with equal vividness is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied.

items.title: Visualization is just weak sensation — there is no separate category.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: An imagined color is just a faint version of seeing that color. A remembered melody is just a quiet version of hearing it. "Visualization" is sensation at low intensity, not a distinct type.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: The difference between perceiving and imagining is intensity, not source.
An imagined color is the same kind of thing as a perceived color, just fainter.
If the only difference is degree, no new category is warranted.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 assumes intensity is the only dimension that could differ — likely because intensity is the most *obvious* difference.

But the source also differs: sensation in perception comes from current stimulus; visualization comes from imagination — information assembled from memory. The intensity may overlap (a vivid imagination can be stronger than a dim perception), but what distinguishes them is what they are the sensation OF.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The distinction is not about intensity but source. A visualization is the sensation (1.2.5.2.2) of an imagination (1.2.5.6.1), just as a perception (1.2.5.2.3) is the sensation of an observation.
