They may feel similar, but one is of what is currently present and the other is of what is mentally assembled.

nodes.claim: A thought is a set of imaginations and their associations.
nodes.soWhat: Names the structured mental experience of connected imaginations. Possibility and future build on this, and later, concepts, statements, and arguments are specific kinds of thoughts.
nodes.search: thought think thinking idea mental content structured imagination

sections.title: Observations
items: "The cat is on the mat."
Planning what to eat for dinner.
Weighing two options before choosing.
Following a story with characters and events.

items.text: A thought is a set of imaginations and their associations.
items: A "thought" is multiple imaginations (1.2.5.6.1) connected by associations (1.1.4). "The cat on the mat" is a thought: an imagined cat, an imagined mat, associated by spatial position.

What makes a thought distinct from a single imagination: a pink elephant is one imagination. "A pink elephant flying over a city" is a thought — multiple imaginations (elephant, wings, city) with associations (flying over, spatial arrangement).

items.title: Multiple imaginations have no unified structure
items.detail: Without recognizing thought, multiple imaginations co-occurring have no connected whole. "The cat on the mat" is just three separate imaginations — cat, mat, spatial position — with no recognition that they form a single structured experience. Possibility, which depends on evaluating structured mental content against known patterns, has nothing to evaluate.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Thought" / "think" / "thinking" — a set of imaginations connected by associations.
Also grounded: "idea" (a thought).
The next step: a thought constrained by recognized patterns (possibility, 1.2.5.6.4).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: There is no structured mental content — imaginations occur but never form connected wholes.
Thoughts require something beyond imaginations and associations — a special mental faculty or medium.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not thoughts require language or occur without words — deferred to later analysis.
What determines which imaginations associate into a thought.

items.title: Abstract thought requires language — the Sapir-Whorf challenge.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: 'The cat is on the mat' works as a visual scene. But 'if the cat were not on the mat, fewer mice would be caught' does not. Counterfactuals, negation, and quantification ('all,' 'none,' 'most') seem to require linguistic scaffolding — there is no obvious way to picture 'not,' to visualize 'all possible cats,' or to imagine 'if things were otherwise.'
The strong Sapir-Whorf hypothesis may be overstated, but the weaker claim — that certain *types* of abstract structure depend on language — is well-supported.
If thought is 'imaginations and their associations,' where do negation and counterfactual structure live?

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Certain abstract structures (negation, counterfactuals, quantification) cannot be represented non-linguistically.
If these structures are constitutive of certain thoughts, then those thoughts require language, and the definition must acknowledge this.
Defining thought without mentioning language excludes the thoughts that most need explaining — the abstract, structured ones.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 is the load-bearer, and the objector is right that simple spatial examples don't fully address it. The hard case is a thought like 'not every belief is justified, but if some were unjustifiable in principle, coherentism would fail.' That has nested quantification, conditionality, and abstract predication. Can this be non-linguistic?

Here is why the hard case doesn't break the definition: the question is not whether or not language helps structure complex thoughts (it does), but whether or not language is the *source* of the structure or a *medium* for it. Consider: a bilingual person can think the same counterfactual in English and French. The linguistic structure changes entirely; the thought is the same. What persists across the two languages is the associative structure between the imagined components — the same relationships, expressed through different words. If language were constitutive of the thought, switching languages would produce a different thought. It doesn't.

Commitment #2 is right that some thoughts are most *naturally* expressed linguistically. But 'most naturally expressed in' is not 'constituted by.' Mathematical insight is often non-linguistic (spatial, structural) and then translated into symbols. Musical composition is non-linguistic and richly structured. These are not lesser forms of thought; they are thought structured through non-linguistic associations.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Language is one powerful medium for structuring associations between imaginations — but the structure it expresses is not created by the language.

The same thought persists across translations, which means the thought's identity is in its associative structure, not in its linguistic form. The definition captures this: a thought is imaginations connected by associations. Some associations are linguistic; others are spatial, temporal, qualitative, or structural.

items.title: This makes every mental event a 'thought' — the definition is too broad.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Any time multiple imaginations co-occur with associations, it is a thought? Daydreaming, idle mental chatter, random associative cascades — all thoughts? The definition captures too much and distinguishes too little.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: A definition that captures daydreaming, idle chatter, and rigorous reasoning under one label is too coarse to be useful.
Types should carve at joints — a definition this broad doesn't.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 assumes that the broadest type-level definition should also be the most discriminating. But "quality" (1.1.3) names any distinct phenomenon — that's maximally broad and still useful because later nodes narrow it (association, feature, pattern, etc.).
"Thought" names the general type; specific kinds of thought — possibility, concept, argument — are distinguished by later nodes that add further constraints.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The definition is broad by design. "Thought" (1.2.5.6.3) names the general type, just as "quality" (1.1.3) names any distinct phenomenon. Specific kinds of thought are distinguished by later nodes.

nodes.claim: A possibility is a thought that matches recognized patterns.
nodes.soWhat: Grounds the experience of 'could happen' — a thought constrained by what is already known. The future, and later the formal definitions of possible and impossible (1.4.4.1–2), build on this.
nodes.search: possibility possible might could plausible conceivable feasible pattern match

sections.title: Observations
items: A coin in the air: heads or tails, not landing as a fish.
Clouds overhead, and the thought "it might rain."
Imagining a chess move that follows the rules.
A glass near the edge of a table, and the thought of it falling.

items.text: A possibility is a thought that matches recognized patterns.
items: A "possibility" is a thought (1.2.5.6.3) that matches (1.2.3) recognized patterns (1.2.5.3.5, 1.2.1.6). Heads-or-tails is a possibility for a flipped coin because both match recognized patterns of coins. A coin landing as a fish does not match any recognized pattern.

What makes a possibility distinct from a thought: every possibility is a thought, but not every thought is a possibility. A thought assembles imaginations in any way. A possibility is constrained — it matches patterns already recognized from experience.

items.title: All thoughts have equal standing
items.detail: Without recognizing possibility, a thought that fits every recognized pattern and one that fits none are indistinguishable. There is no difference between "what might happen" and "what cannot happen." The future — which depends on possibility — collapses: anticipation, planning, and prediction all lose the constraint that separates them from idle fantasy.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Possibility" / "possible" / "possibly" — a thought that matches recognized patterns.
Also grounded: "might," "could" (in the epistemic sense — consistent with recognized patterns), "plausible," "feasible."
The next step: a possibility about what comes next in sequence (the future, 1.2.5.6.5).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: All thoughts are equally plausible — there is no way to distinguish "might happen" from "cannot happen" based on recognized patterns.
Possibility is unrelated to experience — what is possible is determined by something other than pattern recognition.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: How closely a thought must match patterns to count as a possibility — the boundary between barely possible and impossible. Refined later (1.4.4.1–1.4.4.2) with contradiction vocabulary.
Whether or not possibility admits degrees — deferred to later analysis.

items.title: Matching recognized patterns is just probability in disguise.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: What is called "possible" is really just "probable given past patterns." This definition reduces to Bayesian reasoning, which is far more complex than what is being presented.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Possibility reduces to probability — "could happen" means "likely to happen given patterns."
If pattern-matching is the basis for both, the qualitative version (possibility) and quantitative version (probability) are the same thing.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 conflates having the same basis with being the same concept. Possibility is binary — a thought either fits recognized patterns or it doesn't. Probability is scalar — it measures *how well* a thought fits. The experience of "this could happen" comes before any quantification of how likely it is.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This describes the experiential act of recognizing that a thought fits known patterns — not the calculation of how well it fits. The experience comes first; the quantification comes later.

items.title: Dreams feel possible — this makes possibility unreliable.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: In a dream, flying feels possible. Talking animals feel possible. The dreamer's pattern-recognition accepts them without resistance.
If possibility is just 'matches recognized patterns,' then dream-possibilities and waking-possibilities have equal standing — both match the patterns currently active.

But we know dream-possibilities are unreliable. A concept of possibility that can't distinguish reliable from unreliable instances is epistemically dangerous — it gives you no basis for preferring waking judgments over dream judgments.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: A useful concept of possibility must include a reliability dimension — possibility should track what *actually could* happen, not just what *feels like* it could.
If dream-possibilities and waking-possibilities are structurally identical (both match active patterns), the concept has no built-in quality control.
A concept without built-in quality control is epistemically worthless for action or planning.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 is correct and important: dream-possibilities and waking-possibilities ARE structurally identical at this level. The objector is right to notice this. But commitment #3 proves more than the objector intends.

Apply the same test to perception: in a dream, you perceive a dragon. Waking, you perceive a table. The perceptual mechanism is the same (sensation occurring). Dream-perception is unreliable. Does the objector conclude that the *concept of perception* is epistemically worthless? No — the concept is sound; the environment changes. The same applies to possibility.

The objector wants a concept that comes with a built-in reliability marker — a concept that distinguishes good possibilities from bad ones at the moment of occurrence. But no experiential concept works this way. Perception doesn't come with a 'this is veridical' tag. Memory doesn't come with a 'this is accurate' tag. The experience happens; the reliability assessment is a separate, later operation.

Commitment #1 asks possibility to be self-certifying in a way that no other experiential concept is. What the objector actually wants is *judgment* (the assessment of which possibilities are reliable), which is a different, downstream concept.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Dream-possibilities and waking-possibilities are structurally identical — just as dream-perceptions and waking-perceptions are. The concept identifies the phenomenon; reliability is a separate assessment applied afterward.

No experiential concept comes pre-labeled as reliable or unreliable — that assessment requires comparing the experience against other information, which is a later operation the tree can build from this foundation.

nodes.claim: The future is a possibility of what occurs after the present.
nodes.soWhat: Names the temporal application of possibility — 'what comes next.' Expectation, prediction, and planning all depend on having this concept.
nodes.search: future upcoming what will happen next anticipation prediction plan forward

sections.title: Observations
items: A ball rolling toward the edge of a table, and the thought of it falling.
Wondering what the weather will be like tomorrow.
Expecting the next note in a familiar melody.
Anticipating the taste of food being prepared.

items.text: The future is a possibility of what occurs after the present.
items: The "future" is a possibility (1.2.5.6.4) about what comes after (1.2.5.3.2) the present (1.2.5.3.1). What happens when the ball reaches the edge, tomorrow's weather, the next note — each is a thought about what comes next, constrained by recognized patterns.
The future is not a place or a thing. It is a type of possibility — the type that is about sequence, specifically what follows the present.

items.title: No possibility is about what comes next
items.detail: Without recognizing the future, there is no label for possibilities about what follows the present. Expectations, plans, and predictions — all of which are about what has not yet occurred — have no unified concept to reference. Anticipation is indistinguishable from imagination that is not about sequence.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Future" — a possibility about what occurs after the present.
Also grounded: "upcoming," "what will happen," "what comes next," "ahead" (in the temporal sense).
With imagination, visualization, thought, possibility, and future established, the full vocabulary of mental phenomena is grounded — the parent node (1.2.5.6) synthesizes these.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: There is no meaningful distinction between possibilities about what comes next and other possibilities — "tomorrow's weather" and "a pink elephant" are the same type of thought.
The future has no connection to temporal sequence — it is just any imaginable scenario.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not the future is determined or open — deferred to later nodes on causation and reality.
How far into the sequence "future" extends — immediately next or indefinitely ahead.

items.title: The future does not exist — naming it gives it unwarranted ontological status.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Presentists (Prior, Bigelow) hold that only the present exists. The past no longer exists; the future does not yet exist.

By naming 'the future' as a category, the node gives ontological weight to something that has no reality. Even calling it a 'possibility' implies it has some status — possible things have a kind of being.
A strict presentist would say: there are present thoughts *about* what might come next, but there is no 'future' for those thoughts to be about. The node reifies a projection.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Naming 'the future' as a category gives it ontological status — it treats the future as something that exists in some sense.
Even 'possibility' implies a kind of being — possible things occupy a modal space that the presentist denies to non-present entities.
A phenomenological description of future-directed thought should describe the *thinking* without committing to the existence of what is thought *about*.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #3 describes exactly what the node does — and the objector hasn't noticed. The node defines the future as 'a possibility of what occurs after the present.' A possibility (from 1.2.5.6.4) is a *thought* that matches recognized patterns. So the future, on this definition, IS a type of thought — a present mental phenomenon. It is not a domain, a place, or a time that exists separately from the present.

Commitment #1 reads the definition through the lens of ordinary language, where 'the future' suggests a real domain ahead of us. But the node's definition explicitly reduces 'the future' to a present phenomenon: a thought about what comes after now.

The presentist should find this congenial — the future is identified as something that exists *presently* (as a thought), not as something that exists *futurally*. Commitment #2 overreads 'possibility': as defined by the tree, a possibility is a thought matching patterns, not an entity in modal space.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The node does not claim the future exists as a domain or a time. It defines the future as a type of present thought — a possibility (a thought matching recognized patterns) about what occurs after the present.

The future, on this definition, is a mental phenomenon occurring now. The presentist's ontological claim (only the present exists) is compatible with this definition, because the future IS a present phenomenon.

items.title: Not all predictions are temporal — this definition is too narrow.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Some predictions are structural, not temporal — "if this is pushed, it falls" is about structure, not sequence. By tying future exclusively to temporal ordering, the definition misses non-temporal applications of possibility.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: Temporal and conditional predictions should not be separated — both are about "what will happen."
A definition of "future" that excludes structural predictions is missing a core use of the concept.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 conflates two different structures: temporal succession (what comes *next*) and conditional implication (what follows *from*). These overlap in everyday use ("what will happen") but have different structures. The future is specifically the temporal application of possibility.
Structural predictions are a different application, addressed by later nodes on conditions and implications (1.4.4).

subSections.label: Correction
items: The future is one application of possibility — the temporal one. That other applications exist (structural, conditional) does not make this definition too narrow. It makes it specific, which is the point.

nodes.claim: A correlation is when one event often follows another.
nodes.soWhat: Names the experience of recurring sequential connection between events — 'this tends to follow that.' Expectation, independence, consistency, and cause all build on this.
nodes.search: correlation pattern connection between events follows often regularity tends associated

sections.title: Observations
items: Lightning, then thunder — again and again.
Touching a hot surface, then a sharp pain.
Dark clouds appearing, then rain falling.
A dog barking at the same time each day, then a door opening.

items.text: A correlation is when one event often follows another.
items: A "correlation" is when one event (1.2.5.3.9) regularly follows another in sequence (1.2.5.3.2). Lightning followed by thunder, dark clouds followed by rain — the same pairing, recognized (1.2.5.3.5) across multiple occurrences.
What makes correlation distinct from a single sequence: any event can follow another once. A correlation is the recognized pattern of that specific pairing repeating — "often," not "once."

items.title: Recurring sequences have no unified label
items.detail: Without recognizing correlation, lightning followed by thunder today and lightning followed by thunder yesterday are just separate sequences — there is no way to recognize that the same pairing keeps happening. Expectation, which depends on noticing what tends to follow what, has nothing to build on.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Correlation" / "correlate" — when one event often follows another.
Also grounded: "tends to," "regularly," "associated with" (in the sequential sense).
The next step: a possibility based on a correlation (expectation, 1.2.5.7.2).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Recurring sequences are just coincidences with no recognizable connection — the same events following each other repeatedly has no significance beyond each individual occurrence.
Connections between events require an underlying mechanism to be meaningful — without explaining *why* thunder follows lightning, the recurring sequence is meaningless.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: How many repetitions are needed before a sequence is recognized as a correlation — whether or not there is a threshold or a gradual recognition.
Whether or not a correlation implies a necessary connection or just a recognized pattern — deferred to later nodes on causation (1.2.5.7.8).

items.title: This is just pattern recognition applied to sequences — no new concept is needed.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Pattern recognition is already established. Noticing that lightning is followed by thunder is just recognizing a pattern in a sequence. Naming it "correlation" adds a label but no new conceptual content.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Pattern recognition already captures everything correlation describes.
2. If the phenomenon is fully described by existing terms, naming it adds no conceptual value.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 is partially right — correlation does combine pattern and sequence. But the specific combination — a recognized pairing between *events* across a sequence — is not captured by either term alone.

"Pattern" names similarity across features. "Sequence" names temporal ordering. "Event" names a transition. Correlation names the specific phenomenon where a particular event-to-event pairing is recognized as repeating — lightning then thunder, clouds then rain. Expectation and independence both need this specific combination, not just the general components.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Correlation is a specific application of pattern recognition to sequential events. The components are prior, but their combination names a distinct recognizable phenomenon — one that expectation, independence, and cause all require as their foundation.

items.title: A single vivid sequence feels like a correlation — "often" is too restrictive.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Touch a hot surface once and feel pain — that single pairing feels immediately significant, not like a mere sequence waiting for repetition. The definition requires "often," implying multiple occurrences are necessary. But a single striking event can feel just as connected as a repeated pattern.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. A single vivid sequence of events can constitute a correlation.
2. The felt significance of a single pairing is the same experience as recognizing a repeated pattern.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 conflates two different experiences. A single vivid sequence produces salience — a strong reaction to what just happened. A correlation produces recognition — the sense that "this is what happens."

Consider the observations: lightning then thunder *again and again* is what makes it a correlation, not any single flash-and-boom. The hot surface example feels immediate because similar pairings — touching hot things, then pain — were already recognized before this particular instance. The single event draws on a previously recognized correlation, not on itself alone.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The felt significance of a single vivid pairing draws on previously recognized correlations, not on that instance alone. Correlation names the recognized pattern of recurrence — the "often" — not the intensity of any single occurrence.

nodes.claim: An expectation is a possibility based on a correlation.
nodes.soWhat: Names the experience of anticipating what comes next based on recognized patterns — 'this happened, so that will follow.' Prediction, preparation, and later inference all depend on this.
nodes.search: expectation anticipation predict anticipate based on correlation pattern regularity what comes next

sections.title: Observations
items: Dark clouds overhead, and the thought "it will rain."
Hearing footsteps approach a door, and waiting for it to open.
A glass tipping off a table edge, and bracing for the crash.
A familiar melody playing, and already sensing the next note.

items.text: An expectation is a possibility based on a correlation.
items: An "expectation" is a possibility (1.2.5.6.4) that forms because of a recognized correlation (1.2.5.7.1). Dark clouds have often been followed by rain — so when dark clouds appear, the thought "it will rain" arises. The correlation is what gives the possibility its direction.

What makes an expectation distinct from a possibility: every expectation is a possibility, but not every possibility is an expectation. A possibility is any thought that matches recognized patterns. An expectation is a possibility prompted specifically by a correlation — "this happened before, so that will follow."

items.title: Correlations generate no anticipation
items.detail: Without recognizing expectation, correlations are backward-looking only — they describe what has tended to happen, but generate no thought about what will happen next. Dark clouds arrive, and the recognized pattern of clouds-then-rain produces nothing forward-facing. Preparation, prediction, and any response to what is coming all lose their basis.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Expectation" / "expect" — a possibility based on a correlation.
Also grounded: "anticipate," "predict," "likely" (in the experiential sense — what a recognized correlation prompts).
The next step: a possibility based on a want rather than a correlation (hope, 1.2.5.7.3).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Recognized correlations have no forward-facing application — noticing that clouds are often followed by rain produces no thought about whether or not rain will come now.
Expectations arise from something other than recognized correlations — anticipation is unrelated to what has tended to happen before.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not expectations come in degrees — whether or not a stronger correlation produces a stronger expectation. Deferred to later analysis.
What happens when an expectation is not met — the experience of surprise or violated expectation is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied.

items.title: This is just the future (1.2.5.6.5) applied to a correlation — no new concept is needed.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The future is already defined as a possibility about what comes next. An expectation is a possibility about what comes next, prompted by a correlation. The only difference is the source — but the *experience* of anticipating what follows is the same either way.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. The future already captures the experience of anticipating what comes next.
2. Adding a source-constraint ("based on a correlation") does not produce a recognizably different experience.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 does not hold against the observations. "It will rain" prompted by dark clouds feels different from "maybe it will rain" prompted by nothing in particular. The first carries a directedness — a specific thought, pointed at a specific outcome, because of a specific recognized pattern.

The future names any possibility about what comes next. Expectation names the subset where a correlation is doing the prompting — where the thought is not free-floating but pulled toward a particular outcome by recognized experience.

subSections.label: Correction
items: The future is the general category; expectation is a specific kind within it. The difference is experiential: a correlation-prompted possibility carries a felt directedness toward a particular outcome that an unconstrained future-possibility does not.

items.title: Expectations can form from a single event — they do not require a correlation.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Touching a hot surface once produces an immediate expectation: "if touched again, it will hurt." No repeated sequence is needed — a single vivid event is enough. Requiring a correlation ("often follows") sets the bar too high for expectation.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. A single vivid event is sufficient to produce an expectation.
2. The experience of "this will happen again" does not require recognizing a repeated pattern — one occurrence is enough.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 underestimates what is already present in a "single" event. Touching a hot surface and feeling pain is not an isolated first encounter with the pattern — prior correlations between contact and pain, heat and discomfort, already exist from accumulated experience.

The single event feels sufficient because it activates recognized correlations that were already in place. A genuinely first-ever event — one with no prior pattern to draw on — produces surprise, not expectation.

subSections.label: Correction
items: What feels like a single-event expectation draws on correlations already recognized from prior experience. A genuinely novel event — with no recognized correlational basis — produces surprise, not anticipation.

nodes.claim: A hope is a possibility based on a want.
nodes.soWhat: Names the experience of imagining what is wanted as something that could happen — 'maybe it will go the way I want.' Distinguishes want-driven anticipation from pattern-driven anticipation.
nodes.search: hope wish want desire possibility longing optimism want-driven anticipation

sections.title: Observations
items: Wanting sunny weather for an outdoor event, and imagining it happening.
Waiting for test results, and the thought of passing.
Planting seeds, and the thought of flowers growing.
A child blowing out birthday candles, and the thought of getting a wished-for gift.

items.text: A hope is a possibility based on a want.
items: A "hope" is a possibility (1.2.5.6.4) that forms because of a want (1.2.5.1.1). Wanting sunny weather and imagining it happening — the want is what gives the possibility its direction.

What makes hope distinct from expectation (1.2.5.7.2): an expectation is prompted by a correlation — what has tended to happen. A hope is prompted by a want — what is desired. Hoping for sunshine does not require any pattern suggesting sunshine is likely. Expecting rain does not require wanting rain.

items.title: Want-driven possibilities are indistinguishable from pattern-driven ones
items.detail: Without recognizing hope, there is no way to distinguish a possibility that arises because of what is wanted from one that arises because of what has been observed. Imagining sunshine because the weather pattern suggests it and imagining sunshine because it is wanted are the same thing. The difference between wishful thinking and evidence-based anticipation — which matters for evaluating whether or not beliefs are grounded — cannot be articulated.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Hope" / "hoping" — a possibility based on a want.
Also grounded: "wish," "long for" (in the sense of imagining a wanted outcome as possible).
The next step: when variations in one set of features do not correlate with another (independence, 1.2.5.7.4).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: There is no distinct experience of want-driven possibility — wanting something and imagining its occurrence is the same experience as expecting it based on patterns.
Hope requires evidence — a possibility cannot be prompted by a want alone without some correlational basis.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not hope and expectation can conflict — wanting one outcome while a correlation suggests another. The experience of conflicting anticipation is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied.
Whether or not hope comes in degrees corresponding to the intensity of the want — deferred to later analysis.

items.title: Hope is just expectation colored by desire — not a separate concept.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: When hoping for sunshine, there is always *some* pattern in the background — past sunny days, weather tendencies, seasonal patterns. Hope never operates in a pure vacuum of evidence. What is called "hope" is really just an expectation that happens to align with a want.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Every hope has a correlational component — there is always some pattern supporting it.
2. If every hope includes a pattern-based component, hope reduces to expectation-plus-wanting, not a distinct type of possibility.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 does not survive counterexample. Consider: hoping for a wished-for gift while blowing out birthday candles. There is no correlation between candle-blowing and gift-receiving — the hope is entirely want-driven. Or hoping to win a lottery with no pattern of winning.

When a correlation is absent, the possibility still arises — driven by want alone. This is the experience hope names. That hope and expectation can overlap does not make them the same concept, just as a thought that is both a possibility and about the future does not make possibility and future the same concept.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Hope and expectation can overlap — a hoped-for outcome may also be expected. But hope can arise without any supporting correlation, driven by want alone. The two have different sources and can point in different directions.

items.title: Hope without evidence is irrational — giving it conceptual status legitimizes wishful thinking.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Naming "hope" as a type of possibility gives it standing alongside expectation, which is pattern-based. This implicitly elevates wishful thinking to the same conceptual level as evidence-based anticipation. A responsible epistemology should distinguish grounded from ungrounded anticipation, not give both equal labels.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Naming a phenomenon gives it epistemic legitimacy.
2. Want-driven possibilities should not be placed alongside pattern-driven ones because they are epistemically inferior.
3. A responsible framework would distinguish the two by privileging the evidence-based one.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 confuses naming with endorsing. Naming hope does not claim it is reliable — it identifies a recognizable experience. The observations show it: imagining sunshine because it is wanted, imagining passing a test because it is wanted. These happen. Naming them does not say they should be trusted.

Commitment #3 is exactly what this node enables. Without recognizing hope as distinct from expectation, the framework *cannot* distinguish want-driven from pattern-driven anticipation — the very distinction the objector wants.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Naming hope is what makes the distinction the objector wants possible. Without it, want-driven and pattern-driven possibilities are invisible as different types — and the epistemological evaluation the objector values cannot even begin.

nodes.claim: Independence is when the variations in one set of features do not correlate with the variations in another.
nodes.soWhat: Names the experience of disconnection between sets of features — 'these have nothing to do with each other.' Distinguishing what is connected from what is not is the basis for isolating causes, identifying objects, and separating domains.
nodes.search: independence independent unrelated disconnected unconnected separate no correlation varies separately

sections.title: Observations
items: The flavor of a meal and the loudness of traffic outside — one changes without affecting the other.
The color of a wall and the temperature of a room.
The pitch of a bird's song and the brightness of the sun.
The texture of a fabric and the smell of nearby flowers.

items.text: Independence is when the variations in one set of features do not correlate with the variations in another.
items: "Independence" is when variations in one set of features do not correlate (1.2.5.7.1) with variations in another. The flavor of a meal changes — sweet, salty, bitter — while traffic sounds change on their own schedule. Neither set of variations follows the other.

What makes independence distinct from mere difference: two things can differ without being independent. A bright sky and warmth differ, but they correlate — one tends to follow the other. Independence is the specific recognition that the variations in one have nothing to do with the variations in another.

items.title: Connected and unconnected variations are indistinguishable
items.detail: Without recognizing independence, there is no way to distinguish features that vary together from features that vary separately. The correlation between clouds and rain would have the same standing as the non-correlation between wall color and room temperature. Isolating what is relevant from what is irrelevant — the basis for identifying causes, defining objects, and separating one domain from another — becomes impossible.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Independence" / "independent" — when variations in one set of features do not correlate with variations in another.
Also grounded: "unrelated," "separate" (in the sense of non-correlating variation), "irrelevant" (one set has no bearing on another).
The next step: sameness across a sequence (consistency, 1.2.5.7.5).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: All features are connected — there is no such thing as variations that have nothing to do with each other.
The absence of correlation is unrecognizable — only positive connections between features can be noticed, not their absence.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not independence is ever absolute or just reflects unrecognized correlations — the possibility that apparently independent features are connected in ways not yet recognized. Deferred to later analysis.
How many correlated variations are needed before independence is ruled out — the boundary between independence and weak correlation is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied.

items.title: Everything is ultimately connected — independence is just ignorance of the connection.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Maybe the flavor of food and the loudness of traffic seem unconnected — but both depend on physical processes, environmental conditions, and countless shared factors. What looks like independence may just be a failure to see the deeper connection. A holistic view of reality would say nothing is truly independent of anything else.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Apparent independence is always reducible to hidden connection.
2. If a deeper analysis could reveal a connection, the experience of independence is unreliable and should not be given conceptual status.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 applies an unreachable standard. Whether or not a hidden connection exists at some deeper level, the experience being named is concrete: flavor varies without following traffic, wall color varies without following room temperature. These are recognizable phenomena.

The objection also proves more than intended. If apparent independence is unreliable because hidden connections might exist, then apparent *correlation* is equally suspect — any observed correlation might be coincidental, with the real connection lying elsewhere. The objector's standard, consistently applied, eliminates both independence and correlation.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Independence names a recognized phenomenon — that variations in one set of features do not follow variations in another. Whether or not a deeper connection exists is a separate question. The same standard, applied to correlation, would make correlation equally unrecognizable.

items.title: Independence is just the absence of correlation — naming an absence adds nothing.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Correlation is the positive phenomenon — two things vary together. Independence is just "not that." Naming every absence of a concept produces infinite labels — not-hot, not-loud, not-correlated. Independence has no positive content of its own.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Independence has no positive experiential content — it is purely the absence of correlation.
2. Naming absences does not ground new concepts because they carry no recognizable experience.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 does not survive the observations. Consider: the flavor of a meal and the loudness of traffic. The experience is not a blank — not just the failure to notice correlation. There is a positive recognition that these *have nothing to do with each other*. That recognition is what allows separating relevant from irrelevant features.

Compare: "not-hot" does not point at a recognizable experience distinct from other non-hot things. But independence does — the positive experience of recognizing that two sets of variations are disconnected. Without it, every pair of features would need to be evaluated for correlation, with no shortcut for the ones that plainly have nothing to do with each other.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Independence is not the bare absence of correlation but the positive recognition that two sets of variations are disconnected. This recognition has experiential content — it is what allows isolating relevant features from irrelevant ones.

nodes.claim: Consistency is sameness across a sequence.
nodes.soWhat: Names the experience of something remaining the same over successive occurrences — 'it stays.' Distinguishing what persists from what varies is the basis for identifying fundamental and superficial features.
nodes.search: consistency consistent stable unchanged persists remains same steady reliable sameness over time sequence

sections.title: Observations
items: The color of a wall, the same from moment to moment.
A heartbeat maintaining its rhythm across many steps.
The sweetness of honey — the same each time it is tasted.
The shape of a rock, unchanged across repeated encounters.

items.text: Consistency is sameness across a sequence.
items: "Consistency" is sameness (1.2.1) that persists across a sequence (1.2.5.3.2). The color of the wall is the same at this step, the next step, and the step after — the sameness holds across sequential occurrence.

What makes consistency distinct from sameness: sameness names similarity across features. Consistency names that sameness holding across a sequence — not just that two things share a quality, but that the quality persists step after step.

items.title: Persistence and change are indistinguishable
items.detail: Without recognizing consistency, there is no way to distinguish a feature that stays the same across a sequence from one that changes. The wall's color remaining from step to step and the sky's color shifting from step to step have the same standing. Fundamental features — those that persist — cannot be separated from superficial ones, and reliability has no experiential basis.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Consistency" / "consistent" — sameness across a sequence.
Also grounded: "stable," "steady," "unchanged," "persists," "remains" (in the sense of a quality holding across sequential steps).
The next step: a feature that is consistent (fundamental, 1.2.5.7.6).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: There is no recognizable difference between a feature that holds across a sequence and one that does not — persistence is undetectable.
Sameness is only recognizable at a single moment, never across sequential steps.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: How many sequential steps are needed before sameness counts as consistency — whether or not there is a threshold or it is recognized gradually.
Whether or not consistency admits degrees — whether or not something can be "more consistent" or "less consistent" across a sequence. Deferred to later analysis.

items.title: This is just memory applied to sameness — no new concept is needed.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Recognizing that the wall is the same color as before just is remembering its color and comparing. Memory (1.2.5.3.4) and sameness are already established. "Consistency" adds a label to their intersection but no new experiential content.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Memory plus sameness already captures the experience of a quality persisting across steps.
2. If the components fully account for the experience, a new label adds no conceptual value.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 applies the same standard that was raised at correlation (1.2.5.7.1) — and fails for the same reason. The specific combination names a distinct recognizable experience that the components separately do not capture.

Memory says "this was." Sameness says "these are alike." Consistency names the specific recognition that a quality holds step after step — the experienced reliability of a feature persisting. Fundamental and superficial features both depend on this specific recognition, not on memory or sameness alone.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Consistency names the specific experience of sameness persisting across sequential steps. The components are prior, but their combination — experienced persistence — is what fundamental and superficial features require as their basis.

items.title: Nothing is truly consistent — everything changes at some scale.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: The wall's color is not really the same — light shifts, paint fades, perception varies. The heartbeat is not really steady — it speeds up, slows down, skips. At sufficient resolution, nothing is the same from one step to the next. Naming "consistency" treats an approximation as though it were exact.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. True sameness across a sequence never occurs — all apparent consistency involves unnoticed variation.
2. A concept based on an approximation is unreliable and should not be treated as a foundational category.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 may be correct at some level of resolution — but the experience being named does not require absolute sameness. The wall's color is recognized as the same from step to step. That recognition is the phenomenon. Whether or not microscopic changes occur beneath the threshold of recognition is a separate question.

Commitment #2 applies equally to sameness itself — if approximate sameness is unreliable, then sameness as a concept falls too. The objector's standard, consistently applied, eliminates not just consistency but any recognition of similarity.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Consistency names the recognized sameness of a quality across sequential steps — not a claim that nothing changes at every level of resolution. The same standard applied to sameness itself would make all recognition of similarity impossible.

nodes.claim: A fundamental feature is one that is consistent.
nodes.soWhat: Names the features that persist — the ones that make something recognizably what it is. Distinguishing fundamental from superficial features is the basis for identifying what something reliably is versus how it happens to appear.
nodes.search: fundamental essential core consistent persistent defining reliable identity nature

sections.title: Observations
items: Honey is sweet — every time, across every encounter.
A rock is hard — step after step, the hardness persists.
Fire is hot — the heat is there whenever fire is present.
Water is wet — the wetness holds across every instance.

items.text: A fundamental feature is one that is consistent.
items: A "fundamental" feature is a feature that is consistent (1.2.5.7.5) — it persists across the sequence of encounters with that phenomenon. Sweetness is fundamental to honey because it is there every time. Hardness is fundamental to rock because it holds step after step.
What makes a feature fundamental: not its importance or value, but its consistency. A fundamental feature is one that is recognized as the same across sequential occurrences — it is what stays.

items.title: Persistent and non-persistent features have the same standing
items.detail: Without recognizing fundamental features, there is no way to distinguish what consistently characterizes something from what varies. Honey's sweetness and a particular jar's temperature have the same standing — both are just features. Identifying what something reliably is, as distinct from how it happens to appear on one occasion, becomes impossible.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Fundamental" — a feature that is consistent.
Also grounded: "essential," "core," "defining" (in the sense of a feature that persists across encounters).
The next step: variation within a fundamental feature (superficial, 1.2.5.7.7).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: All features have equal standing regardless of whether or not they persist — there is no basis for distinguishing reliable features from transient ones.
What makes a feature fundamental is something other than consistency — e.g. hidden essence, logical necessity, or theoretical importance.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not a feature can be fundamental to one phenomenon and not to another — whether or not fundamentality is relative to what is being characterized. Not addressed here.
Whether or not a feature recognized as fundamental could later be discovered to vary — the relationship between current recognition and deeper investigation is deferred.

items.title: Consistency is just frequency — calling consistent features 'fundamental' imports ungrounded significance.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Honey has been sweet in every past encounter — that is a frequency observation. Calling sweetness "fundamental" suggests it is somehow deeper, more important, or more real than other features. But all you have observed is that it keeps showing up. "Fundamental" smuggles in metaphysical weight that mere consistency does not support.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Consistency is a frequency observation — "this has always been present."
2. Labeling a frequent feature "fundamental" adds metaphysical significance (depth, importance, essence) beyond what frequency alone supports.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 reads into the label what the definition does not claim. "Fundamental" here means exactly one thing: consistent. It does not claim depth, hidden essence, or metaphysical importance — it names the recognized persistence of a feature across a sequence.

The objector's concern is legitimate if "fundamental" carried connotations of necessity or essence. But the definition strips it to its experiential basis: a feature that stays the same, step after step. Nothing more is claimed.

subSections.label: Correction
items: "Fundamental" is defined as consistent — a feature that persists across sequential encounters. No claim of hidden essence, metaphysical depth, or necessity is made. The label names persistence, not importance.

items.title: A feature that has been consistent so far might change — calling it fundamental is premature.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Every encounter with honey so far has included sweetness. But the next encounter might not. Calling sweetness "fundamental" treats an inductive generalization — it has always been sweet — as though it reveals something fixed. The problem of induction applies: past consistency does not guarantee future consistency.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. A feature recognized as consistent could cease to be consistent in a future encounter.
2. A label that depends on induction (past-to-present consistency) should not be applied as though it names something fixed.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 misreads the definition. "Fundamental" does not mean "guaranteed to persist forever" — it means "recognized as consistent." If a previously consistent feature changes, it is no longer recognized as consistent and is no longer fundamental. The label tracks the recognition, not a metaphysical guarantee.

The same concern applies to every recognition-based concept in this branch — correlation, expectation, consistency itself. If the problem of induction disqualifies fundamental, it disqualifies all of them equally.

subSections.label: Correction
items: "Fundamental" tracks recognized consistency, not guaranteed permanence. If a feature that was consistent ceases to be, it is no longer recognized as fundamental. The label describes what is recognized, not what is metaphysically fixed.

nodes.claim: A superficial feature is variation within a fundamental feature.
nodes.soWhat: Names the features that change while something else persists — 'this varies but that stays.' Distinguishing superficial from fundamental features is the basis for recognizing what is incidental versus what is defining.
nodes.search: superficial incidental accidental variable changing surface appearance differs varies within

sections.title: Observations
items: Apples are always sweet — but their shade of red varies from apple to apple.
A heartbeat is always rhythmic — but the exact speed changes with activity.
Fire is always hot — but the color of the flame varies.
A voice is always recognizable — but the loudness changes from word to word.

items.text: A superficial feature is variation within a fundamental feature.
items: A "superficial" feature is variation that occurs within a fundamental feature (1.2.5.7.6). Sweetness is fundamental to apples — it is consistent across encounters. The specific shade of red varies from apple to apple. That variation occurs within the context of something that persists.

What makes a superficial feature distinct from any variation: not all variation is superficial. Superficial variation is specifically the kind that occurs while a fundamental feature holds — it is change within persistence. The shade of red varies, but the sweetness stays.

items.title: All variation has the same standing regardless of what persists
items.detail: Without recognizing superficial features, there is no way to distinguish variation that occurs within something consistent from variation that indicates something has changed fundamentally. An apple being a slightly different shade of red and an apple tasting completely different have the same standing. The distinction between incidental difference and defining change — which matters for recognizing whether or not something is still the same thing — becomes impossible.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Superficial" — variation within a fundamental feature.
Also grounded: "incidental," "surface-level," "cosmetic" (in the sense of variation that does not affect what is consistent).
The next step: a want whose direction correlates with an event (cause, 1.2.5.7.8).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: All variation is equally significant — there is no basis for treating some changes as incidental and others as defining.
Superficial features are unrelated to fundamental features — variation and consistency are independent categories with no connection.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Where the boundary falls between superficial variation and fundamental change — how much variation a fundamental feature can absorb before it is no longer recognized as consistent. Not addressed here.
Whether or not the same feature can be superficial in one context and fundamental in another — deferred to later analysis.

items.title: What counts as superficial depends on the observer — this makes the concept subjective and unreliable.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: A painter might regard the shade of red as fundamental to an apple — it is the defining feature for their purpose. A chef regards sweetness as fundamental. What counts as superficial shifts depending on who is attending and what they care about. A concept that shifts with the observer is not grounding anything stable.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. What counts as superficial depends on the observer's attention and purpose.
2. A concept that varies with the observer cannot serve as a stable foundation.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 is partially correct — what is recognized as consistent can differ between observers. But commitment #2 does not follow. Superficial names a relationship between variation and consistency: variation that occurs within what is recognized as fundamental. The relationship holds regardless of which specific features fill the roles.

The painter recognizes shade as consistent across certain encounters and notices variation within it. The chef recognizes sweetness as consistent and notices variation within that. In both cases, the structure is the same — superficial variation within a fundamental feature. The concept names the structure, not any particular feature.

subSections.label: Correction
items: "Superficial" names a structural relationship — variation occurring within what is recognized as consistent. Which features fill each role can differ, but the relationship itself is the same in every case.

items.title: This creates a false binary — features can be partly consistent and partly varying.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: A heartbeat is mostly rhythmic but occasionally skips. Is rhythm fundamental or superficial? The definition seems to require a clean division — consistent features are fundamental, varying ones are superficial. But many features are neither fully consistent nor fully varying.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Many features are partially consistent and partially varying.
2. A binary classification (fundamental or superficial) cannot accommodate features that are both.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 assumes the classification is binary when the definitions allow for exactly this case. A heartbeat's rhythm is recognized as consistent — it is fundamental. The occasional skip is variation within that consistency — it is superficial. The skip does not make rhythm non-fundamental; it is a variation within what persists.

The boundary between "still consistent" and "no longer consistent" may be unclear in edge cases — this is acknowledged in Unknowns. But the paradigm cases are clear: sweetness stays, shade varies. The edge cases do not eliminate the distinction.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Partial variation within an otherwise consistent feature is exactly what superficial names. A heartbeat that mostly holds rhythm with occasional skips has a fundamental feature (rhythm) with superficial variation (the skips). The boundary may blur in edge cases, but the distinction is clear in the central ones.

nodes.claim: A cause is a want whose direction correlates with an event.
nodes.soWhat: Names the experience of making something happen — 'I wanted this, and it occurred.' Agency, responsibility, and later the distinction between what is controlled and what is not all depend on this.
nodes.search: cause causation agency make happen want direction correlates event produce bring about action

sections.title: Observations
items: Wanting to move an arm, and the arm moves.
Wanting to speak a word, and hearing it spoken.
Wanting to push a door, and the door opening.
Wanting to clench a fist, and feeling the pressure.

items.text: A cause is a want whose direction correlates with an event.
items: A "cause" is a want (1.2.5.1.1) whose direction (1.2.5.1.2) correlates (1.2.5.7.1) with an event (1.2.5.3.9). Wanting to move an arm (the direction) and then the arm moves (the event) — when this pairing is recognized as recurring, the want is a cause of the event.

What makes cause distinct from correlation alone: correlation names any recurring event-to-event pairing. Cause names the specific case where a want's direction is what correlates with the event. The want gives the correlation a source — it is not just 'A follows B' but 'what was wanted is what happened.'

items.title: Wanting something and it happening are indistinguishable from coincidence
items.detail: Without recognizing cause, a want whose direction matches an event that occurs has the same standing as any other correlation. Wanting to move an arm and the arm moving would be no different from lightning followed by thunder — a recognized pattern with no connection to wanting. Agency — the experience of making something happen — has no label and no experiential basis. The distinction between what is done and what merely happens becomes impossible.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Cause" — a want whose direction correlates with an event.
Also grounded: "make happen," "bring about," "produce" (in the agentive sense — a want whose direction correlates with an occurring event), "do" / "action" (in the sense of a want that causes).
The next step: the event that correlates with a cause's direction (effect, 1.2.5.7.9).

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Wanting something and it happening is always coincidence — no want ever has a recognized correlational connection to an event.
Causation is unrelated to wanting — making something happen has nothing to do with the experience of wanting it to happen.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not causation extends beyond wants — whether or not events that follow other events without any want involved are also causes. The definition here grounds cause in the experience of wanting; external or physical causation is not addressed.

Whether or not the correlation between a want's direction and an event implies a necessary connection or just a recognized pattern — the metaphysics of causation is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied.

items.title: Causation exists without wanting — a ball breaks a vase with no want involved.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: A ball strikes a vase and the vase shatters. No wanting is present — yet this is plainly causation. By defining cause through wanting, this excludes the majority of causal relationships in the world. Physical causation, natural processes, and mechanical interactions are all causation without wants.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Physical causation (ball breaks vase) is a genuine case of causation.
2. A definition that excludes physical causation is too narrow to capture what cause means.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 demands a complete definition when the node provides the experiential ground. The experience of causation — the felt connection between wanting and what happens — is where the concept originates. Wanting to move an arm and the arm moving is the paradigm case: the experience of making something happen.

The ball-and-vase case is recognized as causal by extending this experience — seeing the ball "do" something to the vase. But that extension uses vocabulary (physical mechanism, external objects as agents) not yet grounded. The experiential origin — want-direction correlating with event — comes first. Whether or not the concept extends to unwanted events is a separate question addressed later.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This grounds cause where it is first experienced — in the correlation between a want's direction and an event. Whether or not the concept extends to physical interactions without wants is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied. The experiential origin does not exclude later extension.

items.title: Correlation is not causation — this just restates the post hoc fallacy.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Wanting to move an arm and the arm moving could be coincidence — the want might correlate with the movement without causing it. By defining cause as a correlation, the definition cannot distinguish genuine causation from mere coincidence that happens to recur. "After" is not "because of."

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. Genuine causation requires more than correlation — it requires a necessary or mechanistic connection.
2. Defining cause as correlation makes it impossible to distinguish real causes from coincidences that happen to recur.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 asks for necessity or mechanism — but at this level, neither is grounded. Necessary connection is a logical concept (deferred to 1.4). Physical mechanism presupposes external causation not yet established. What IS available is the experience described in the observations: wanting to move an arm and the arm moving, wanting to speak and hearing the word.

The definition does not claim the correlation is necessary or mechanical. It names the recognized phenomenon: a want whose direction matches an event, recurring. Whether or not this correlation reflects a deeper necessary connection is left open. But the experience is there before any theory of mechanism — it is what theories of mechanism are built to explain.

subSections.label: Correction
items: This names the experiential phenomenon — a want whose direction correlates with an event — not a theory of mechanism or necessary connection. Whether or not the correlation reflects something deeper is a separate question. The experience of wanting and it happening is what the concept is grounded in, and it is what theories of causation are built to explain.

items.title: The want might be an after-the-fact fabrication — the event happens, and the want is attributed retroactively.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Research on confabulation suggests that the sense of agency can be manufactured after the fact. The arm moves, and the feeling of "I wanted that" is constructed retroactively. If the want is not genuinely prior to the event, the correlation is illusory — the want is not causing the event but being attributed to it after it occurs.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. The want that appears to precede the event might actually be constructed after the event occurs.
2. If the temporal ordering (want first, event second) is illusory, the correlation does not reflect a genuine want-to-event direction.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 raises a genuine possibility — but it does not affect what the definition names. Whether or not the want is prior, simultaneous, or retroactively attributed, the experience being named is: a want whose direction matches an event, recognized as a recurring pairing.

The confabulation concern is about whether or not the experience accurately reflects the underlying process. That is a question about reliability — parallel to the dream objection at possibility (1.2.5.6.4). The concept names the experience; the reliability of that experience is a separate assessment.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Whether or not the temporal ordering of want and event is veridical, the experience being named is recognizable: a want whose direction matches an event. The reliability of this experience — including whether or not confabulation occurs — is a separate question, just as the reliability of any experiential concept is.

nodes.claim: An effect is an event that correlates with a cause's direction.
nodes.soWhat: Names the other side of the causal correlation — the event that happens when a want makes something happen. Without this, the result of agency has no label distinct from any other event.
nodes.search: effect result outcome consequence event caused produced brought about

sections.title: Observations
items: The arm moving — the event that follows wanting to move it.
The word heard — the event that follows wanting to speak.
The door opening — the event that follows wanting to push it.
The fist clenching — the event that follows wanting to clench.

items.text: An effect is an event that correlates with a cause's direction.
items: An "effect" is an event (1.2.5.3.9) that correlates (1.2.5.7.1) with a cause's (1.2.5.7.8) direction (1.2.5.1.2). The arm moving is an effect — it is the event that correlates with the want to move the arm. The cause is the want; the effect is the event.

What makes an effect distinct from any other event: events happen constantly. An effect is specifically an event that is recognized as correlating with a cause's direction — not just something that happened, but something that happened in connection with what was wanted.

items.title: Results of agency have no label distinct from any other event
items.detail: Without recognizing effect, the arm moving after wanting to move it has the same standing as any event — thunder after lightning, rain after clouds. There is no way to label the event-side of causation. The result of doing something and something merely happening are indistinguishable, and consequences — which depend on identifying what happened because of what was wanted — cannot be tracked.

sections.title: Unlocks

items.text: Vocabulary grounded by this node.
items: "Effect" — an event that correlates with a cause's direction.
Also grounded: "result" (of a cause), "consequence" (in the agentive sense — what happened because of what was wanted).
With cause and effect established, the full relational vocabulary of this branch is grounded — the parent node (1.2.5.7) synthesizes these.

sections.title: Eliminates
items: Events connected to wants and events unconnected to wants are indistinguishable — there is no basis for calling one a result and the other a coincidence.
Effects are identified independently of causes — an event can be recognized as a result without any reference to what was wanted.

sections.title: Unknowns
items: Whether or not effects extend beyond events that correlate with wants — whether or not events that follow other events (without wanting) are also effects. Deferred along with the extension of cause beyond wants.
Whether or not a single cause can have multiple effects, or a single effect can have multiple causes — the structure of causal chains is not addressed here — neither endorsed nor denied.

items.title: Effect is just the event in a causal correlation — it adds nothing to what cause already establishes.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: Cause already names the full correlation: a want whose direction correlates with an event. The event is right there in the definition. Naming the event-side separately as "effect" is redundant — anyone who understands cause already has the concept of what the cause produces.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. The event in a causal correlation is already fully captured by the definition of cause.
2. Naming it separately adds no conceptual content.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #2 assumes that appearing in another concept's definition is the same as being recognized in its own right. Cause names the want-side — it answers "what did the causing?" Effect names the event-side — it answers "what happened as a result?"

Without effect, the event in a causal correlation can only be referred to as "the event that correlates with the cause's direction" — a description, not a label. Consequences, results, and outcomes all need a term for the event-side of causation to be referenced compactly.

subSections.label: Correction
items: Effect names the event-side of the causal correlation — it answers a different question than cause does. Cause identifies what did the causing; effect identifies what resulted. Both sides need labels for the relationship to be referenced from either direction.

items.title: Effects should be defined by what produced them, not by correlation with a want — this makes effects subjective.

subSections.label: Objection Basis
items: An effect should be defined by its connection to what produced it — a mechanism, a process, a physical chain of events. Defining effect through correlation with a want makes it depend on the wanter's perspective. Two people watching the same event could disagree about whether or not it is an effect, because they have different wants. An objective concept of effect should not depend on wanting.

subSections.label: Objection Commitments
items: 1. A proper definition of effect should reference the producing mechanism, not a want.
2. Tying effect to want makes it perspective-dependent and therefore subjective.

subSections.label: What's Missing
items: Commitment #1 requires vocabulary not yet available — mechanism, physical process, and objective production all presuppose concepts not yet grounded. The experience being named comes first: wanting to push a door, and the door opening. The opening is recognized as an effect because it correlates with what was wanted.

Commitment #2 conflates the experiential origin with a limitation. The concept is grounded where it is first experienced — in the connection between wanting and what happens. Whether or not it extends to observer-independent physical chains is a separate, later question — the same deferral made for cause (1.2.5.7.8).

subSections.label: Correction
items: Effect is grounded where it is first experienced — in the event that correlates with a cause's direction. Mechanism and objective production require vocabulary not yet available. The experiential origin does not prevent later extension to observer-independent contexts.

nodes.claim: A description is information about an object.
A definition is a description of an identity.
Descriptions match or mismatch what they describe.
A description is independent from what it describes.
Truth is when a description matches reality.
Falsehood is when a description mismatches reality.
